News.title: Mushroom killer Erin Patterson set to die in prison after appeal spectacularly backfires and increases her sentence
News.content:
Next

MUSHROOM killer Erin Patterson is set to die in prison after her appeal spectacularly backfired and increased her sentence instead.

The triple murderer was jailed for life with a non-parole period of 33 years for serving her estranged husbands relatives poisoned beef Wellingtons laced with death cap mushrooms.



But an Australian appeals court on Friday ordered Erin Patterson to never be released from prison after agreeing with prosecutors that her parole period was inadequate.

The three judges of the Victoria state Court of Appeal also dismissed Pattersons challenge to her convictions that stemmed from a family meal she hosted at her rural home in Leongatha in July 2023.



Patterson, 51, insisted she added death cap mushrooms to the meals accidentally.

Her mum-in-law Gail Patterson, dad-in-law Donald Patterson and Gail’s sister Heather Wilkinson died in hospital within six days of the fatal lunch in July 2023.

Patterson was also convicted for the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, a small-town local pastor who was the sole survivor of the poisoning.

She was sentenced last year to three life sentences for murder and 25 years for attempted murder with eligibility for parole after 33 years.



Patterson appealed the verdict and the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) appealed the sentence, arguing her non-parole period was “manifestly inadequate”.

Central to Patterson’s bid to overturn her conviction was the “catastrophic” decision to place members of the jury in the same hotel as a police witness, journalists and members of the prosecution.

Barrister Richard Edney argued that the move “fatally undermined the integrity of the verdicts” and means the verdicts should be quashed and a retrial should take place “so that justice can be done”.

But Justice Stephen McLeish today dismissed the arguments and denied the appeal.

Instead, the judge sided with the DPP’s appeal, meaning Patterson will spend the remainder of her years behind bars, reports 7News.



McLeish blasted Patterson’s crimes as “extraordinarily cold and calculated” and a “cruel breach of trust”.

Patterson will still be able to challenge the decision at Australia‘s High Court.

During the appeal, the court heard that, despite Edney’s complaints, there was no evidence that the jury came into contact with anyone at trial.



While the defence acknowledged that there was no evidence that the jury spoke with the witness or prosecution, they highlighted that the crossover occurred during jury deliberation week.

Another contentious point concerned the prosecution’s use of evidence about Patterson’s activity on the foraging website iNaturalist and mobile phone tower data.

At the trial, the prosecution argued that Patterson found two sightings of death cap mushrooms reported online near her home.

The court heard how her phone connected to cell towers in both areas, with the prosecution indicating she’d visited both spots.

Hours after visiting one of the locations, Patterson bought a food dehydrator to prepare the mushrooms for the fateful beef Wellingtons.



CCTV captured Patterson travelling to a local dump and disposing of the dehydrator, which was later found to have traces of the deadly mushrooms.

'MUSHROOM' MURDER TIMELINE All the twists & turns that led to Erin Patterson being jailed for life 2021-22 – A 48-year-old man, believed to Patterson’s ex-husband Simon, falls ill after three separate meails. July 29, 2023 – The deadly mushroom lunch takes place July 30 – Gail and Don Patterson & Heather and Ian Wilkinson are rushed to hospital – all die but Ian. August 5-7 – Patterson’s home is searched, she is questions and becomes an official suspect. November 2 – Police arrest and charge Patterson with three counts of murder and five of attempted murder. May 7, 2024 – Patterson pleads not guilty to the eight charges. April 29, 2025 – Her trial begins. The prosecuction drop three charges related to the attempted murder of Simon. July 7, 2025 – The jury finds Patterson guilty. September 8, 2025 – She is sentenced to life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 33 years.

When sentencing Patterson, the judge said that it didn’t necessarily matter where she sourced the mushrooms from as it was abundantly clear that she had.

Patterson has maintained she unknowingly used foraged death cap mushrooms in the meal.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

There were also complaints that prosecutors had been “unfair” in the court proceedings, as they made 35 complaints throughout.

Police have also alleged Patterson may have attempted to poison her ex-husband, Simon Patterson, on three separate occasions between 2021 and 2022.

News.title: Train driver, 36, dead in horror Spain smash that killed 69 is pictured as TV presenter, composer among missing
News.content:
Next

THE train driver behind the wheel in the horror railway crash in Spain has been pictured as heartbreaking details of his “hero” final moments emerge.

Antonio Acedo, 36, was in the cockpit of the Renfe train when it slammed into the back of a Iryo train at 124mph on Wednesday.



At least 69 people were killed in the devastating collision – with rescuers still combing the site for bodies and missing loved ones.

A headmaster, a composer, a TV presenter and a food bank volunteer are among those still missing.



More than 100 people were also injured – some of them critically – when multiple carriages derailed and flipped over down an embankment.

Both Antonio and his fellow trainee train driver sat beside him in the cockpit were killed.

The family of the deceased train driver have described him as a “hero” after revealing that Antonio activated the emergency brake – saving the lives of hundreds of passengers.

But the fate of him and Daniel Muñoz Cob, 31, sat beside him was sealed with a single haunting conversation.



Chilling audio recordings of communications between Madrid’s control room and Antonio reveal the exact moment the deadly mistake was made.

The command centre told him: “Resume [driving] at normal speed.”

“At normal speed?” Antonio asked.



“Yeah” the control worker replied.

The train driver was never informed of the fact that there was another train ahead of him unable to move – despite the fact that the control room knew of the “equipment problems” on the stranded Iryo train.

In a further tragic twist, Antonio had been an active member of the Izquierda Española political party and had warned of the crumbling infrastructure and chronic underfunding of the train system.

His friend, journalist Paula Fraga, said: “Antonio was one of the frontline workers who sounded the alarm over deteriorating rail infrastructure—one of those ignored and dismissed workers who died because officials refused to listen.”

Party leader Guillermo del Valle remembered him as “a good man” and a “cautious, kind and exemplary colleague”.



Previously on social media Antonio had reflected on death, writing: “I imagine that when we reach the end, if we look back and find happiness, we aren’t saddened to leave.”

A former politician died in the tragedy, confirmed by the Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations.

Fátima Báñez served as minister for employment and social security while in government between 2011 and 2018.

A classical music composer is also missing following the disaster.

Friends of María Luisa Manchado have issued appeals to find her after the train operator confirmed she had scanned her ticket for the ride.



A young athlete, 24, and a policeman, 36, also lost their lives in the crash.

Julieta Gallego, a runner for AD Sprint, had her life “unjustly extinguished”, said Raúl Chapado, president of the Royal Spanish Athletics Federation.

Cop José Manuel Chacón was travelling back to his hometown of Seville when he was killed in the horror collision.

He married just four months earlier.

Still among the missing is die-hard Atletico Madrid fan David Martinez Mendez who his family describe as “cheerful and devoted to his loved ones”.



In another heartbreaking case, the family of engineer David Reina Reguera are still searching for their son.

The 22-year-old called his family at 8.30 – less than half an hour before the fatal crash.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Another missing person – architect Alexandra García Bartolomé – also spoke to her family approximately 20 minutes before the collision.

She had been heading to Seville on business when the tragedy unfolded.

News.title: Labourer dies after ‘being hit by HGV’ on Sir Winston Churchill’s family estate
News.content:
'LORRY DEATH' Labourer dies after ‘being hit by HGV’ on Sir Winston Churchill’s family estate







Next

A LABOURER has died after being hit by an HGV on Sir Winston Churchill’s family estate, The Sun understands.

The 50-year-old labourer died on the scene of the lunchtime accident on grand Blenheim Palace in Woodstock, Oxfordshire.

The 12,000-acre estate is the ancestral seat of aristocrat James Spencer-Churchill, 12th Duke of Marlborough.

It hosted US President Donald Trump on his 2018 presidential visit to the UK for a lavish, black-tie diplomatic dinner with ex-PM Theresa May.





The Sun understands the labourer was working on a pathway for construction on the estate.

It is thought the worker, who has not been named, was struck by a heavy goods vehicle and died almost immediately on October 14.

Bosses from the Health and Safety Executive have since launched a probe.

A Thames Valley Police spokesperson told The Sun: “We are working with the Health and Safety Executive to investigate a fatal industrial incident at Blenheim Palace on 14 October.



“We were called at around 1pm that day following an incident involving a heavy goods vehicle in the palace grounds.

“A 50-year-old man sadly died at the scene. A specially trained police officer is supporting his family at this difficult time.”

Blenheim Palace was the birthplace of war hero Churchill and features a dedicated Churchill Exhibition.

The estate features over 2,000 acres of landscaped parkland and formal gardens plus water terraces, a Walled Garden, and a butterfly house.



The Duke of Marlborough has been tied to the estate for over 300 years, and James Spencer-Churchill, 70, is thought to still have a residence there.

Visitors can tour the opulent State Rooms, the Long Library, housing over 10,000 books, and a permanent exhibition dedicated to Sir Winston Churchill.

The palace recently underwent a massive £12million restoration “Glow Up” project to repair the palace’s roof which concluded in October.

DBR Limited, the contractor for the restoration project, said the accident was not on their site but involved another project.

There are other restoration works at the palace as part of a ten-year £40million conservation project which started in 2017.



They include work on the estate’s “Queen Pool” and its 300-year-old chapel.

Dominic Hare, Chief Executive of Blenheim Palace, said: “We are deeply saddened by the death of a man who was working for a contractor on a construction site on the wider Blenheim Estate on Wednesday 14 October.

“Our heartfelt condolences are with his family, friends and colleagues at this extremely difficult time.

“We are supporting Thames Valley Police and the Health and Safety Executive with their investigation, and it would not be appropriate to comment further while that continues.”

News.title: John Healey seemed adamant about cutting welfare bill… but Labour’s position has descended into chaos
News.content:
Next

LABOUR’S position on cutting the benefits bill has descended into chaos.

Chancellor John Healey appeared to be adamant on the BBC yesterday morning at 6am that the benefits bill would be cut before the next election.



But a couple of hours later, Treasury sources disputed the story saying his words had been incorrectly interpreted.

The fuss all kicked off after the Chancellor was asked whether there would be a cut in the bill before the next polling day.



He replied: “There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we’ll do that in a Labour way.”

Bear in mind that the Budget watchdog said on Wednesday that the bill would hit an eye-watering £430billion by the start of the next decade.

Then shortly before 1pm, Number 10 told journalists that they had never set a target date.

Andy Burnham popped up in the afternoon saying the government was working “flat out” and the bill would come down “as soon as possible”.

Fast forward to 4pm and the Chancellor tells Channel 4 that Labour will not bring down the welfare bill in this Parliament – scheduled at the moment to end in 2029.

An about-turn in just a matter of hours.



Two big reviews on the welfare system – from Alan Milburn and Sir Stephen Timms – will help frame the debate.

But after Labour shied away from benefits cuts last year it seems Andy Burnham doesn’t want to have the fight.

Mr Healey said cutting the welfare bill will be done in the Labour way – and it could take years.

Labour insiders are happy with how the Budget has gone this week. After all, the bond markets and the Parliamentary Labour Party are on side.

The trouble is how much patience do taxpayers have to keep paying for Benefits Street?

News.title: Passenger jet’s nose caves in & windscreen cracks after flying through storm but is able to finish journey
News.content:
Next

THE nose of a passenger jet has been completely bashed in and its windscreens cracked after it was battered by a ferocious hailstorm.

Terrifying turbulence struck the Yemeni Airways flight while it was travelling from Yemen to Jordan – sparking safety fears.



Heavy showers of hail pummelled the passenger jet on Monday as the crew desperately fought to land the stricken plane.

Shocking photos show huge spiderweb cracks splintering across the pilot’s windscreen and the front nose of the plane completely caved in.



Scratches and peeling paint can also be seen on the pockmarked body of the damaged plane.

Passengers aboard the stricken flight described feeling fearful as the jet entered the raging storm.

But the captain calmly reassured them that everything was under control and that they would land safely.

Airline spokesperson Hatem al-Shaabi described the terrifying weather turbulence as a “hail strike”.



He praised the jet’s captain Basim Fareed and his crew for their skill in bringing everyone to ground safely.

The passenger plane landed without incident at Queen Alia International Airport and is being inspected for further damage.

No passengers or crew were injured during the mid-air ordeal.

The damaged aircraft, registered 7O-AFB, remained on the ground in Amman on Tuesday while engineers assessed the hail damage.

Earlier this month a passenger plane travelling though India was pummelled by a hailstorm.



The IndiGo flight was also reportedly struck by lightning during the terrifying turbulence.

Despite damage to the plane’s nose, it landed safely at Chaudhary Charan Singh International Airport eight minutes ahead of schedule on October 7.

All 104 passengers and six crew walked away from the scare unhurt.

Meanwhile, a passenger jet was gripped by terror when oxygen masks suddenly dropped and the plane plunged 23,000ft in a matter of minutes.

The LATAM Airlines flight was cruising at an altitude of 33,000ft after taking off from Lima in Peru when the horrifying scare unfolded.



Panicked flyers were forced to strap on oxygen masks as the crew declared a general emergency following a sudden technical failure.

A MAN has been accused of poisoning and secretly filming three women in a seven-year campaign of abuse.

Cops said they found a vile stash of 2.5million images of the alleged abuse when they raided the home of Christopher Ridings, 39, in Tumbi Umbi, north of Sydney.



Ridings has been hit with more than 200 domestic violence-related sex offence charges.

The charges include 109 counts of intentionally recording an intimate image without consent and 57 counts of accessory to sexual intercourse without consent.



He has also been hit with 12 counts of aggravated sexual assault and 10 counts of sexual intercourse without consent.

Cops said Ridings targeted three women between the ages of 29 and 31, recording images of the crimes over seven years.

Just hours before his arrest on December 10, 2025, prosecutors said he detained a victim and assaulted her mother, according to court documents seen by the Daily Mail.

The horror started in the early hours of the morning with Ridings allegedly assaulting the woman’s mother between 12.30am and 1.20am while the woman was tied up.

From 1am to 1.20 he is also accused of assaulting the tied-up woman.

Alongside the escalating suspected violence, prosecutors allege Ridings filmed a third woman engaging in a “private act” without her consent for his sexual arousal.



Following the alleged ordeal Ridings was slammed with charges including detaining a person with the intent to sexually assault her and assault causing bodily harm.

The suspected rapist has also been accused of stalking and intimidating the woman and her mother.

Disturbing posts from what is believed to be Riding’s social media account reveal a slew of sexist and violent material.

The last public post read: “My demons will bend your demons over”.



His arrest followed investigations into domestic violence – only for police to allege they found a massive stash of secretly filmed sexual abuse images across 120 electronic storage devices.

It comes after police alleged that Ridings sexually assaulted both women in front of others and sexually assaulted a person under the age of 16.

The suspected abuser has also been accused of poisoning with the intent to injure or cause distress – though it is unclear who or how many people he drugged.

Ridings remains in police custody and is due to appear in Wyong Local Court on December 8.

Police confirmed that a second man has also been arrested in connection with the Ridings investigation.

News.title: Nigel Farage warns Budget hike to betting taxes will devastate UK’s high streets
News.content:
Next

NIGEL Farage has warned that a Budget hike to betting taxes will devastate the UK’s high streets.

And the Reform UK leader said further closures of bookies will push more punters towards the black market.



The extra levies on slot, quiz and fruit machines risk 9,000 jobs and 1,000 outlets, according to analysis by audit giants EY.

Those closures could in turn hit horse racing for £57million.



Mr Farage said: “One, it’s more empty shops on the high street.

“Two, it is damage to the racing industry.

“And three, all you do is you drive people to the black market.”

He said tough restrictions on traditional bookmakers already meant many big wagers were going to illegal operators overseas.

And he insisted: “This just drives things further and further in that direction.”

Chancellor John Healey upped Machine Games Duty from 20 to 25 per cent.



The move came despite The Sun’s Save Our Bets campaign calling for an end to Labour’s tax hikes.

The owners of Mecca Bingo and Grosvenor Casinos say the rise will cost them £9million a year.

News.title: Moment boy, 7, is hit by disqualified driver on e-bike and left in coma for 3 months as dad blasts ‘they’re a weapon’
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment a seven-year-old boy was hit by a disqualified driver on a e-bike, leaving him in a coma for three months.

Michael Hill was 23 when he ploughed into the boy with his Surron bike on Westminster Road in Middlesbrough in August last year.



He and his accomplice, Lee Oliver, had previously been riding around the area on electric bikes without driving licences or insurance.

Hill was a disqualified driver and both riders fled the scene straight after the horror collision took place.



The schoolboy was taken to hospital where he was in an induced coma for three months.

The seven-year-old became entirely dependent on his parents, who had to travel to the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle to see him every day.



The two devastated parents made the round trips whilst also looking after his siblings and continuing to work.

Hill, who is currently serving a four-and-a-half year jail sentence for the collision, has now warned others about e-bikes.

Speaking with regret, he said: “I wish I didn’t go out on the bike that day.

“People just jump on and think they are fun. They are very dangerous truthfully – they are a weapon. They’re very dangerous, they’re a weapon.”



He added: “It has affected me, it has affected the child, it has affected the parents. I can’t sleep on a night, I still get dreams about what happened, what I had done.

“It’s just a blur truthfully, it just all happened so fast. I was literally going down the road, say not even 20mph, cruising down the road then all of a sudden the little boy runs in between two parked cars from the path and into the handlebars of my bike.

“And that’s when I realised I had ran a child over. I couldn’t do anything – I took off because I was scared.”



The boy’s father, speaking via an actor, pleaded with people not to get on an e-bike.

He said: “Even if one rider just stopped and thought ‘I’m not going to do this, I’m not going to cause harm to the people around me it will mean a step in the right direction’.”

The dad revealed his son had sustained a traumatic brain injury, leaving him unable to care for himself.

He added: “Every day for us now is a constant struggle.

“His general quality of life has been diminished. He has lost his independence.”

News.title: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
News.content:
At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.

Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.

However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And for the second time in its history as a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago.

Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments.

By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.

Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of s it was able to sell during the quarter.

The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business.

Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."

Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year.

News.title: Australian mushroom murderer loses appeal to overturn convictions
News.content:
Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison.

Erin Patterson, 51, was found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023. Her life sentence included a non-parole period of 33 years.

In Victoria's Court of Appeal on Friday, three judges threw out her appeal against her convictions and agreed with the prosecution that her sentence was inadequate, as it allowed for the possibility of freedom.

Patterson's crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms," they said.

"We have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," Justice Peter Kidd told the court, on the panel's behalf.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms.

Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.

He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face.

News.title: Crypto worth billions frozen after suspected Binance hack
News.content:
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that it has frozen digital assets worth around $3bn (Â£2.24bn) to prevent them from being stolen while it investigates a security issue.

The company said as part of a series of alerts online that all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while its teams conduct security checks and that the firm will "cover all losses".

Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they have also frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.

Binance has not said how much has potentially been stolen but some crypto experts have put the figure at well above $5bn.

The security incident concerns Binance.com, while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US which provides trading services specifically for American residents, said its platform is not affected by the issue.

"It does look like a hack," Binance's former boss Changpeng Zhao said on X.

Zhao no longer manages the firm but remains a key shareholder.

Glassnode, a digital asset advisory firm, estimated the hack concerns a total of $5.3bn in crypto.

Meanwhile, New York-based blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimated that more than $5.9bn has been stolen.

That amount is nearly four times the value of crypto stolen from Dubai-based crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 - a record-breaking incident that has been attributed to hackers linked to North Korea.

Binance said the amount of funds frozen may continue to increase as its teams work closely with law enforcement and other partners to trace and seize additional assets.

"We are working around the clock and will share a full post-mortem once the investigation is complete. Please rely only on official Binance channels for updates," the firm said, adding that users' funds are safe.

Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.

Bitcoin dropped by around 5% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire said his firm is "closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance" and that his company has frozen more than $800m in assets linked to the incident.

Circle is the issuer and co-creator of the USDC, one of the world's largest US dollar-backed cryptocurrencies.

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said his firm has frozen around $1.6bn "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."

"Protecting the industry and our partners is our main priority," said Ardoino, whose company issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT.

Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.

News.title: Bombshell confession in The Traitors as faithfuls finally turn the screw
News.content:
As ever, James B was as far off the pace as me in the year 11 cross-country race.

When Leigh-Anne Pinnock, probably the most astute faithful of the series, brought up James A being a potential traitor over breakfast, James B sarcastically replied: "I think that's a good theory to start banishing the most innocent."

Sharon - aka Poundland Poirot - failed to appear in the dining room, having been chosen for the chopping block so soon after escaping banishment, throwing all the faithfuls into more confusion. She was getting a bit stressed, so it was probably for the best.

Michael had a warning for the traitors though, giving his most rousing oratory since his motivational speech for the Welsh football team ahead of the 2022 World Cup.

"Traitors... today is going to be a living hell for you, I am going to push and push and push and you are going to suffer today. This is the apocalypse.

"Vengeful daddy is in the house today."

Theories were soon flying left right and centre, with Bash throwing the spotlight on "the head of the round table" Michael, Kenny putting suspicion on James B, while Romesh pointed the finger at actual traitor Maya, shock, horror.

And the obsession with the peacock perfume wasn't going anywhere.

Finally Michael 'Vengeful Daddy' Sheen seemed to be on to something, telling a shell-shocked Maya in the kitchen: "I think you could be a brilliant traitor, and if you and Kenny paired up, amazing."

She was probably relieved when the jeeps turned up for another day trip, and Romesh was all of us with his hilarious reaction to news of yet another insane mission.

On being told by host Claudia Winkleman that they had to find the severed heads of some of the murdered celebrities and reunite them with the head of the buried body, he got the giggles: "It's just so ridiculous. I love it though!"

James B tried to get one group in the Frankenstein-style lab to sing his hit Beautiful - which had Leigh-Ann and Michael bopping along but by the puzzled look on Kenny's face, he had clearly never heard it. Awks.

This mission was a bit of a rehash of the wailing in the well challenge from the first Celebrity Traitors series, with Claudia going full headteacher and cheering - or should we say, shouting - the teams on.

Digital versions of the dead celebs in bell jars had to be matched to the correct gravestone in the castle gardens.

"Seeing Ross's face when he was alive was enough to give a man pause, let alone when his dismembered head is looking out at you from a pickle jar," quipped Michael.

Back at the castle, it seemed that Michael wasn't the only one starting to turn up the heat on Maya.

Romesh and Bash decided she had gone under the radar long enough: "One of the greatest gliders in the game. Maybe Olympic level gliding," mused Bash. And King Kenny was also in their sights.

And so to the penultimate round table. (A shout out to Claudia's sequin-tastic midnight blue trouser suit).

Michael was under the spotlight first due to his presence, intelligence and status as "the father of the table."

In turn, he first went back to his previous suspicion of Leigh-Anne on the night of the murder in plain sight, accusing her again of using her Big Mix dance with Miranda as a distraction.

Romesh put heat on James B due to his vocal accusations, which were often wrong.

The quiet ones - traitors James A and Maya - were then questioned by Michael and James B, who soon honed in on the murder in plain sight, working out that Maya, Kenny and James A were in the library at the end of the night when Ross was killed.

Vengeful Daddy was indeed in the house, and James B was on the money for once. Credit where it's due.

Then the bombshell of the series - something that has never happened before in the history of the show.

James A, who failed dismally to defend himself against Michael's accusations, clearly couldn't take any more and confessed he was a traitor at the table.

"I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped.

"I've had a unique experience on this that no-one has had before, I wanted to be a faithful and that's all I wanted to be. But I couldn't just say 'guys, vote for me.'"

At least no-one had to explain their decision when they all wrote his name down on the boards.

And as Michael and Maya stood round the firepit before heading to bed - or the turret in Maya's case - she looked like a dead woman walking. And DSI Sheen is on her case.

News.title: What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spoken of their desire for the benefits bill to come down, but the government has not yet laid out a timetable for any reductions.

Their political opponents have criticised them for a lack of detail on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, accusing the government of delaying difficult decisions over cuts.

Official forecasts released alongside the Budget indicate welfare spending is going to increase by Â£79bn in cash terms over the next few years.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers behind this thorny political issue and some of the difficult options the government have to bring down welfare costs.

News.title: Hyrox athlete who soiled herself in race tells BBC she put others at risk but says backlash was traumatic
News.content:
An Australian athlete has admitted putting others at risk by continuing to race after soiling herself during an endurance sports event.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC ahead of her return to the sport, Joanna Wietrzyk suggested her determination to win the Hyrox race in Beijing in September had clouded her judgement: "It was my decision to continue racing so I take full responsibility for that."

Challenged over why she carried on, she said: "I didn't really think about those around meâ¦ the decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry for everyone that I did affect."

The 24-year-old said that the experience and subsequent backlash was "traumatic". She also said she had considered walking away from the sport, in which she holds a world record.

Hyrox sees participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.

The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, in northern Germany, and is now held across the world.

News.title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
News.content:
The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.

Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.

These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.

The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.

Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.

He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."

Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.

"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."

News.title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
News.content:
People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.

Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by Â£1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.

Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.

The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.

In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a Â£100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.

But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.

"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.

"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.

However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.

News.title: CCTV shows frying pan used to stop train attacker
News.content:
CCTV footage of a crew member using a frying pan to fend off a knifeman aboard a train has been shown in court.

Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said Samir Zitouni showed "sheer courage and bravery in seeking to save lives and defend others", during the mass stabbing on the Doncaster to London King's Cross train.

Jurors at Cambridge Crown Court saw footage of Zitouni using the pan against Anthony Williams, before the train made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies attempting to murder 10 people aboard the train, three people in Peterborough the day before and a boy at a London railway station.

The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks was not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals.

News.title: Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the government is "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse.

The prime minister called for answers over why an offer to buy the business from its current owners, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.

"This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families," Burnham told the BBC.

The discount chain is teetering on the edge after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).

Burnham said: "We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn't been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case.

"We stand ready to support the workforce however we can."

The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.

The move comes after managing director Barry Williams told its 12,000 staff the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales.

It is understood Gordon Brothers wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds earlier said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal Â£1. A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale.

Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer, which has left it on the brink of collapse.

It could still be purchased out of administration in a so-called pre-pack deal, but the most likely option is for it to be broken up and for Poundland's stores to be sold off.

Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.

It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz.

It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.

News.title: Hundreds of GP practices lose online services after collapse of tech firm
News.content:
Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.

Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England â just under 10% of the total.

Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk, have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.

GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.

Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.

Since last year, all practices in England have had to offer online appointment booking. Currently, more than 40% of appointments are made that way.

An NHS England spokesperson said while "the majority" of GP practice websites were running as normal, some using Silicon Practice will be affected.

"If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."

News.title: Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
News.content:
A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.

The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.

Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.

The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".

The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."

Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.

However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph, external.

The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.

Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.

In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.

"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.

"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."

Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there â but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."

Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."

News.title: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
News.content:
Laura Brand said she knew before they met that "he liked women", and found out that while they were dating that he had been having sex with others.

"I wasn't interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people", she said.

"I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."

She said she remained friends with Brand while he was married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012, and got back together with him in 2015.

Asked if she was "aware of his promiscuity" during their time apart, she said: "I was very aware of it. I could read about it regularly in the papers, so I was aware of it and he also told me."

Turning to their relationship now, she said: "We have a very honest, frank, and clear relationship and marriage.

"It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest."

The charges against Brand relate to allegations made by six female complainants spanning a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The entertainer has displayed little emotion during the course of his trial, but was seen smiling broadly during parts of his wife's evidence.

He let out a laugh when she told the court: "We do have many friends and there are colleagues, and we are grateful for those people."

Her evidence came a day after the star appeared in the witness box himself.

He told the jury the allegations had a "devastating" impact on his relationships with friends and colleagues, meaning they would not touch him "with a bargepole".

He also said on Wednesday he had been promiscuous but believes sexual consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".

On Thursday, the court also heard statements from two of Russell Brand's ex-girlfriends

Elia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, and described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".

She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with".

"When I said no, however, he accepted it," she said in a statement.

Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.

Amanda Alguero Alejos told the court in a statement that Brand had also repeatedly cheated on her.

"He was undoubtedly promiscuous, never in front of me and never when I was around. That was not what mattered to me at the time," she said.

She recalled women "circling" around Brand "like birds", even when they were out as a couple.

The trial continues, with the jury likely to retire to consider the verdicts on Tuesday.

News.title: Ex-Top Gear host Richard Hammond's 'brave' new Welsh life wild swimming and running
News.content:
Former Top Gear star Richard Hammond says he has swapped vintage cars for food festivals and running as he settles into life in a Welsh market town.

The 56-year-old bought a Â£2m Georgian mansion in Llanwenarth, near Abergavenny in Monmouthshire, in November 2025 following his divorce from wife Mindy after 23 years.

The presenter previously told BBC Wales he had "never been happier" since moving into the 19th Century home, and each week he has discovered a new reason to be "delighted that I live there".

With Bannau Brycheiniog - Brecon Beacons - in his back garden, Hammond told the High Performance Podcast he had taken up open water swimming as he becomes "braver" than he has ever been.

News.title: Call of Duty maker slammed for using footage of real-life crowd disaster in game
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 remove real footage of the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush from the video game, after players identified scenes from the disaster in its opening sequence.

Released worldwide last week, the first-person shooter opens with a montage of news reports about North Korea invading South Korea.

Among the clips is around three seconds of real broadcast footage showing a paramedic performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on a person lying in the street.

Other shots show bodies on the road and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.

South Korean players identified the footage as images from the Itaewon disaster, according to broadcaster SBS.

The crowd crush happened on 29 October 2022, when thousands of people gathered for Halloween celebrations in Itaewon, a popular nightlife district in Seoul.

Revellers were packed into a narrow, sloping alley near the area’s bars and clubs when a surge of people triggered a crush, leaving many unable to move or breathe.

The disaster killed 158 people, with two further deaths later recognised as resulting from trauma caused by the incident.

open image in gallery Among the clips is around three seconds of real broadcast footage showing a paramedic performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on a person lying in the street ( Youtube/Activision )

The use of the footage in the game has drawn condemnation from bereaved families and civic groups in the run-up to the fourth anniversary of the disaster, with relatives demanding its removal and saying survivors and witnesses continue to suffer from trauma.

“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Council and the Citizens’ Countermeasures Meeting for the Itaewon Disaster said in a joint statement.

The groups said people who had witnessed the disaster or taken part in rescue efforts continued to suffer from trauma.

They also warned of further harm to victims and their families, saying that “hateful comments that disparage the Itaewon disaster” were spreading online in connection with the game’s setting.

Cho In Young, co-director of the Joint Action for the October 29 Itaewon Disaster, said the decision to use the footage showed that the makers were “insensitive to the anguish felt by the bereaved families, victims and citizens upon seeing the disaster site as it was, and failed to consider the dignity of the victims”.

“Foreign bereaved families are currently visiting South Korea to participate in the memorial service, and we plan to gather signatures from the bereaved families and raise the issue officially,” she said.

open image in gallery A woman burns incense to pay her respects on a wall in an alleyway in Seoul, the site of the tragic crowd crush that killed 159 people during Halloween celebrations, in Seoul's popular Itaewon nightlife area two years ago ( AFP/Getty )

The Korea Game Users Association called on Activision to apologise to the bereaved families, saying: “There must be a clear explanation of the circumstances and an apology regarding the fact that tragic disaster footage unrelated to the game’s progression context was used, causing harm to the bereaved families and others.”

The association urged Activision to replace the footage in an update, but cautioned that “this controversy must not be expanded into demands for censorship or unjustified restrictions on the content of the game itself”.

Activision said in a statement to The Independent: “In developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, we approached the subject matter with care and respect. The game’s opening cinematic utilises some real world news coverage to establish the game’s fictional narrative. It is not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form.”

Before Modern Warfare 4 was released, opposition lawmaker and former justice minister Han Dong Hoon urged President Lee Jae Myung to play it, arguing that its depiction of a North Korean invasion raised questions about South Korea’s military preparedness.

Modern Warfare 4 has performed strongly since its release, topping South Korea’s Steam sales chart four days after launch and overtaking PUBG: Battlegrounds, according to The Chosun Daily.

News.title: Patrick Stewart death updates: Best friend Ian McKellen, Hollywood pays tribute to 86-year-old Star Trek and X-Men star
News.content:

Sir Patrick Stewart, who was known for his roles in X-Men and Star Trek, has died at the age of 86, his family announced Thursday.

The English actor died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” his longtime spokesperson announced Thursday.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” the statement said. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

The Emmy-winning actor rose to fame for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the 1987 hit Star Trek: The Next Generation. He later became known for playing Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men movie franchise.

In the years before he became a movie star, Stewart was already a revered theater veteran in Britain, having made his first stage appearance in 1959.

Stewart was 86 years old ( AFP/Getty )

He started working with the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966 and performed with actors including Helen Mirren and Ben Kingsley, according to the New York Times. In 1986, he won the London Fringe Theater best actor award for his performance as George in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? He also won Olivier Awards for his performances in two Shakespeare plays: Antony and Cleopatra in 1979 and Hamlet in 2009.

He is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, and his two children, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.

News.title: The roof of a water tower in Manhattan where a rare family of barn owls nested has been removed
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The roof of a water tower where a family of celebrity barn owls had been nesting in Manhattan’s Upper West Side has been removed, sparking outrage among New Yorkers who have been captivated by the elusive birds.

The barn owl family was discovered weeks ago, drawing crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the birds, including nature photographers. It is believed to be the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history.

Jessica Wilson, the executive director of NYC Bird Alliance, said that she saw one barn owl fledgling Thursday on the roof of a nearby building after the roof of the water tower, which is located atop a building, was removed. Barn owl fledglings “should not be out in the middle of the day” because barn owls are nocturnal, she said.

“It had been disturbed from the nest,” Wilson added. “We didn’t see any more fledglings.”

NYC Bird Alliance received reports Thursday morning from residents and birders of work happening at the top of the tower, Wilson said. When Wilson got to the building, no workers were present. Enforcement police with the state Department of Environmental Conservation also arrived, Wilson said, and they all were able to access the building's roof with the permission of the building's superintendent. Wilson saw that the top of the water tower where the barn owls had been nesting was gone.

The New York Department of Environmental Conservation said in a statement that its police officers “investigated the area and found that the roof of the water tower on the building was removed, exposing the barn owl nest.”

The officers told the building owner to “halt demolition of the water tower until further notice” while the department investigates any potential violations, the department added.

Reached by phone, the building's superintendent declined to comment. It's not immediately clear who owns the building or ordered the removal of the water tower's roof.

Thomas Obersteiner, an Upper West Side resident, said he saw a man with an extension cord climbing down from the water tower around noon on Thursday.

The news of the water tower roof removal prompted criticism.

“I am outraged by reports that construction work on an Upper West Side water tower destroyed part of the structure that was home to Manhattan’s first Barn Owl nest, potentially endangering a pair of owls and their several fledglings," New York State Sen. Erik Bottcher said in a social media post, adding that “active migratory bird nests” are protected by state and federal law.

“Our city’s wildlife deserves protection, and there must be accountability when these protections are violated," Bottcher said.

“That nest was well-known, incredibly well-known, written about widely,” said David Barrett, a Manhattan-based birder who runs the popular social media account, Manhattan Bird Alert. "It should never have happened.”

Barrett said he observed the water tower Thursday and saw that the roof had been removed.

Birds have captivated New Yorkers in the past. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan’s Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring. After Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year. Then there was Pale Male, a red-tailed hawk who nested above Fifth Avenue for three decades before dying in 2023.

Barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl’s range and the barn owl population has declined “at an alarming rate” over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation.

Barn owl fledglings depend on their parents to hunt for them because they don't know how to hunt yet, Wilson said. The fledglings' parents bring them food at their nest. Without the nest, Wilson added, "we’re worried that these barn owl fledglings might not survive.”

___

Kelety reported from Phoenix.

News.title: Is Bigfoot hiding out in New Jersey? These Sasquatch hunters have a hunch
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A group of Sasquatch hunters has been investigating Bigfoot sightings in New Jersey, with the hope of solving a mystery that has bewildered many for decades.

While Bigfoot, the big and hairy bipedal, is more tied to the Pacific Northwest, Sasquatch hunter Mike Familant believes there is more to discover on the opposite coast.

Mike Familant, who documents his investigations into reported Bigfoot sightings on his online series, In the Shadow of Big Red Eye, has mentioned forests around High Point State Park, Stokes State Forest, and the Delaware Water Gap as some of New Jersey’s hotspots.

The Bigfoot hunter recently told NJ.com about a bizarre sound his team recorded in 2022 after mimicking a barrel owl call at High Point.

open image in gallery The Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization has listed 79 reported Bigfoot sightings in New Jersey on its website, including 18 in Sussex County, 16 in Burlington County and 11 in Ocean County. ( Getty Images )

A military linguist “came back with a report that said it was outside of human vocal range and wasn’t any known animal from northwestern New Jersey,” Familant said.

The Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization has listed 79 reported Bigfoot sightings in New Jersey on its website, including 18 in Sussex County, 16 in Burlington County and 11 in Ocean County.

Outdoorsman Jacob Korbel, an investigator for the research organization, was initially a Bigfoot skeptic.

In 2021, he joined an expedition in the Pine Barrens to check out the organization’s work.

open image in gallery Mike Familant, who documents his investigations into reported Bigfoot sightings online, has told local media that forests around High Point State Park, Stokes State Forest and the Delaware Water Gap are some of the state's hotspots ( AFP via Getty Images )

“About 100 yards away in front of us, there’s this whoop response,” Korbel told NJ.com. “And right away, I’m like, that’s nothing that I’ve ever heard before. That’s not an owl, that’s not a coyote, fox.”

“And you could hear it slowly getting closer to our position, like it was coming in to check us out. Like we were almost getting flanked,” he recalled.

With no solid evidence of the Sasquatch, it remains unclear whether Bigfoot is simply elusive or just bogus.

While public polling on the matter is scant, a 2012 Angus Reid Public Opinion survey found that 29 percent of Americans believed Bigfoot is “definitely” or “probably” real.

News.title: North Korea's Kim calls for rapid expansion of drone technology and observes weapons tests
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for rapidly expanding the country's drone technology and observed tests of various weapons, state media reported Friday, as his nation remains embroiled in a standoff with rival South Korea along their heavily fortified border.

The report came a day after South Korea's military said North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea in what were its first ballistic weapons firings in 17 days.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said that Kim on Thursday visited an exhibition of a variety of attack and other drones that show recent achievements in the field of unmanned aeronautical technology.

In a speech at the exhibition, Kim stressed the need to seize “the absolute superiority in the drone technology” and announced unspecified steps needed to “rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology,” KCNA said.

To mark the event, KCNA said that North Korea later conducted test-launches of various drones, missiles and weapons from the 600 mm-calibre ultra-precision multiple rocket launchers. KCNA photos showed Kim watching soaring weapons or him clenching his fist while his teenage daughter was clapping her hands beside him. South Korea's spy agency assesses that the girl, reportedly about 13, is likely Kim's heir.

Tensions between the two Koreas are running high since last month's land mine blasts at their border that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. But Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.

Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.

North Korea has pulled out of talks with the U.S. and South Korea after Kim's high-stakes diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to boost its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim.

On Saturday, Kim made a surprise visit to a Chinese border town via a newly opened bridge and vowed to develop bilateral ties. Kim has recently taken steps to cement ties with China, North Korea's economic pipeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia, including by sending troops and ammunitions to support its war against Ukraine.

News.title: Peru's Fujimori becomes latest Latin American leader to visit notorious Salvadoran prison CECOT
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori on Thursday visited the maximum-security mega-prison built by Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, known as the Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT). She is the latest Latin American leader to visit the prison that Bukele said is meant to house the most dangerous gang members.

The prison gained international attention when the Trump administration sent more than 250 Venezuelan deportees with alleged ties to Tren de Aragua, without providing evidence.

Fujimori, who assumed the presidency in July, had expressed her interest during her election campaign in building a prison like the one in El Salvador, amid an internal security crisis in her country caused by rampant extortion and a rise in homicides.

Her visit to CECOT comes more than a week after Costa Rican President Laura Fernández toured the mega-prison as part of a trip to meet with Bukele. The Costa Rican leader recently i naugurated a maximum-security prison amid an increase in drug-related violence.

Fujimori, who is scheduled to meet with Bukele later, was received by the Salvadoran Ministers of Security and Justice, Gustavo Villatoro, and of Defense, Francis Merino Monroy.

They explained to the president and her delegation, in one of CECOT’s halls, the design of the infrastructure, surveillance protocols and mechanisms to isolate gang members.

The meeting addressed an agenda aimed at deepening technical exchange between the two nations, and discussions focused on the transfer of expertise in citizen security, digital security, and the modernization of state services, according to a statement from the Salvadoran Presidential Communications Secretariat.

Fujimori praised the security efforts undertaken by the Bukele administration, calling them a “successful model, a very useful model.”

“As is public knowledge, Peru also faced historical challenges in the 1980s and early 1990s, confronting two major terrorist groups,” she noted during the meeting with the Salvadoran officials.

More than 90,000 people have been imprisoned in El Salvador under a state of exception, an emergency measure that began in March 2022 and suspends certain constitutional rights to fight gangs. The measure has come under scrutiny by human rights organizations, which have documented thousands of cases of arbitrary arrests.

The Central American country now has the highest incarceration rate per capita, with about 1.5% of its population behind bars.

The CECOT opened in 2023 and can hold up to 40,000 inmates. It gained international attention in 2025 when more than 250 Venezuelans and some Salvadorans, including Kilmar Abrego Garcia, were sent there. They were later released and allege they were beaten and tortured.

News.title: British soldiers ‘told to take screen breaks and use emojis to help with stress in new guidance’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

British soldiers have been encouraged to take 10-minute screen breaks every hour and use emojis in internal messages to combat stress under new health and safety guidance introduced by the Ministry of Defence (MoD), according to a report.

The policies apply to UK-based service personnel and civilian defence staff, including those deployed on drone operations, cybersecurity defences, and intelligence analysis, The Times reported.

Military chiefs have ordered the measures in an effort to combat “visual fatigue and mental stress”, instructing managers to intervene directly if staff fail to step away from their workstations in addition to their standard lunch breaks.

Troops have also been advised to swap long-winded messages for concise updates accompanied by emojis to reduce strain.

open image in gallery The new guidance offers military personnel a range of advice to reduce strain, including encouraging the use of emojis ( Getty )

The Independent has contacted the MoD for comment.

According to the new internal rulebook circulated to personnel, display screen equipment (DSE) users are instructed to take short intervals away from their desks rather than saving up rest periods.

“You should allow yourself short natural breaks (ten minutes in every hour) away from the DSE,” the document states.

It adds: “A break of [five to ten] minutes duration should be taken every hour, breaks should not be accumulated into one longer break (for example, 30 minutes after [four] hours) … If a DSE user is not taking regular breaks, then the manager is to explain the need for regular breaks and make sure that they are taken.”

The extensive guidance also covers everyday workplace etiquette, advising personnel to avoid crossing their legs or ankles to prevent posture complications and to ensure their feet remain flat on the floor. Personnel are also urged to adopt the “20-20-20” eye-care guideline by looking at an object seven metres (20 feet) away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes.

Beyond workstation setups, the rulebook discourages personnel from looking at mobile phones while walking to reduce the risk of “slips, trips, and falls”, and warns against charging devices via extension leads due to fire hazards.

It also stipulates that formal risk assessments must be completed before electrical appliances such as kettles, toasters, coffee machines, or desk fans are introduced across the MoD estate.

open image in gallery The policy applies to UK-based service personnel at the forefront of digital and drone warfare ( Reuters )

The detailed guidance has drawn sharp criticism from military veterans, who have questioned the tone and priorities of the directives.

Stuart Crawford, a former lieutenant colonel who served 20 years in the Royal Tank Regiment, told The Times the guidance amounted to a “nanny state” intervention.

“I think it’s ludicrous. I think it’s really stupid. ‘Don’t cross your legs’? Sorry, I can’t stop laughing at it,” Mr Crawford said. “I can just imagine going to my blokes 20 years ago and saying, ‘Oh, by the way, you’ve crossed your legs’. I would have been laughed out of court.”

He questioned the MoD’s rationale regarding mental strain, telling the outlet: “It is highly likely most of the mental stress will be coming from soldiers physically fighting. I don’t think we should play that down. That’s why so many former military people suffer from various levels of PTSD and so on.

“Sitting in a container somewhere on an airfield in the UK, looking at a computer screen or governing a radar, cannot be at the same level of stress as being in combat on the ground. There is a bit of nanny state about that.”

An MoD spokesperson said that guidance on screens has been in place since 2016, and is one of a “range of measures to keep its staff fit, ready and able to perform at their best.”

News.title: Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot
News.content:
David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

News.title: Trump administration loses grip on bird flu, experts warn
News.content:
The Trump administration has been criticised for losing control of a bird flu outbreak that has spread among mink and cattle farms across the United States.

The H5N1 virus has infected around 1,000 people since it was first detected in the late 1990s, killing roughly half of them. While it currently does not spread among humans, scientists have long worried that it could trigger a pandemic, and that each human infection raises the risk of the virus mutating.

A new variant emerged in 2020 and has since spread to millions of birds and hundreds of animal species across the globe, leading to devastating losses in both wildlife and farmed livestock and poultry.

While some countries have introduced tough measures to curb its spread, including mandatory culls of infected animals, “flockdowns” (where birds are kept indoors) and vaccination of farm workers who handle at-risk livestock, experts say the US is allowing the virus to run rampant.

For more than two months, an outbreak has raged unchecked on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur, news outlet ProPublica reported last week.

Mink in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of the farms give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate.

Mink have very similar respiratory systems to humans, increasing the risk that a virus can spread between the animals and people, and undergo a process known as “reassortment”, when two or more viruses mix together to make a new, more dangerous strain.

Thanks for joining me. John Healey has ruled out making “crude cuts” to welfare after he failed to tackle the rising benefits bill in Wednesday’s Budget.

The Chancellor acknowledged last night that the current benefits system is “unsustainable” but said he will only look to make cuts “in a Labour way”.

Speaking to the BBC in the wake of Wednesday’s Budget, Mr Healey promised that “there will be a reduction in the benefits bill” before the next election.

However, he said this will not include “crude cuts” to payments.

He said: “We will do that in a Labour way, and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain, or progressive, to have a bigger and bigger benefits bills.

“This system is unsustainable. I’ve been clear about that. The Prime Minister’s been clear about that. It’s what you do about it.”

He added: “We have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures.”

His comments on welfare come after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch accused Labour of presiding over a Government that had left Britain “overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system”.

She said: “Next year, under Labour, the tax burden will be the highest in our country’s history and our benefits bill is going up by tens of billions of pounds because this Government has put welfare first.”

The latest figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility released on Wednesday revealed that benefits spending is expected to jump by almost 30pc to £431bn by 2032.

Almost half the total is pensions and disability benefits for pensioners, despite the planned abolition of the triple lock. Here is what you need to know.
