Budget reaction in the defense world One of the SDR authors and former Nato secretary general Lord Robertson of Port Ellen said: ”John Healey is acting in the national interest – and has done exactly what he said was needed for defense in his resignation letter, by setting a head-mark for 3% in 2030.

“I am strongly in favor of innovative ways of financing defense – and this is a credible route to get more into UK defense. Today’s announcements strengthen UK leadership in NATO once again.”

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey pressed the Government to push for a “European rearmament bank” which he said would “bring our allies together behind a shared vision of defence investment to protect our continent from Putin”.

Former defense secretary and Scots Guards officer Sir Ben Wallace was quick to criticize the Budget, highlighting the way he said it would affect people like Mr Healey's own son, who is a member of the Army Reserve.

Sir Ben posted on X: ”The MOD faces a real term cut to day-to-day spending of nearly 0.5% (RDEL) in 27/28.That's money we spend on training, ammunition, maintenance and operations. So the Chancellor's son in the reserves will have even less training and ammo.“

His comments were echoed by Afghanistan veteran Mike Martin, who said: ”The Chancellor has handed another year to Putin by deferring decisions to increase defense spending in today's Budget.

“The Government says we should prepare for war with Russia in three years, but is totally comfortable wasting one of those years standing still as it defers increasing defense spending until the next Spending Review.

”By then it will be 18 months since the Chancellor resigned as defense secretary over the Government's failure to reach 3% of GDP.”

Mr Healey also announced plans that will see the Government work with private and international finance. A defense finance taskforce is being set up ahead of next year’s spending review. (Forces.net by Sian Grzeszczyk Melbourne).

World.title: IMF expects Brazil to become the 8th largest economy in the 2027 ranking
World.content:
IMF expects Brazil to become the 8th largest economy in the 2027 ranking

29th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:33 UTC Full article

Brazil in 2026 figures as the tenth largest global economy

Brazil is expected to return to eighth place in the global GDP ranking for 2027, overtaking Russia and Italy, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and its World Economic Outlook report, released this month.

IMF points out that Brazil’s GDP, which measures the value of goods and services produced in the country, is expected to reach US$2.80 trillion next year. This year Brazil is expected to finish in tenth place. A trillion in 12 zeros.

Likewise for 2027, United States is expected to remain the world’s largest economy, followed by China, Germany, India, UK. Follows the IMF top ranking for next year,

1. United States: US$ 34.44 trillion

2. China: US$ 22.94 trillion

3. Germany: US$ 5.66 trillion

4. India: US$ 4.52 trillion

5. United Kingdom: US$ 4.49 trillion

6. Japan: US$ 4.47 trillion

7. France: US$ 3.65 trillion

8. Brazil: US$ 2.80 trillion

9. Italy: US$ 2.77 trillion

10. Russia: US$ 2.68 trillion

11. Canada US$ 2.63 trillion

According to the IMF’s projections, Brazil is expected to maintain that position through 2031, the final year covered by the forecast. Brazil’s highest position in the global GDP rankings was seventh, a ranking it held in 1995 and from 2010 through 2014.

The rising star. One of the highlights of the IMF’s forecast is India, which is expected to jump from sixth to fourth place, overtaking the United Kingdom and Japan. By 2031, India is projected to move into third place, ahead of Germany.

The United States and China are expected to retain the top two positions, in that order, through 2031.

World.title: Tabasco residents prepare to contain the damage caused by climate-change-induced coastal erosion
World.content:
As the Gulf of Mexico encroaches on the Tabasco coastal plain, some communities are working to recover natural barriers that protect the coast from erosion.

Residents of Barra de Santa Ana — a sandy strip of land separating the Gulf from the Carmen-Pajonal-Machona Lagoon System — have received training from Eni Mexico (the Mexican subsidiary of an Italian multinational energy company) and UNESCO to revegetate coastal dunes.

Climate change and the resulting rise in sea level threaten Santa Ana and other coastal communities and has resulted in the erosion of 85% of the 30 kilometers of coastline between Boca de Santa Ana and Boca de Panteones.

Up to 3.5 meters of shoreline are lost each year, prompting the development of the Dunas Vivas project (Living Dunes), which includes a temporary paid-work scheme to carry out its activities.

The project is part of a plan to reduce disaster risk and strengthen community resilience through science-based solutions and sustainable management of natural and cultural heritage. Community participation is critical to these restoration processes, ensuring ownership and long-term continuity.

With the additional help of local universities, ejido authorities and government officials, a 30-member brigade selected by the community was given a crash course in strategic planting to rebuild the vegetative barrier and the installation of sand catchers made from organic materials (to facilitate dune formation).

Additionally, the brigade will operate botanical nurseries and collect the germplasm (seeds, plant tissues, pollen, DNA, etc.) needed for the controlled propagation of species ideal for revegetation.

Coastal dunes are among the main natural defenses against hurricanes and storm surges, while also protecting communities, infrastructure and mangroves.

El Heraldo de Tabasco newspaper reported that the state has 50,044 hectares of mangrove forest, but large stretches of these coastal intertidal zones have scarce vegetation.

Government mapping of the area last year identified 2,179 hectares of disturbed mangrove compared to 406 hectares in the 2020 assessment.

A January 2026 report outlined the vulnerability of the Tabasco coast and the problems affecting the areas between the Gulf and lagoons.

In August 2026, a report prepared by the Navy warned of critical levels of erosion in El Alacrán, near La Machona Lagoon, as well as in Barra Santa Ana and in Paraíso further to the east.

With reports from UNESCO, Prevention Web and El Heraldo de Tabasco

World.title: Cartel roadblocks paralyze Matamoros after arrest of Gulf Cartel leader’s son
World.content:
Alleged cartel members set up roadblocks in Matamoros, Tamaulipas, on Monday after federal forces arrested a high-level criminal target in the northern border city.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch confirmed Thursday afternoon that Axel Alfredo Cárdenas Rodríguez, son of a Gulf Cartel leader known as “El Contador” (The Accountant), had been detained earlier in the day. El Contador is José Alfredo Cárdenas Martínez, nephew of Osiel Cárdenas Guillén, a former Gulf Cartel leader and founder of Los Zetas criminal organization.

Como resultado de trabajos de inteligencia militar de @Defensamx, Fuerzas Especiales del Ejército Mexicano y de la @GN_MEXICO_ detuvieron en Matamoros, Tamaulipas, a dos personas, entre ellas Axel Alfredo “N”, alias “Axel”, identificado como segundo al mando de la célula delictiva “Ciclones”. Axel Alfredo “N” está relacionado con homicidios, secuestro, extorsión y tráfico de drogas, armas y personas hacia Estados Unidos. También es señalado como responsable de la agresión contra integrantes de @SSPCMexico, ocurrida el pasado 17 de mayo, en la que lamentablemente perdió la vida un compañero y varios más resultaron heridos. Su memoria y el compromiso de quienes arriesgan la vida para proteger a la ciudadanía nos obligan a continuar las investigaciones hasta detener a todos los responsables. No permitiremos que esta agresión quede impune. Durante la acción se aseguraron armas, cargadores, cartuchos, droga y un vehículo. Ambos detenidos fueron trasladados por la @FuerzaAereaMx a la Ciudad de México. — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) October 29, 2026

On Thursday afternoon, the Tamaulipas government’s security spokesperson’s office announced the arrest of a “priority target” on social media, but didn’t identify the suspect.

“In Matamoros, federal forces detained a priority target linked to an organized crime group,” the office said, adding that the suspect “was extracted from the area” prior to being turned over to “the relevant authorities.”

“As a result of these events, blockades have occurred at various points in Matamoros and Río Bravo,” the office said, referring in the latter case to a border municipality and city west of Matamoros.

“The public is advised to exercise caution, avoid the affected areas, use alternate routes, stay informed through official channels and follow the instructions of security authorities.”

🚨 La ciudad fronteriza de #Matamoros, Tamaulipas, registra bloqueos y quema de vehículos tras la detención de un integrante del Cártel del Golfo. La policía de Brownsville, Texas, informó que los puentes internacionales están cerrados por un “incidente de seguridad. 📹 Especial — La Silla Rota (@lasillarota) October 29, 2026

Blockades were also reported on the highway between Matamoros and Reynosa and the highway between Matamoros and Ciudad Victoria. The newspaper Reforma reported that main roads in Matamoros — located opposite Brownsville, Texas — were blocked.

“To block traffic, the criminals used public transport and cargo vehicles, as well as vehicles from which they had forced the drivers out,” Reforma reported.

In addition, “alleged organized crime accomplices … threw tire spikes on avenues in Reynosa and in the area around the [city’s] airport,” the newspaper wrote.

In addition to roadblocks, gunfire was reported in Matamoros and other parts of Tamaulipas, where criminals reportedly clashed with security forces.

Early Thursday afternoon, the Brownsville Police Department announced on social media that all international bridges between Brownsville and Matamoros were “closed due to an active security incident in Matamoros.”

However, later in the afternoon, it said that all bridges had “resumed normal operations.”

The Tamaulipas Ministry of Education canceled classes in Matamoros for students who start school in the afternoon (turno vespertino) in order to “protect the physical safety of school communities.”

The Gulf Cartel, one of eight Mexican criminal groups that the U.S. government has designated as foreign terrorist organizations, is one of the two main criminal groups that operate in Tamaulipas, the other being the Northeast Cartel.

According to the think tank and media organization Insight Crime, the Gulf Cartel is “one of Mexico’s oldest criminal groups, but it no longer operates as a unified organization.”

“… The Scorpions and the Cyclones are the most powerful factions. From the border, these groups smuggle migrants and drugs into the United States, move weapons and cash into Mexico, and operate complex extortion schemes,” Insight Crime says.

According to a report by the El Economista newspaper, Cárdenas Martínez is the leader of the Cyclones, while his son — who was detained today — is second-in-command.

With reports from Reforma and Aristegui Noticias

World.title: Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, who helped end decades of one-party rule in Mexico, dies at 92
World.content:
Listen to this article

Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Solórzano, a three-time presidential candidate, a central figure in Mexico’s democratic transition and son of former president Lázaro Cárdenas del Río, died in Mexico City on Wednesday. He was 92.

The cause of Cárdenas’ death was not immediately clear. He reportedly passed away in the Ángeles Metropolitano Hospital in the Roma Sur neighborhood of the capital.

President Claudia Sheinbaum and former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador acknowledged Cárdenas’ death in social media posts on Wednesday night.

Sheinbaum called him “a man of steadfast principles who transformed the political life of our country.”

López Obrador said Cárdenas was “a precursor of the democratic movement in Mexico’s recent history.”

“Without him, the country’s political reality would be different,” he wrote.

La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum encabeza la guardia de honor ante el féretro de Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, histórico líder de la izquierda mexicana, acompañada por la familia del fallecido político. Más información en López-Dóriga Digital https://t.co/rSlCjtnTUo — Joaquín López-Dóriga (@lopezdoriga) October 29, 2026

Cárdenas is credited with helping to end the Institutional Revolutionary Party’s decades-long rule in Mexico, which spanned much of the 20th century. He was a member of the PRI for more than 30 years, but left the party in 1987 and ran in the 1988 presidential election as the candidate for the National Democratic Front, a coalition of left-wing parties. Cárdenas is widely believed to have won that election, but the PRI’s Carlos Salinas de Gortari was declared the winner.

He would go on to contest the 1994 and 2000 elections as the candidate for the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), which he co-founded. The 2000 election was won by the National Action Party (PAN) candidate Vicente Fox, who became the first president of Mexico from outside the PRI or its predecessors in 71 years.

The early years

Cárdenas was born in Mexico City on May 1, 1934, exactly two months before his father, Lázaro Cárdenas, won the 1934 presidential election with more than 98% of the vote. His mother was Amalia Solórzano Bravo, who, like his father, was a native of Michoacán.

Cárdenas was not yet four years old when his father nationalized Mexico’s oil industry on March 18, 1938. Lázaro Cárdenas is best remembered for that historic decision, but also oversaw significant land reform, redistributing millions of hectares to small-scale farmers, or campesinos.

Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas spent his early years living at Los Pinos, the erstwhile residence of the president of Mexico. The New York Times reported that “[a] boyhood friend, José J. Altamirano, remembered the young Cuauhtémoc pushing toy trucks around his father’s feet there.”

Cárdenas was educated at private schools before enrolling in a civil engineering degree at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM). He graduated from UNAM in the mid-1950s and worked as a civil engineer before starting his long political career.

Cárdenas wed María Celeste Batel in 1963 and they remained married until her death in 2021. The couple had three children.

A political life

Cárdenas was a member of the PRI from 1954 to 1987. During that period, he served as a federal senator for Michoacán (1976-80) and governor of Michoacán (1980-86).

While in those positions, he was critical of the federal government’s economic decisions — Mexico’s so-called neoliberal period began in 1982 — and the “dedazo,” the colloquial name for the practice in which the sitting president handpicked the PRI’s next presidential candidate.

Before he left the PRI, Cárdenas, Porfirio Muñoz, Ifigenia Martínez and others founded the Corriente Democrática (Democratic Current), a progressive and reformist faction of the PRI.

The 1988 presidential election

Cárdenas had hopes of representing the PRI at the 1988 presidential election, but President Miguel de la Madrid chose Salinas de Gortari — a free trade advocate — as the party’s flag bearer.

Having left the PRI, Cárdenas stood as the candidate for the National Democratic Front, which was backed by the Mexican Socialist Party and the Authentic Party of the Mexican Revolution, among other parties and organizations.

His message of economic nationalism resonated with voters, and early results on the night of the 1988 election showed that he had a significant lead over Salinas. However, later in the night, election officials claimed that the electoral computer system had broken down and they stopped reporting results. Before midnight on July 6, 1988, Salinas was declared the winner with almost 51% of the vote compared to Cárdenas’ 31%, according to the official, but highly questionable, results.

De la Madrid admitted that the results were rigged in his 2004 memoir.

The New York Times reported that Cárdenas’ “sway over the Mexican people was so great that he could have, with a few words, set off a bloody civil war after obvious fraud in the 1988 presidential election robbed him of the victory that many believed was his.”

“But instead of whipping up their anger, he convinced his followers that they could launch a true revolution, not by taking to the streets but by returning to the polls.”

“Se cayó el sistema”. La elección presidencial de 1988 marcó para siempre la trayectoria de Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas. La interrupción del flujo de información, las denuncias de fraude y el triunfo oficial de Carlos Salinas de Gortari abrieron una de las mayores polémicas electorales de México. Así fue aquella histórica elección. @renzochiquito nos cuenta https://t.co/beFZrZj8VB — Azteca Noticias (@AztecaNoticias) October 29, 2026

Cárdenas seeks the presidency again

In 1989, Cárdenas, Porfirio Muñoz, Ifigenia Martínez and Andrés Manuel López Obrador founded the PRD, which became Mexico’s main left-wing party.

Cárdenas represented the PRD at the 1994 and 2000 presidential elections, finishing third in both.

In between his second and third presidential bids, he served as mayor of Mexico City between 1997 and 1999, having won the first direct election of the capital’s head of government, a position previously filled by presidential appointment.

President Sheinbaum used the Mexico City mayorship as a springboard to the presidency, but that wasn’t the case for Cárdenas. Fox took the presidency for the PAN in 2000, which, along with Felipe Calderón’s victory in another controversial election in 2006, left the PRI out of power at the federal level for 12 years. The once-dominant party wouldn’t return to the national halls of power until Enrique Peña Nieto took office in late 2012.

While he didn’t rise to the national leadership position he appeared to be destined for, Cárdenas “was, in a real sense, one of the midwives of Mexico’s democratic transition,” according to University of California political scientist Kathleen Bruhn.

He helped turn the PRD into a competitive political party after the long 20th-century hegemony of the PRI. The party won elections in Mexico City and various states before its recent demise as a result of its poor showing in the 2024 federal elections. Cárdenas left the PRD in 2014, 25 years after co-founding the party, due to differences with its leadership, but he will forever be linked to the party that was Mexico’s preeminent leftist force until the emergence last decade of the National Regeneration Movement, or Morena, which has ruled Mexico since late 2018.

Symbol of the Mexican left

The La Jornada newspaper described Cárdenas as a “symbol of the left in Mexico” and a “historic leader” of the national leftist movement.

“Cárdenas left a profound mark on contemporary political history by leading the most significant rupture of the PRI in the decade of the ’80s, the … Corriente Democrática, and by opening a new stage for the Mexican left,” reported the Mexico City-based daily.

“… He became closely associated with the emergence of an electoral left, the call for free and competitive elections, and the transformation of the Mexican political system. He also supported causes such as those of the EZLN [the Zapatista Army of National Liberation] and the defense of energy resources and national sovereignty,” La Jornada wrote.

El Universal reported that biographers have defined his ideology as “rejection of neoliberalism, defense of the state in strategic sectors, especially energy, austerity, national sovereignty and laicism.”

Cárdenas’ autumn years

Cárdenas remained engaged in Mexican politics in the later years of his life. He spoke out about the need to combat organized crime groups and retake territory they control, and voiced concerns about issues such as low economic growth, the militarization of public security and insufficient funding for education and healthcare.

“I’m very concerned about the situation we’re living, the situation that the country is going through,” he said during a meeting with a cross-party group of senators in 2022. He made those remarks while his former PRD colleague, López Obrador, was in office. Like Cárdenas, AMLO contested three presidential elections, but, in contrast to his political associate, won on his third attempt.

In 2011, Cárdenas, at the age of 77, was awarded the Belisario Domínguez medal, the Mexican Senate’s highest honor, in recognition of his political career and contributions to public life. Among those contributions are several books he authored.

Cárdenas is survived by his three children Cuauhtémoc, Camila and Lázaro Cárdenas Batel, and his grandchildren. Lázaro, governor of Michoacán between 2002 and 2008, is President Sheinbaum’s chief of staff.

With reports from La Jornada, Reforma, El Economista, El Universal and The New York Times

World.title: After a surprisingly strong start, Chipotle plans more restaurants in Nuevo León and Mexico City
World.content:
Chipotle, the U.S. fast-casual food chain inspired by Mexican and Tex-Mex food, plans to open more restaurants in Mexico after its first branch in the country exceeded expectations.

Mexico’s first Chipotle restaurant opened in July 2026 in the border state of Nuevo León, in the high-end municipality of San Pedro Garza García, part of the greater Monterrey area.

Alsea, a Mexican company that operates the U.S. brand, said it plans to open between three and four additional locations in Nuevo León during the first quarter of 2027, while also preparing for its entry into Mexico City that same year.

According to Alsea CEO Christian Gurría, the public’s positive response to the first restaurant exceeded the “honeymoon effect” associated with the initial excitement surrounding an opening.

“Now that our operation is consolidating and the flow of customers is stabilizing, we remain above [expectations],” Gurría said during a call with analysts cited by Bloomberg Línea.

Chipotle arrived in the country after other Tex-Mex food chains tried—and failed—to establish a market there, including U.S. fast-food mainstay Taco Bell, which attempted to expand into Mexico in the 1990s and the 2000s.

Gurría attributed the favorable reception of Chipotle to a combination of price, quality, and portion size. According to Bloomberg Línea, the bowls, burritos, and salads on the Mexican menu cost between 150 and 200 pesos (US $7.98 and $10.64).

The expansion of Chipotle is part of the renewal of Alsea’s portfolio in Mexico, which also includes preparations for the arrival of Raising Cane’s, a U.S. chain specializing in breaded chicken tenders. According to Gurría, the brand’s first branch is set to open in the first quarter of 2027.

Beyond Mexico, Alsea operates and develops restaurant and coffee shop chains in other parts of Latin America and Europe. Its portfolio includes brands such as Starbucks, Domino’s Pizza, Burger King, Vips, Chili’s, Italianni’s, P. F. Chang’s, and The Cheesecake Factory.

According to Alsea’s latest financial report cited by specialized media Merca 2.0, Starbucks remains one of its largest-scale operations with 1,983 coffee shops across 12 countries, including 976 located in Mexico.

The company operates more than 4,800 units across 12 countries, and trades on the Mexican Stock Exchange.

With reports from Bloomberg Línea and Merca 2.0

World.title: Mexico City Grand Prix: Everything to know for the year’s premier motor sports event
World.content:
Formula 1 — the world’s most popular motorsport series — is in Mexico City this week for the 21st race of its 2026 season.

Widely viewed as one of the most vibrant, high-energy and uniquely festive spectacles on the F1 calendar, the Mexico City Grand Prix is expected to attract 400,000 fans to the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez this weekend.

For most in Mexico, Guadalajara native Sergio “Checo” Pérez is the star attraction of this year’s F1 event and will be competing in his 10th Mexico City GP. Checo — who missed last year’s race after being released by Red Bull following the 2024 season — will be racing for Cadillac, a constructor in its first year of competition.

Helping make his return to his home country extra special, Cadillac announced on Wednesday that it had signed Checo to a contract extension, keeping the six-time Grand Prix winner with the team through the 2029 season.

Checo has another reason to celebrate. Sunday’s race will be his 300th F1 race, making him the seventh driver in history to reach that number. As if getting to achieve that milestone at home is not enough, Checo also made a special appearance in the capital on Wednesday.

Driving a modified Formula 2 car, Pérez rumbled along the Paseo de la Reforma avenue in front of an estimated 100,000 onlookers. He burned rubber while performing donuts near the Diana roundabout, then stopped at the Angel of Independence Monument to acknowledge the fans.

“I know some of you have been here since last ​night. I really appreciate it,” Checo told the crowd. “You guys are one of the main reasons I ​came back.”

The what, when and where of the F-1 weekend

For those planning on attending the F-1 race, the Hermanos Rodríguez circuit is inside the Ciudad Deportiva de la Magdalena Mixhuca public park located at the eastern terminus of the Viaducto Río de la Piedad (Viaducto Miguel Alemán). It can also be reached by Metrobus (Line 2) and Metro (Line 9).

Tickets are available via the Official Mexico GP Website, the Formula 1 Official Ticket Portal or through verified secondary resale markets like StubHub.

As for the event, drivers will take two practice runs on Friday, while the third practice run and qualifying take place Saturday.

The Mexico City GP, featuring 71 laps of the 4.3-kilometer (2.6-mile) track, begins at 2 p.m. Sunday.

Of note, Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, 20, could become the youngest champion in series history by finishing in the top nine.

Also competing is five-time Mexico City GP winner Max Verstappen (2017, 2018, 2021, 2022, 2023). Sergio Pérez was Verstappen’s teammate from 2021 through 2024.

With reports from The Associated Press, Reuters, The Straits Times and Grand Prix 247

World.title: MND Local CDMX: Rent reforms, a viral Tesla crash and possible Cowboys game
World.content:
Mexico City is tackling a range of issues this week, from housing affordability and suspected dog poisonings to a dramatic car crash caught on camera. Meanwhile, Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones has teased a future NFL game in the capital, adding to the growing buzz around U.S. sports in Mexico.

Let’s get into it.

Morena’s housing bill aims to curb rent hikes and gentrification

The ruling Morena party and Mayor Clara Brugada put forth a framework on Oct. 22, aimed at stabilizing Mexico City’s ongoing housing rental affordability crisis.

Dubbed the Law on Tenant Relations and Fair, Reasonable and Affordable Rents, the reforms include capping rent increases, prohibiting excessive requirements to obtain a rental, creating an official government office tasked with handling tenant-landlord relations, and building more affordable housing.

In a news release, the administration said the bill is aimed at “curbing gentrification and guaranteeing the right to housing.”

According to the mayor’s office, roughly 2 million people rent their homes in the capital, representing a 54% increase over the past 15 years. Rent, meanwhile, “frequently exceeds 30% of the family income,” a benchmark set by the United Nations in 2020, with prices in some high-demand areas skyrocketing between 100% and 200% over the past decade.

Mexico City’s government already passed a 2024 law capping rent increases relative to inflation. However, the new legislation goes a step further, barring landlords from raising a property’s rent when it changes from one tenant to another. There is an exception for landlords who undertake significant renovations to a property.

Other reforms included in the legislation

A Bill of Rights protecting renters from excessive rental requirements and discrimination. A Tenant Relations Ombudsman tasked with providing free legal advice and resolving disputes. A Digital Registry of Contracts and a one-year lease requirement. A Social Support Office for Evictions, tasked with ensuring the eviction process is “peaceful and respects human dignity.” An affordable housing project that aims to build 80,000 new units alongside 120,000 improvement and expansion projects in low-income neighborhoods. A Public Housing Observatory tasked with monitoring land prices and rental prices across Mexico City’s 16 boroughs.

According to the International Business Times, Morena is gathering signatures for the bill, which it will present to the Mexico City Congress as a show of public support. The proposal is currently being considered by the joint Housing and Administration and Justice committees.

Authorities investigate suspected dog poisonings at Parque España

We reported on this in Mexico News Daily’s regular coverage. However, some stories are so important, we felt it prudent to reiterate here: Authorities are investigating suspected dog poisonings at Parque España in the capital’s Condesa neighborhood.

Simply put, if you or someone you know is a pet parent in the capital (cat walkers, we see you too), please be aware and spread the word.

In a news release published Oct. 27, the Attorney General’s Office of Mexico City announced it is launching an investigation and preventative measures after several dogs became fatally ill while spending time in the park, which features a popular off-leash dog area.

According to the AG’s office, the Citizen Security Ministry (SSC) was called to a nearby veterinary clinic that was treating the dogs. The SSC subsequently canvassed the park and found a blue pill wrapped in a piece of sausage. The pill, which is currently being investigated, has not been definitively linked to the suspected poisonings.

The case is being treated as potential animal abuse and cruelty. While the park is still open, the dog run and children’s areas were closed for cleanup.

“Citizens are urged to report any situation that could put the integrity of animals at risk to 911 or to the SSC Secretary’s Contact Unit, at telephone 55 5208 9898,” the Attorney General’s Office wrote in its news release, “as well as through the accounts @SSC_CDMX and @UCS_GCDMX.”

Tesla crash in affluent Mexico City neighborhood goes viral

A viral video of a shocking car crash in western Mexico City is making the rounds, roughly a week after the incident.

According to video obtained by U.S. media outlet TMZ, a Tesla careens off the road in Cuajimalpa, smashes through a gate and part of another structure before launching off a side patio and ultimately landing somewhere off-screen.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by TMZ (@tmztv)

A time stamp on the footage, taken from what appears to be a home surveillance video, dates the incident to Oct. 19. The incident occurred in Cuajimalpa’s affluent Lomas del Chamizal neighborhood.

International Business Times reports that the cause of the crash, as well as the condition of those involved, is unknown.

Dallas Cowboys tease future game in Mexico City

With the NFL’s first Mexico City series game of the season less than a month away, Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones suggested his team could soon be coming to the capital.

During a post-game interview with ESPN’s John Sutcliffe on Monday, Oct. 26, Jones was asked, on a scale of one to 10, about the likelihood of the Cowboys playing at Mexico City’s Estadio Azteca (also known as Estadio Banorte).

“One,” Jones said several times before catching his mistake and changing his answer to an emphatic 10. “We’re coming,” he added.

Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott doubled down on the enthusiasm, telling Sutcliffe a game in Mexico City would be “exciting.”

“I know the atmosphere would be electric,” Prescott said. “Viva Mexico!”

U.S. sports have had something of a moment in Mexico as of late.

Ticket demand for the Nov. 22 Week 11 match-up between the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings was extraordinary, with some 840,000 fans registering to get a highly coveted seat, as Mexico News Daily previously reported.

Meanwhile, NBA Commissioner Adam Silver suggested last week that Mexico City could be considered for a future league expansion, telling the Pat McAfee Show, “It’s a shorter flight from New York to Mexico than from New York to Los Angeles, so you can see why we’d be interested.”

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How does Mexico’s education system compare to other countries?
World.content:
Last week, we published Part 2 of the MND Mexico Well-being Series, which focused on eight education indicators, including expenditure on education as a percentage of GDP, average class sizes in primary and secondary schools and Mexico’s scores in the 2025 PISA tests.

This “Mexico in Numbers” article is a condensed version of that report — a concise presentation of the key data, complemented by visual features.

As we have previously noted, the MND Mexico Well-being Series — a collection of articles on a range of topics related to well-being — draws on the most recent internationally comparable data, as well as data from the past decade, to assess the state of well-being in Mexico today, and to see what has changed in Mexico during the eight years that the ruling Morena party has been in office.

Without further ado, let’s take a look at the key data from Part 2 of the series.

* The data in this article comes from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Education at a Glance 2026 report and the OECD’s PISA 2025 Results report.

Early childhood education enrollment rates

Just 4% of two-year-olds in Mexico were enrolled in early childhood education programs meeting International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED) criteria in 2024, compared with an OECD average of 50%, placing Mexico last among 30 countries assessed.

Enrollment among children aged 3 to primary-school entry was 75%, versus an OECD average of 90%, ranking Mexico 42nd of 46 countries.

Both rates declined from 2015, when they stood at 5% and 79%, respectively, widening Mexico’s gaps with the OECD averages.

Expenditure on education as a percentage of GDP

Mexico’s government spent the equivalent of 2.9% of GDP on education in 2023, below the OECD average of 4.2%, ranking it 39th of 42 countries, or fourth-lowest.

Mexico’s spending on education fell from 4.4% of GDP in 2015 — when it matched the OECD average — a decline of 1.5 percentage points.

Educational attainment rates

In 2025, 40% of Mexicans aged 25–34 lacked an upper secondary qualification, down from 55% in 2015 but still well above the OECD average of 12%, leaving Mexico fourth-worst among 47 countries.

Tertiary attainment among the same age group rose from around 21% to 29% over the decade.

In 2025, 28% of young men and 30% of young women held tertiary qualifications — 12 and 24 percentage points below the respective OECD averages — ranking Mexico 39th of 45 countries for both sexes.

Teacher qualifications

In 2024, 82% of preschool teachers, 92% of primary teachers and 87% of lower secondary teachers in Mexico met national minimum educational attainment requirements. Mexico exceeded the OECD average only at primary level, by four percentage points, while trailing it by five points at preschool level and two points at lower secondary level.

All three rates declined between 2017 and 2024, falling by five, five and six percentage points, respectively.

Average class sizes in primary and lower secondary education

Mexico’s primary school classes averaged 23 students in 2024, while lower secondary classes averaged 25 — both two students above the respective OECD averages. Mexico’s classes were larger than those in 30 of 38 countries assessed at primary level and 27 of 38 at lower secondary level.

Since 2015, average primary class sizes increased by one student, while lower secondary class sizes fell by three.

PISA scores

Mexican 15-year-olds scored below OECD averages in all four areas assessed in PISA 2025: reading (408 points), science (414), mathematics (388) and computational problem solving (453), with gaps ranging from 47 to 75 points.

Mexico ranked equal 52nd of 90 countries and jurisdictions in reading, equal 63rd of 91 in science and equal 64th of 90 in mathematics.

Since 2015, Mexico’s average reading score fell by 15 points, its math score declined 20 points and its science score dropped two points. Nevertheless, the gaps between Mexico’s scores and OECD averages narrowed as OECD scores declined more sharply between 2015 and 2025.

Students’ exposure to bullying

In 2025, 19.5% of Mexican students aged 15 and 16 reported being bullied at school at least a few times a month, just below the OECD average of 19.6%. Mexico had the 38th-lowest bullying rate among 88 countries and jurisdictions.

Mexico’s bullying rate declined from 20.2% in 2015 — a fall of 0.7 percentage points — allowing it to move from above to slightly below the OECD average.

NEET rate

In 2025, 19% of Mexicans aged 18–24 were neither employed nor in education or training (NEET), five percentage points above the OECD average of 14%, giving Mexico the joint ninth-highest rate among 41 countries. The rate was 29% for young women, compared with 10% for young men.

Mexico’s overall NEET rate fell from 23% in 2015, narrowing its gap with the OECD average from seven to five percentage points.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Sheinbaum and cabinet pay tribute to Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🕊️ Government pays tribute to Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas after his death: The centerpiece of Thursday’s mañanera was a tribute to Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate, co-founder of the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD) and former Mexico City mayor, who died at age 92. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said “Mexico is in mourning,” while Minister for Women Laura Itzel Castillo praised his commitment to democracy and social justice. Asked what legacy Cárdenas leaves for “the left” in Mexico, Sheinbaum answered: “Honesty and democracy.”

The centerpiece of Thursday’s mañanera was a tribute to Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate, co-founder of the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD) and former Mexico City mayor, who died at age 92. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said “Mexico is in mourning,” while Minister for Women Laura Itzel Castillo praised his commitment to democracy and social justice. Asked what legacy Cárdenas leaves for “the left” in Mexico, Sheinbaum answered: “Honesty and democracy.” 🗳️ Sheinbaum says Taddei “betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico”: Three days after Guadalupe Taddei resigned as president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), the president offered a blunt assessment of her conduct. Taddei stepped down after media reports that companies linked to a businessman close to her received lucrative INE contracts. Sheinbaum noted that Taddei was chosen by the Chamber of Deputies, not by the president, and reiterated her support for a comprehensive audit of the INE by the Federal Auditor’s Office.

Three days after Guadalupe Taddei resigned as president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), the president offered a blunt assessment of her conduct. Taddei stepped down after media reports that companies linked to a businessman close to her received lucrative INE contracts. Sheinbaum noted that Taddei was chosen by the Chamber of Deputies, not by the president, and reiterated her support for a comprehensive audit of the INE by the Federal Auditor’s Office. 🖨️ Sheinbaum wants state-owned printer Talleres Gráficos de México to supply “most electoral materials”: The president asserted that “two or three” INE suppliers of items such as ballot papers and ballot boxes are “intermediaries” that don’t produce the materials themselves. Sheinbaum said that next week her government will formally propose turning the government-run printing agency Talleres Gráficos de México into a state-owned company with its own board of directors and “external observation.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Thursday morning press conference came the day after the death of Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Solórzano, a three-time presidential candidate (1988, 1994 and 2000), a co-founder of the leftist Democratic Revolution Party (PRD) and the son of former President of Mexico Lázaro Cárdenas del Río.

Cárdenas, a major figure in Mexican politics who served as a federal senator in the 1970s, governor of Michoacán in the 1980s and mayor of Mexico City in the 1990s, passed away at the age of 92.

Sheinbaum acknowledged his death in a social media post on Wednesday night.

“With deep sorrow, we lament the passing of the engineer Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Solórzano, a man of steadfast principles who transformed the political life of our country,” she wrote.

“His role in Mexico’s contemporary history is fundamental. In 1988, he led a peaceful democratic movement that channeled the yearning for change of millions of Mexican women and men. That historic electoral day, in which he should have been recognized as president, marked the beginning of the democratic transformation,” Sheinbaum wrote, alluding to allegations that Cárdenas was denied victory in the 1988 presidential election by electoral fraud.

A tribute to Cárdenas was the centerpiece of today’s mañanera, at which government officials honored his life and political legacy.

Beyond the tribute, Sheinbaum spoke about the allegedly corrupt conduct of Guadalupe Taddei, former president of the National Electoral Institute (INE).

Taddei resigned earlier this week after media outlets reported that companies linked to a businessman with whom she has a close personal relationship had received lucrative INE contracts.

‘Mexico is in mourning,’ says Interior Minister Rosa Rodríguez

Sheinbaum announced at the start of the press conference that the government would pay tribute to “the engineer” Cuauhtémoc Cardenas Solórzano, who obtained a degree in civil engineering from the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

“From here we send an affectionate hug to Lázaro, Cuauhtémoc and Camila, his children, and to all the people who were close to the engineer,” she said.

#LoÚltimo 🕊️La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum anunció que la mañanera de este jueves estará dedicada a rendir homenaje a Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, tras darse a conocer su fallecimiento a los 92 años. “Hasta siempre, Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas”, expresó la mandataria. https://t.co/DNTvdCAtcq — xevt – xhvt (@xevtfm) October 29, 2026

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez was the first official to speak at length about Cardenas.

“The journey of Cuauhtémoc Cardenas Solórzano has historical significance for Mexico and for the people of the Americas and the world,” she began.

Rodríguez said that his political “struggle” greatly influenced “the Mexico of today.”

Cárdenas was a man who “shaped the transition to democratic life” in Mexico and he “left a mark on the transformation of our country,” she said.

“His example demonstrates that convictions take on meaning when they are placed at the service of the people,” Rodríguez said.

At the end of her address, the interior minister said that “Mexico is in mourning,” but added that Cárdenas’ “teachings, his love of the homeland, his principles and his ideals will remain with us.”

“Long live the great democrat of Mexico, Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Solórzano,” Rodríguez said.

Minister for Women Laura Itzel Castillo called Cárdenas “a great Mexican” and a “dear friend” of her family.

She said his life was “marked by the strength of his convictions and his commitment to democracy, social justice and the defense of national sovereignty.”

“His career is part of the contemporary history of Mexico. His struggle opened paths for democratic participation and he contributed to the transformation of political life in our country,” Castillo said.

After a video tribute to Cárdenas was played, a reporter asked Sheinbaum about the legacy he leaves for “the left” in Mexico and Latin America.

“Honesty and democracy,” she responded.

“Democracy that comes from below, not democracy of the elites,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum: ‘I believe that Guadalupe Taddei betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico’

Three days after Guadalupe Taddei resigned as president of the INE, Sheinbaum offered a blunt assessment of Taddei’s conduct.

“I believe that Guadalupe Taddei betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico,” she said. “That’s the way it has to be said.”

Sheinbaum reiterated that Taddei was elected by the Chamber of Deputies, rather than by the president. She also reiterated her support for a comprehensive audit of the INE by the Federal Auditor’s Office.

In 2023, during the presidency of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, Taddi was elected via sortition — also known as selection by lottery — as none of the candidates for president of the INE had the support of the required two-thirds of lawmakers in the lower house of Congress. At the time of her election, questions were raised about her family links to both the government and Morena.

Sheinbaum says state-owned company should supply ‘most electoral materials’

Electoral materials suppliers linked to José Alfredo Hernández Casillas — the businessman who is reportedly a close friend of Taddei — received lucrative INE contracts.

Sheinbaum asserted that “two or three” companies that received contracts to supply materials such as ballot papers and ballot boxes to the INE didn’t actually produce the materials themselves but rather acted as “intermediaries.”

She told reporters that “most electoral materials” should in fact be made by Talleres Gráficos de México, a government-run printing agency.

To that end, Sheinbaum said that next week her government will formally propose turning Talleres Gráficos de México into a state-owned company with its own board of directors and “external observation.”

Oil — the daily wrap.

Key Facts Brent oil, the global benchmark, rose about 0.6% to roughly US$111 a barrel on Thursday, October 29, and US crude (WTI) gained about 0.7% to near US$103.

on Thursday, October 29, and US crude (WTI) gained about 0.7% to near US$103. The US oil fund USO gained 0.97% to US$168.19 and the Brent fund BNO rose 0.88%, in line with the futures.

and the Brent fund BNO rose 0.88%, in line with the futures. Latin American producers fell: Argentina’s YPF lost 3.12% and Colombia’s Ecopetrol 2.26%, while Brazil’s Petrobras slipped 0.59% in New York.

Argentina’s YPF lost 3.12% and Colombia’s Ecopetrol 2.26%, while Brazil’s Petrobras slipped 0.59% in New York. US crude stocks fell by 1.9 million barrels in the week to 23 October, to 410.6 million barrels, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) reported on Wednesday.

to 410.6 million barrels, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) reported on Wednesday. Prediction markets: Polymarket, a prediction market, puts 33.5% on WTI crude touching US$105 and 27.5% on falling to US$100 at some point in October, as of 29 October 2026, 8:45 pm ET.

Today’s Focus Oil edged higher at very high levels on Thursday. Brent futures rose about 0.6% to roughly US$111 a barrel, and US crude (WTI) gained about 0.7% to near US$103. Latin America’s listed producers had a poor day: YPF, Argentina’s state-controlled oil company, fell 3.12%, and Ecopetrol, Colombia’s, 2.26%. What matters today. Oil at more than US$100 a barrel feeds US petrol prices and the budgets of Brazil, Colombia and Argentina, so even small daily moves matter to both producers and US drivers.

01 The session in one read

Brent closed near US$111.4, up about 0.6% from about US$110.8, and WTI near US$102.7, up about 0.7%, according to futures prices.

The USO fund closed at US$168.19, up 0.97%, and the BNO fund, which tracks Brent, at US$70.76, up 0.88%.

Energy shares in the US rose modestly, with the XLE fund up 0.38% to US$68.71.

Assessment — Oil steady, Latin American producers lower MEDIUM The benchmarks rose about 0.6% to 0.7% and US oil funds gained close to 1%, but the shares of YPF and Ecopetrol fell by 3.12% and 2.26%, so the weakness was local to those companies and their markets. The variable to watch is whether Brent holds above US$110.

on Thursday, October 29, and the copper-miners fund COPX lost 1.21% to US$75.90. Freeport-McMoRan, a US-listed miner with large Peruvian and Indonesian mines, fell 0.69% to US$66.14; Southern Copper, the Peru- and Mexico-focused miner, lost 1.11% to US$191.75.

Today’s Focus Copper gave back Wednesday’s gains on Thursday. The US-listed copper fund CPER, which tracks copper futures, fell 1.49% to US$39.73, and the miners fund COPX lost 1.21%. Miners fell across the board. Southern Copper dropped 1.11%, Freeport-McMoRan 0.69% and BHP, the Australian giant, 0.49%, while Rio Tinto, the Anglo-Australian miner, lost 3.12%. The weaker dollar did not help: the dollar index fell 0.33%, yet copper still declined. What matters today. Copper is Chile’s and Peru’s biggest export and a key input for US power grids and electric vehicles, so a falling price weighs on both producer currencies and Latin American mining shares.

01 The session in one read

Copper ended Thursday lower. CPER closed at US$39.73, down 1.49% from US$40.33, and COPX, a fund of copper-mining companies, fell 1.21% to US$75.90.

US growth was the day’s main data point. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), the US statistics agency, said the economy grew 3.4% at an annual rate in the third quarter, above the 3.2% forecast in the RT economic calendar.

China, the world’s largest copper buyer, had no major data on the RT economic calendar for 29 October.

Assessment — A softer metal despite a softer dollar MEDIUM Copper fell 1.49% on a day when Wall Street also fell, with the S&P 500 down 0.30% and the Nasdaq down 1.38%. A weaker dollar normally helps metals, so the drop looks tied to risk appetite rather than the currency. We could not confirm a single trigger. The variable to watch is China’s demand data, since the country takes roughly half of the world’s refined copper.

03 What moved it

The dollar index slipped 0.33% to 101.85, which usually supports dollar-priced metals, but copper fell anyway.

Stronger US growth cuts two ways. It supports demand for copper in power grids and construction, but it can also keep US interest rates high, which slows building and manufacturing.

04 The Latin American read

Chile, the world’s largest copper producer, saw its stock index fall 1.25% on Thursday, while its peso was roughly flat near 988 per dollar. The IPSA’s decline matched copper’s weakness.

Peru, the second-largest producer, is home to Southern Copper’s mines and to Cerro Verde, a large mine run by Freeport-McMoRan. Southern Copper’s shares fell 1.11% in New York.

Mexico’s Grupo México, which owns Southern Copper, fell about 0.7% in Mexico City.

05 The names to watch

Freeport-McMoRan is the cleanest US-listed play on copper, and it fell less than the sector.

For investors who want exposure without single-company risk, CPER tracks futures and COPX holds miners, and both fell on Thursday.

06 The outlook

Copper is likely to stay tied to risk appetite and the dollar in the short term. A weak Wall Street can drag the metal lower even when the dollar eases.

The next catalysts are China’s industrial data and any news on US tariffs, as prediction markets still see about a one-in-four chance of Section 232 tariffs (national-security tariffs) on copper cable by the end of 2026.

No. CPER tracks copper futures contracts, not the spot price of physical copper.

It is an input for power grids, electric vehicles and data centres, and a gauge of global industrial demand.

Which countries produce the most copper?

Chile is the world’s largest producer and Peru is the second-largest.

Freeport-McMoRan fell 0.69%, Southern Copper 1.11%, BHP 0.49% and Rio Tinto 3.12%.

Today’s Focus Precious metals had their worst day of the week on Thursday. Spot gold ended near US$4,010 an ounce, down about 1.3%, and spot silver fell about 3.5% to roughly US$52. Mining shares fell more than the metals. The GDX fund of gold miners lost 3.12%, and Agnico Eagle, a large Canadian producer, dropped 3.93%. The fall came even though the dollar eased and US Treasury yields fell, which normally helps gold. What matters today. Gold usually rises when the dollar and yields fall, so a drop on a day when both eased suggests investors were selling to raise cash, not reacting to rates.

01 The session in one read

Spot gold ended Thursday near US$4,010 an ounce, down about 1.3% from about US$4,055 on Wednesday. Silver lost about 3.5% to roughly US$52.

In New York, the gold fund GLD fell 1.32% to US$368.57 and the silver fund SLV 3.63% to US$47.28.

Wall Street also sold off. The S&P 500 lost 0.30% and the Nasdaq 1.38%, so metals did not act as a refuge on the day.

Assessment — A broad sell-off, not a rates story MEDIUM The dollar index fell 0.33% and the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.94% from 5.02%, yet gold and silver still dropped. We could not confirm the cause. A common reading is that investors sold winners as stocks fell, but that is an interpretation, not a fact. The variable to watch is whether gold holds US$4,000, a level traders watch closely.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Cambronero Bridge to Reopen
World.content:
The Cambronero bridge on Route 1 is scheduled to reopen Tuesday, November 3, restoring traffic through a stretch of the Inter-American Highway closed since a truck damaged the structure in September. The reopening is planned for noon, nearly two weeks ahead of schedule. The bridge is at kilometer 71, on the road connecting San Ramón, Alajuela, with Esparza, Puntarenas.

The crossing has been closed since the night of September 7, when a tractor-trailer struck the modular steel bridge. Crews had to dismantle parts of the structure, replace damaged components and remove and reinstall the bridge deck. Before those repairs could begin, workers built a support tower to hold the bridge’s weight while damaged pieces were removed. Some parts of that temporary support had to be manufactured specifically for the work.

Additional work will continue after the bridge reopens, but those remaining tasks are not expected to interrupt traffic. Drivers should slow down and use caution around crews at the site. The reopening will restore passage through Cambronero while preparations continue for a permanent solution to the ground instability affecting this section of Route 1.

Bids for that project are under review, with construction expected to begin in early 2027. The planned work includes stabilizing the slope, removing the modular bridge and restoring the road’s two lanes. A possible third lane is also being studied, but it has not been approved for construction.

World.title: Tamarindo Celebrates Halloween Weekend With Costume Surfing, Parades and Beach Parties
World.content:
Tamarindo is getting ready for a Halloween weekend that promises everything from surfers riding waves in costumes to trick-or-treating, costume contests, live music and beach parties. The popular Guanacaste destination will host the fifth annual Tamarindo Halloween Fest, with its main celebrations taking place this Friday and Saturday.

Organized by the Tamarindo Development Association (ADIT), the festival brings together local families, tourists, businesses and community organizations for two days of activities designed to offer something for just about everyone. There will be events for children, contests for pets, a nighttime running race and plenty of entertainment for adults looking to celebrate Halloween at the beach.

The celebration has grown since it began in 2022, with Tamarindo’s hotels, restaurants and local businesses joining the festivities. Organizers hope the event will also bring more people to the community before Costa Rica’s busy tourism season gets underway. This year, Halloween falls on a Saturday, giving everyone a full weekend to enjoy the celebrations without having to rush home the next morning.

The main family activities begin Friday at 5 p.m. with a costume parade through downtown Tamarindo, starting near Hotel Tamarindo Diria and continuing toward Parque Oneida, where much of the evening’s entertainment will take place. Children and adults are encouraged to dress up, with costume competitions planned for kids and families. Even dogs will have their chance to compete, as organizers invite pet owners to bring their four-legged companions dressed in Halloween outfits.

The Friday celebration will feature a crazy hair competition, trick-or-treating, music and activities for younger children. The traditional Payasos Los Alegres will also join the parade, bringing a touch of Costa Rican entertainment to the festivities. For those who prefer something a little scarier, Journey School will operate a haunted house at Parque Oneida beginning at 6 p.m. Admission to the haunted house carries a fee, with proceeds supporting scholarships for students at the school.

Those looking for food will find local vendors participating in the Tama Market, offering a variety of dishes and refreshments throughout the evening. A dance competition will add another element to the celebration, with participants performing routines inspired by Halloween characters and popular horror-themed entertainment. Organizers are encouraging groups to put together their most creative performances for a chance to win prizes.

Friday will also feature a recreational 5-kilometer (3.1-mile) race organized by Tama Run. The event combines exercise with Halloween fun, rewarding runners who show up wearing the most creative costumes. After the family celebrations, Tamarindo’s nightlife will take over. Crazy Monkey will host its Haunted Paradise party on Friday beginning at 9 p.m., featuring several DJs and three stages with dancehall, reggaeton and electronic music.

The festivities continue Saturday morning with a free Halloween reading event at the Tamarindo Children’s Community Library. From 10:30 a.m. until 12:30 p.m., children can enjoy themed stories and collect candy. One of the weekend’s most unusual events takes place Saturday afternoon when surfers head into the Pacific Ocean wearing Halloween costumes.

The costume surfing event is scheduled from 3:30 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. in front of Witch’s Rock Surf Camp, bringing together local surfers, instructors, residents and visitors for an afternoon of waves, music and prizes. Participants will be judged in different categories, adding a playful twist to a sport that has helped make Tamarindo one of Costa Rica’s best-known surfing destinations.

Several local surfing organizations are participating, including the Tamarindo Surf Association, the Tamarindo Sports Committee and the North Pacific Surf Association. For anyone who would rather watch than paddle out, the beach will provide a chance to see surfers attempt to catch waves while dressed in costumes not normally associated with the ocean.

Saturday evening will bring another round of parties and competitions. Sharky’s is planning a Halloween celebration with $1,500 in costume prizes, while Iguana Surf and NAIA restaurant will hold a sunset gathering featuring music and additional costume contests. A pickleball tournament organized by 15 Love Tamarindo is also part of the festival’s activities, with prizes that include a two-night hotel stay for two people.

Beyond the entertainment, the festival is intended to support Tamarindo’s tourism businesses during a traditionally slower period of the year. Hotels including Pasatiempo, Mar Rey, Hideaway Costa Rica and Las Guapas are offering special accommodation promotions, with some deals extending into November.

Restaurants and shops are also participating, giving everyone more reasons to spend the weekend in town. Several beachwear and fashion retailers have announced discounts ranging from 10% to 70%. Elizabeth Cole, president of the Tamarindo Development Association, said the goal is to make the community a destination people associate with Halloween celebrations in Costa Rica.

The combination of beaches, restaurants, nightlife and family entertainment makes Tamarindo well suited for a festival that appeals to different age groups, while providing additional business for local merchants ahead of the high season. Although many of the community activities are free, some attractions, races and private parties may require advance registration or paid admission.

Anyone planning to attend should check individual event details, particularly for nighttime entertainment and competitions with limited participation. The main family celebration at Parque Oneida runs from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. Friday, while the Saturday program offers activities from the morning through late evening.

For travelers already visiting Guanacaste, Halloween weekend provides another reason to spend time in Tamarindo. And for those living in Costa Rica who want something different from the usual Halloween party, watching costumed surfers catch waves in the Pacific might be difficult to beat.

The complete schedule, registration details and any last-minute changes are available through the Tamarindo Development Association’s official website and its social media accounts.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Native Stingless Bees at Center of Supreme Court Fight
World.content:
Costa Rica’s tiny native bees have become the center of a legal battle that could affect beekeepers, honey producers and efforts to protect some of the country’s most important pollinators. The Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court (Sala IV), has agreed to review a challenge against government regulations that limit the commercial use of native stingless bees. The case raises questions about whether the rules are protecting biodiversity or making it unnecessarily difficult for people who have raised these insects for generations.

Costa Rica is home to 58 recorded species of native stingless bees, but regulations introduced in November 2025 allow commercial production without additional scientific studies for only two species. Anyone hoping to commercially produce honey, wax or other products from the remaining species must first provide scientific evidence showing that doing so will not threaten their survival.

The legal challenge was accepted last week following a complaint filed by Yandry Johanna Alvarado Castro. The lawsuit questions several provisions of the Executive Decree which regulates facilities where stingless bees are raised and managed. Unlike the familiar European honeybee, Costa Rica’s native stingless bees lack a functional stinger. Many are much smaller, and some live in colonies inside hollow trees, fallen logs and other natural cavities.

Two of the best-known species are the mariola (Tetragonisca angustula) and soncuano (Scaptotrigona pectoralis). Both are included among the species permitted for commercial production under the regulations. Their honey is produced in relatively small quantities and has long been valued by Costa Rican families, particularly in rural communities where raising native bees has been passed down through generations.

The practice is known as meliponiculture, a type of beekeeping that focuses on stingless bees rather than the imported honeybees commonly used in large-scale commercial honey production. But these insects do much more than produce honey. They pollinate native plants and agricultural crops, helping forests regenerate and supporting the reproduction of vegetation throughout the country.

That ecological importance is one reason the government introduced the regulations. Officials say the rules are intended to protect native bee populations, prevent overexploitation and preserve genetic diversity. However, beekeepers and researchers have questioned whether some of the restrictions are supported by sufficient scientific evidence.

One of the most controversial measures limits commercial operations to 30 colonies and noncommercial operations to just five. The legal challenge argues that these limits fail to consider differences between species, regional environmental conditions and the availability of food sources.

A beekeeper working in the humid forests of Limón, for example, may face very different conditions from someone maintaining colonies in the dry forests of Guanacaste. Critics argue that applying identical limits to both operations may not make sense without additional research.

The regulations also require beekeepers to maintain minimum distances between their colonies and agricultural operations using pesticides. Depending on the size of the bee species, those distances range from 500 meters (1,640 feet) to 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles). Even greater distances are required in some circumstances, including where aerial spraying takes place.

Although the intention is to protect bees from potentially dangerous chemicals, the lawsuit questions how those distances were established and whether they are practical for small farmers and rural families. Researchers at the National University’s Tropical Bee Research Center (CINAT) have also raised concerns about the scientific basis for the restrictions.

Of the 58 native stingless-bee species recorded in Costa Rica, researchers have documented 20 species being maintained in managed colonies. That is considerably more than the two species covered by the regulation’s simpler commercial approval process. Specialists agree that native bees need protection but have warned that more information is required before deciding how many colonies should be allowed or which species are appropriate for commercial production.

For traditional beekeepers, the rules could have financial consequences. Some families maintain several species and depend on the sale of small quantities of honey and other products to supplement their income. Others raise bees primarily to preserve traditional knowledge and maintain healthy populations of pollinators on their properties.

The National Chamber of Stingless Beekeepers has previously called for additional species to be included in the regulations, particularly the jicote gato (Melipona beecheii) and jicote barcino (Melipona costarricensis). The organization and other critics argue that overly restrictive rules could discourage beekeepers from registering their operations and push some producers into the informal market.

Another concern involves potential penalties. The lawsuit challenges provisions that refer violations to Costa Rica’s Wildlife Conservation Law, arguing that beekeepers could face legal uncertainty over activities involving insects that naturally move between managed colonies and the surrounding environment. The case now moves forward in the Constitutional Chamber, where judges will examine whether the disputed rules comply with Costa Rica’s Constitution and environmental protections.

The court has given the Attorney General’s Office and the ministries of Environment and Energy and the Presidency 15 days to respond to the legal challenge. Importantly, accepting the case does not mean the judges have ruled against the regulations. The existing requirements remain in effect while the court considers the arguments.

Beekeepers also face a registration deadline in November 2026, when the 12-month period established under the regulations is scheduled to expire. The dispute comes at a time when Costa Rica is already confronting broader concerns about the survival of native bees. Earlier this year, the Constitutional Chamber ordered authorities to enforce a nationwide ban on insecticides containing fipronil after a separate case involving damage to bee colonies in Lepanto, Puntarenas.

The complainants in that case reported losing at least 24 native bee colonies and serious damage to hundreds of additional hives. The ruling highlighted the risks that agricultural chemicals can pose to pollinators and reinforced the importance of protecting native insects that play an essential role in Costa Rica’s ecosystems.

For now, the latest legal dispute presents a difficult question for authorities: how to protect native bees without placing unnecessary burdens on the people who raise and care for them. With dozens of native species, a long tradition of small-scale beekeeping and an economy closely connected to agriculture and conservation, Costa Rica has considerable interest in finding the right balance.

The Supreme Court’s eventual ruling could help determine how the country manages its native bees for years to come, affecting not only honey producers but also the forests and farms that depend on these small but valuable pollinators.

World.title: Costa Rica’s President Invites Pope Leo XIV to Visit in 2027
World.content:
President Laura Fernández formally invited Pope Leo XIV to visit Costa Rica during a private audience at the Vatican, proposing a trip in 2027 that would make him the first pontiff to set foot in the country since John Paul II in March 1983. Fernández delivered the invitation in a letter and handed it to the pope in person at the Apostolic Palace. In it, she extended what she called a fraternal and respectful invitation on behalf of the people and government of Costa Rica, describing the country as a land where work and peace prevail.

The letter ties the proposed visit to two anniversaries Costa Rica will mark in 2027. One is the 203rd anniversary of the declaration of Our Lady of the Angels, known here as La Negrita, the patron saint. The other is the 180th anniversary of the Constitution recognizing Catholicism as the official religion of the state.

No date has been set and the letter leaves the timing to the pope, and Fernández offered to coordinate preparations for an eventual pastoral and official visit through the Vatican’s Secretariat of State and the Apostolic Nunciature in San José. The Vatican has not said whether the pope will accept.

Fernández also presented the pope with a replica of the Virgin of the Angels and coffees from several Costa Rican growing regions. It is not the first time Costa Rican coffee has reached Leo XIV. Speaking to Catholic media after the meeting, Fernández said she had invited the pope to come and greet La Negrita, and that it would be very special for Costa Rica to receive a pope again after 1983. She said the conversation lasted about 30 minutes, that she told him Costa Ricans had been praying for him, and that she felt at home.

She added that the pope appeared in good spirits and in good health following a recent medical procedure, though she said the two did not discuss his recovery directly. The Holy See Press Office said in a statement after the audience that Fernández also met with Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, and Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, secretary for relations with states and international organizations.

According to the statement, those talks highlighted good relations between the Holy See and Costa Rica and between the state and the local Church and covered social and political issues in the country and the region, particularly security and migration. Fernández said she discussed with the pope the situation of Nicaraguan migrants, the largest migrant group in Costa Rica, as well as cooperation with the United States on people going through deportation proceedings.

On security, she said her government pairs investment in education, health and support for young people with measures against organized crime, including efforts to stop inmates from directing violence from inside prisons. The audience came two weeks after Fernández toured El Salvador’s CECOT mega-prison, and as Costa Rica moves inmates into its own maximum-security facility, the CACCO.

Bishop Bartolomé Buigues of Alajuela, vice president of the Costa Rican Episcopal Conference, said closer engagement between the Church and civil authorities is of great importance. The bishops’ conference thanked the president for promoting the meeting. The Vatican stop opened Fernández’s third official trip abroad since taking office in May, following visits to El Salvador and Colombia. Her schedule in Rome also includes a meeting with Italian President Sergio Mattarella.

She then travels to Madrid for the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government on Nov. 4 and 5 and is scheduled to return to Costa Rica on Nov. 6. A papal visit would carry particular weight in a country where devotion to La Negrita draws pilgrims from every province to the Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels in Cartago each August. John Paul II’s 1983 stop, part of a tour of Central America, remains the last time a pope visited the country.

World.title: 46 US Veterans Tried Ayahuasca in Costa Rica, Where Rules Remain Murky
World.content:
Forty-six American military veterans and first responders spent a week at an ayahuasca retreat in Guanacaste in September, hoping the Amazonian brew would ease trauma they carried home from combat zones and emergency scenes. Their accounts, published Wednesday by the New York Post, describe former Army Rangers and Navy SEALs weeping in ceremony tents and returning home calmer.

The stories are moving. They also land in a place where the Ministry of Health has spent nearly two years warning the public against therapeutic ayahuasca use, while the best-known center that serves it holds a ministry authorization the ministry itself tried, and failed, to cancel.

The retreat ran from Sept. 5 to 12 at Rythmia Life Advancement Center near Tamarindo, in the area of Santa Cruz, spanning the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. It was organized with The Coming Home Project, a nonprofit founded in 2021 by Navy SEAL veteran Nate Brown to combat veteran suicide, and funded largely by the Birds Eye View Project, a Texas veterans charity, according to the organizers.

The Post put the group at 46, while a September press release from the organizers said 47 took part. Days combined yoga, individual and group counseling, classes and meditation, with ayahuasca ceremonies held at night in tents. Rythmia and Coming Home reviewed each participant’s medical history, medications and mental health beforehand, the Post reported.

The need behind such efforts is stark. A 2026 Department of Veterans Affairs report counted 6,488 veteran suicides in 2024, an average of nearly 18 a day. Participants described the week as a turning point. A 44-year-old firefighter and former Army Ranger, identified only as Dave L., told the Post that the constant inner conflict he lived with had grown much quieter since he returned home. He stopped short of calling a single retreat a cure.

Jeff McNairy, Rythmia’s chief medical officer and a psychiatrist, told the paper that trauma is the condition he considers ayahuasca best suited to treat. He said roughly half the participants vomited on any given night, a reaction the center describes as a psychosomatic release of trauma.

What the coverage does not include is outcome data. No standardized symptom scores, follow-up assessments or comparison group were reported for the group. Rythmia advertises a self-reported success rate above 97% among more than 23,000 guests since 2016, a figure drawn from its own guest surveys rather than independent clinical measurement.

The broader research is promising but young. An observational study run with the nonprofit Heroic Hearts Project followed 58 veterans who attended ayahuasca or psilocybin retreats in Peru and Jamaica between 2021 and 2024. Its research director, neuroscientist Grace Blest-Hopley, has said more than 80% of those who entered with PTSD no longer met the diagnostic criteria afterward.

The study’s published averages were more modest, with PTSD symptom scores falling about 26% among the ayahuasca group. Researchers at the University of Texas are now studying how brain responses in combat veterans change after ayahuasca treatment. None of this yet amounts to the large controlled trials regulators require before approving a treatment.

The risks are well documented. About 70% of users experience acute nausea and more than half report unsettling psychological effects, according to research cited by the Post. Combined with common SSRI antidepressants, the brew can trigger serotonin syndrome, which can be fatal, and it can provoke prolonged psychosis in people with underlying psychiatric vulnerabilities.

Those medications and histories are common among veterans with PTSD, which is why screening matters as much as the ceremony itself. Costa Rica has no law written for this industry. In January 2025 the Ministry of Health issued a health warning on ayahuasca and ibogaine, urging the public not to consume or promote either for therapeutic purposes, not to join rituals that use psychoactive substances for healing, and to report anyone offering them.

The ministry said no product based on either plant holds the sanitary registration it requires. Rythmia is the exception, and an awkward one. The center promotes itself as the world’s only medically licensed ayahuasca center, with a round-the-clock medical team that McNairy said includes five doctors and 12 registered nurses.

According to a February 2025 opinion from the Attorney General’s Office (PGR), the Ministry of Health told Rythmia in July 2022 that it could keep using ayahuasca for therapeutic purposes on a temporary basis until a regulation was issued. In October 2024, Health Minister Mary Munive asked the PGR to endorse annulling that authorization.

The PGR declined and said the ministry’s request contained extremely serious errors, including a failure to identify which rules the authorization violated, and noted that no regulation governed or banned ayahuasca when the permission was granted. It is not clear whether the ministry has revisited the case since.

Elsewhere, safeguards vary widely. A study published in January in JAMA Network Open interviewed representatives of 49 publicly advertised psychedelic retreat organizations, most of them based in the United States. About seven in 10 worked with a licensed health professional or someone trained in emergency response, but only about two-thirds had such a person present at retreats even some of the time.

By one estimate, Costa Rica hosts about 80 psychedelic retreat centers, some 60 of them offering ayahuasca, making it the second most popular destination for this kind of travel after Peru.

The consequences of thin oversight have already been felt here. Lauren Levis, a 40-year-old social worker from New Mexico, died in August 2024 after taking iboga at Soul Centro, a retreat in Paquera on the Nicoya Peninsula. Her brother has said she collapsed in a shower after an all-night ceremony, and that an electrocardiogram taken before the retreat showed marked abnormalities, yet she was allowed to attend.
