Judicial investigators sent their findings to prosecutors in March 2025, nearly eight months after her death. A Norwegian woman died after taking ibogaine at another facility near Liberia in 2014. The veterans’ relief may prove genuine, and researchers are working to measure how much of it lasts. For now, the safeguards around ayahuasca in Costa Rica depend largely on the operators who serve it.

Researchers who study the retreat industry advise anyone weighing one to ask for a written medical screening that covers heart conditions, psychiatric history and every medication, a medical professional on site rather than on call, a clear emergency plan with transport to the nearest hospital, and straight answers about the legal status of what is being served. Medical experts also warn that safely tapering off antidepressants can take six to 12 weeks under supervision, far longer than many retreats allow.

World.title: All Three VIP Lounges at Juan Santamaría Airport Close Sunday
World.content:
If you are flying out of Juan Santamaría International Airport this Sunday, Nov. 1, plan on waiting at the gate. All three VIP lounges at Costa Rica’s main airport will be closed that day, and one of them has no date to reopen. The closures start Saturday, Oct. 31, and each lounge is on a different schedule. BAC Credomatic said the special hours are the result of an operational adjustment scheduled by the airport’s management and outside the bank’s control.

Here is how each lounge is affected:

Lounge BAC closes at 6 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31, two hours earlier than usual. It reopens at 4 a.m. Monday, Nov. 2. That is 34 hours without service.

closes at 6 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31, two hours earlier than usual. It reopens at 4 a.m. Monday, Nov. 2. That is 34 hours without service. VIP Santamaría , next to Gate 5, closes for Sunday, Nov. 1, only.

, next to Gate 5, closes for Sunday, Nov. 1, only. VIP Lounge Costa Rica, the Mastercard lounge that also operates as the Copa Club, closes Saturday, Oct. 31, until further notice.

That last closure is the one to watch. If you usually get in with a Mastercard card or a Priority Pass membership, you will lose that option for an open-ended period. The lounge’s own notice gives no reopening date, and Priority Pass now lists it as temporarily closed from Oct. 31 until further notice.

Aeris, the company that runs the airport, has not said what the adjustment involves. Asked whether the lounges would change operators, the company said it recognizes the lounges as an important part of the airport experience. It added that any official information will be released through its own channels.

The lounges normally open from 4:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Priority Pass also lists VIP Santamaría as undergoing renovation work, and warns that space may be limited even when it is open. Nothing announced so far affects flight schedules. If you were counting on lounge food or a quiet place to work this weekend, eat before you head to the airport and bring a charged phone and laptop.

Check with your bank or lounge program before you leave home, since access rules differ from one lounge to the next. If you are heading to the United States, you will also need to sign a new passenger form starting Nov. 3. The lounge closures come a week after a power failure disrupted the airport’s control tower. From Monday, the BAC and VIP Santamaría lounges are expected back on normal hours. The Mastercard lounge may stay closed well beyond that.

World.title: Elena Rybakina Clinches Year-End World No. 1 Ranking After Tokyo Victory
World.content:
Elena Rybakina has won the year-end World No. 1 ranking for the first time in her career, defeating fellow Kazakh Yulia Putintseva 6-2, 6-3 at the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo on Thursday. The 27-year-old needed just one more victory to guarantee that Aryna Sabalenka could not overtake her before the end of the season. She accomplished that in 70 minutes, adding another milestone to a remarkable year that has already brought her two Grand Slam titles.

Rybakina becomes the 17th woman in WTA history to finish a season ranked No. 1 and the first player representing Kazakhstan, male or female, to achieve the year-end top ranking in singles or doubles. Thursday’s result also means Rybakina will enter the 2027 season at the top of women’s tennis, regardless of what happens at next month’s WTA Finals in Indian Wells, California.

Her performance against Putintseva was convincing from the start. Rybakina never lost her serve, fired six aces and faced only one break point, which she saved in the final game before closing out the match. The victory extended her winning streak to five matches following last week’s title at the Ningbo Open in China.

Rybakina’s rise to the top has been one of the biggest stories in women’s tennis this season. She began 2026 by winning the Australian Open, defeating Sabalenka in the final to claim her second Grand Slam title. Her first major championship came at Wimbledon in 2022. In September, she added the US Open title, again beating Sabalenka in the championship match. That victory brought her Grand Slam total to three and helped her take over the World No. 1 ranking for the first time, ending Sabalenka’s 99-week run at the top.

But Rybakina’s success has extended well beyond the Grand Slams. She has won four singles titles this season, more than any other player on the WTA Tour, with victories at the Australian Open, Stuttgart, US Open and Ningbo. She has also reached six finals and recorded a tour-leading 54 match wins.

Her consistency has been particularly important in the race for the year-end ranking. Despite finishing runner-up at major tournaments in Indian Wells and Toronto, Rybakina continued collecting ranking points throughout the season, gradually building an advantage over her closest rivals.

There were setbacks along the way. After winning the US Open, she lost her opening match in Beijing and missed the Wuhan Open because of a leg injury. She responded by successfully defending her Ningbo title, the first time in her career she had won the same tournament in consecutive years.

That victory left her needing only one more match win to secure the year-end No. 1 ranking, and she wasted little time accomplishing that goal in Tokyo. “I’m really proud of what I’ve achieved this season and the consistency I’ve shown throughout the year,” Rybakina said in a statement released by the WTA.

She now advances to the Tokyo quarterfinals, where she will face Canada’s Leylah Fernandez in a rematch of last week’s Ningbo final. Fernandez earned her place by defeating Belgium’s Elise Mertens 6-2, 7-6 (8) on Thursday. Rybakina won their previous meeting 6-2, 6-2 and holds a 4-2 career advantage over the Canadian.

A title in Tokyo would give Rybakina her fifth trophy of 2026 and the 16th singles title of her career. Beyond Tokyo, her next major challenge will be the WTA Finals, scheduled for November 8–15 at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden in California. The tournament brings together the eight leading singles players of the season and features a round-robin format before the semifinals and final.

Rybakina enters as the defending champion after winning the 2025 WTA Finals in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. She will attempt to become the first player since Serena Williams to successfully defend the season-ending championship. She will also receive the Chris Evert WTA No. 1 Trophy during a presentation at Indian Wells, recognizing her achievement as the world’s top-ranked player at the end of the season.

Although her position at No. 1 is now secure, Rybakina still has an opportunity to finish an already historic season with another major championship.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Nosara Free Nature Trails Through Forests and Wetlands
World.content:
Nosara is best known for its beaches, surfing and laid-back lifestyle, but visitors to this popular destination on Costa Rica’s Nicoya Peninsula have another way to enjoy the outdoors without spending a dollar. A network of 18 kilometers (11.2 miles) of free walking trails connects tropical forests, wetlands, beaches and public spaces, offering a different look at one of Guanacaste’s most visited coastal communities.

The network brings together nine routes ranging from 500 meters (0.3 miles) to 4 kilometers (2.5 miles), giving you a choice between short nature walks and longer hikes through the surrounding countryside. Some trails wind through patches of tropical dry forest, while others pass streams, mangroves and areas where native vegetation is slowly reclaiming previously disturbed land.

The project is coordinated by the Nosara Civic Association (NCA), with support from Costa Rica’s National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) and the Municipality of Nicoya. Rather than operating as a traditional national park, the trail network connects several existing conservation and community areas, including the association’s private reserve, sections of the Ostional National Wildlife Refuge and the embankment along the Nosara River.

For those who want to see wildlife, the trails offer opportunities to see animals that are commonly found in this part of Costa Rica. Howler monkeys can often be heard calling from the treetops, while white-nosed coatis, deer and blue morpho butterflies are among the species that inhabit the surrounding forests. Large guanacaste trees, mangroves and other native plants provide shelter for wildlife and help maintain the natural landscape.

One of the biggest bonuses is the price. All nine routes are free to use, thanks to financial support from local hotels, businesses and families who help cover maintenance costs. That arrangement allows residents and tourists to enjoy the trails without paying the entrance fees commonly associated with Costa Rica’s national parks and private nature reserves.

The initiative also serves a practical purpose for the community. Some routes connect residential neighborhoods with public spaces, beaches and commercial areas, giving people an alternative to traveling short distances by car. That is particularly useful in Nosara, where growing tourism and residential development have increased traffic on roads that were originally built for a much smaller population.

The trail system is not a newly opened experience. Nosara has maintained a network of nature paths for years, and the latest effort brings renewed attention to how these routes are connected and maintained. Local conservation organizations have worked to preserve public access to forests and other natural areas even as the surrounding community continues to grow.

That growth has brought both opportunities and challenges. Nosara has become an international destination for surfing, yoga and wellness tourism, attracting visitors and property buyers from around the world. At the same time, new construction has placed increasing pressure on wildlife habitats, roads and public infrastructure.

Maintaining natural corridors is especially important in a region where animals move between forested areas, waterways and the coast. Keeping those habitats connected gives wildlife room to move while allowing residents and visitors to experience the environment without having to travel far from town.

The trail network has also attracted interest as an example of community planning. The Municipality of Nicoya presented the initiative at an international urban landscaping conference in San José in 2025, highlighting the value of connecting public spaces through walking routes rather than relying entirely on roads.

Anyone going is encouraged to stay on marked paths, respect protected areas and avoid disturbing wildlife. The Nosara Civic Association recommends using the trails during daylight hours, keeping noise to a minimum and taking any trash back out. Dogs are permitted on leashes, and people using bicycles are asked to give way to walkers.

Anyone planning a hike should also remember that conditions can change during the rainy season, when some paths become muddy and streams can rise. Comfortable walking shoes, drinking water and insect repellent are sensible additions for exploring the area.

For tourists who usually spend their time around Playa Guiones or Playa Pelada, the network offers a chance to see another side of Nosara. A short walk away from the busy beach areas can lead into forests filled with birdsong, monkeys and the sights and sounds of tropical Costa Rica.

For those that live in the area, the trails offer something equally important: access to green spaces in a community where development continues to reshape the landscape.

Visitors can consult the Nosara Civic Association’s official trail map for routes and guidelines before heading out. The network shows how a coastal community can make nature part of everyday life while protecting the forests and wildlife that helped make Nosara such an attractive place to begin with. And unlike many tourist activities in Costa Rica, enjoying it doesn’t cost anything.

World.title: Police recover SUV and detain two suspects after three armed men rob Orange Walk businessman of jewelry
World.content:
Police recover SUV and detain two suspects after three armed men rob Orange Walk businessman of jewelry

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have impounded a vehicle and detained two persons in connection with Wednesday evening’s armed robbery of an Orange Walk businessman, who was held up by three gunmen outside his establishment on the Belize-Corozal Road.

The robbery occurred around 6 p.m. on October 28, when an SUV approached the businessman’s premises and three armed men exited the vehicle.

According to Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith, the men proceeded to rob the businessman of several items of jewelry before fleeing the scene.

Breaking Belize News first reported the robbery on Wednesday night, after obtaining footage showing the armed men arriving in a white SUV and confronting the owner of a used clothing business along the Belize-Corozal Road.

During Thursday’s police briefing, Smith confirmed that investigators had recovered what they believe to be the SUV used in the commission of the robbery.

Two persons have also been detained as police continue their investigation.

Authorities have not disclosed the identities of those detained, the value of the stolen jewelry, or whether any of the stolen property has been recovered.

Police have not announced any formal charges in connection with the incident.

World.title: Police suspect gang involvement after 26-year-old Tafaree Sanchez shot; Third Belize City shooting on Thursday alone
World.content:
Police suspect gang involvement after 26-year-old Tafaree Sanchez shot; Third Belize City shooting on Thursday alone

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police believe gang activity may have been behind the shooting of 26-year-old Tafaree Sanchez, who was attacked by an armed individual in Belize City on Thursday.

According to Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith, the incident occurred shortly before noon on October 29, when officers on patrol heard gunshots in the vicinity of Periwinkle Street.

Investigators established that Sanchez was standing near the intersection of Periwinkle and Poinsettia Streets when an armed individual approached and fired several shots in his direction, injuring him.

Sanchez was transported for medical treatment and is reportedly in stable condition.

Smith confirmed that investigators believe the attack may have been gang-related, although police have not disclosed the circumstances leading up to the shooting or identified any suspects.

The incident was among three shootings reported in Belize City on Thursday morning, including the murder of 19-year-old Dodrick Madrill on Freedom Street and another shooting that injured 19-year-old Troydon Conorquie near a basketball court on Wagner’s Lane.

Despite the close timing of the incidents, Smith said police have not established any clear connection between the attacks.

The violence follows another shooting reported by BBN on October 28, in which 20-year-old Michael Casires and a 17-year-old minor were injured on Cairo Street. Police had previously indicated that they were monitoring increased criminal activity in that area.

Investigations into the shooting of Sanchez remain ongoing.

World.title: Gunman approaches 19-year-old near basketball court on Wagner’s Lane and shoots him
World.content:
Gunman approaches 19-year-old near basketball court on Wagner’s Lane and shoots him

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Belize City resident is recovering after he was shot by an armed individual near a basketball court on Wagner’s Lane on Thursday morning.

Police identified the victim as Troydon Conorquie, who was reportedly in the vicinity of the basketball court when he was approached by a gunman who opened fire, striking him.

According to Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith, officers were alerted to the shooting at approximately 11:35 a.m. on October 29.

Conorquie was transported for medical treatment and is listed in stable condition.

Police have not disclosed a motive for the attack or indicated whether any suspects have been identified.

The shooting occurred just hours after 19-year-old Dodrick Madrill was murdered on Freedom Street earlier that morning.

When questioned about whether Thursday’s shootings were connected, Smith said investigators had not established any clear information suggesting a link between the incidents.

Investigations continue.

World.title: Gunman exits vehicle and shoots 19-year-old Dodrick Madrill dead on Freedom Street; Police identify vehicle and seek suspects
World.content:
Gunman exits vehicle and shoots 19-year-old Dodrick Madrill dead on Freedom Street; Police identify vehicle and seek suspects

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are searching for several persons of interest following the murder of 19-year-old Dodrick Salvador Miguel Madrill, who was gunned down on Freedom Street in Belize City on Thursday morning.

According to Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith, officers patrolling the area around 7:20 a.m. on October 29 were alerted to gunshots and subsequently discovered that Madrill had been fatally wounded.

Preliminary investigations indicate that Madrill was walking along Freedom Street when a vehicle approached. An individual exited the vehicle and fired several shots at the teenager, causing his fatal injuries.

Smith confirmed that investigators have made progress in identifying the vehicle believed to have been used in the murder, as well as several persons of interest who are now being sought by police.

Madrill was previously before the courts on firearm-related charges. In February 2025, Breaking Belize News reported that Madrill, then 18, was remanded to prison after pleading guilty to possession of an unlicensed 9mm pistol and 13 live rounds of ammunition.

The firearm had been discovered during a police search at a Freedom Street residence on January 29, 2025. Madrill was charged alongside three relatives but accepted responsibility for the weapon. During the proceedings, his attorney told the court he was a first-time offender, while Madrill expressed remorse and appealed for leniency.

Asked whether Madrill had any other criminal charges on record, Smith said she had not researched his background and could not provide further information.

Police have not established a motive for Thursday’s murder, and investigations remain ongoing.

World.title: Belize promotes Nautical Tourism at Fort Lauderdale International boat show
World.content:
Belize promotes Nautical Tourism at Fort Lauderdale International boat show

By Zoila Palma: Belize is promoting its nautical tourism industry at the 67th Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show in Florida through a joint exhibition by the Belize Tourism Board (BTB) and the International Merchant Marine Registry of Belize (IMMARBE).

The partnership aims to attract yacht owners, captains, charter brokers and boating enthusiasts by showcasing Belize as both a destination for sailing and a place to register yachts under the Belizean flag. The event runs through Sunday, November 1, 2026.

At Booth 854 in the Yacht Builders Tent at the Bahia Mar Yachting Center, visitors can learn about the benefits of registering their vessels with IMMARBE and exploring Belize’s coastal and marine attractions. The initiative brings together yacht registration services and tourism promotion, with the goal of expanding opportunities within Belize’s nautical sector and attracting more visitors to its waters.

The Belize Tourism Board (BTB) says that Belize is highlighting its proximity to Florida, with nonstop flights taking approximately two hours from Miami and two and a half hours from Fort Lauderdale. Visitors are being encouraged to explore the Belize Barrier Reef, offshore atolls and coastal marinas, while also experiencing the country’s rainforests, ancient Maya sites and cultural attractions.

BTB is also promoting sport-fishing opportunities, including bonefish, permit and tarpon fishing in destinations such as San Pedro, Placencia, Turneffe Atoll and Punta Gorda, as well as offshore fishing for marlin, sailfish and tuna.

The BTB and IMMARBE partnership seeks to strengthen Belize’s position as a destination for yacht registration, cruising, fishing and marine recreation.

World.title: Team Belize competes in swimming and basketball at World Police Games 2026
World.content:
Team Belize competes in swimming and basketball at World Police Games 2026

By Zoila Palma: Team Belize continued its participation in the World Police Games 2026 in the Dominican Republic on Day 3, competing in the 50-metre freestyle swimming event and the 3v3 basketball quarterfinals.

The Belize Police Department’s delegation is representing the country at the international competition, which runs from October 26 to 30, bringing together law enforcement officers from different countries to compete in various sporting disciplines.

Three Belizean athletes competed in the 50-metre freestyle swimming event, which was conducted as a one-swim final.

The Belize Police Department congratulated the swimmers for their courage, determination and willingness to compete in a sport where Belize has limited competitive opportunities. Their participation is also being viewed as an opportunity to gain experience and encourage greater interest in swimming back home.

In 3v3 basketball, Team Belize faced the New York Police Department (NYPD) in the quarterfinals but lost 15–9, ending its campaign in the event. Despite the defeat, the department praised the players for their teamwork, resilience and determination throughout the competition, noting their efforts to represent Belize with pride on the international stage.

Team Belize will now turn its attention to the 10-kilometre run, which is scheduled as its next and final event. The department has encouraged Belizeans to continue supporting the athletes as they complete their participation in the games.

World.title: New Police Sub-Station inaugurated in San Narciso, Corozal
World.content:
New Police Sub-Station inaugurated in San Narciso, Corozal

By Zoila Palma: A new police sub-station was officially inaugurated in San Narciso Village, Corozal District, today, October 29, strengthening citizen security and law enforcement services in northern Belize. The facility is expected to serve 13 surrounding communities and improve public safety for approximately 40,000 residents across rural Corozal.

The modern facility was funded under the Belize Integral Security Programme (BISP), a broader BZ$60 million initiative supported by the Central American Bank for Economic Integration (CABEI).

The sub-station includes dedicated spaces for a domestic violence unit, secure evidence storage and private interview rooms to support police operations and the handling of sensitive cases.

The inauguration marks an investment in strengthening police infrastructure and improving access to security services for communities in the Corozal District.

World.title: Canadian authorities decline to pursue charges against Kennedy Carillo; keeps official post
World.content:
Canadian authorities decline to pursue charges against Kennedy Carillo; keeps official post

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement on the official post of Kennedy Carillo, Belize’s State Representative to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) in Montreal.

The Ministry says that it received formal communication that the Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions of Quebec declined to pursue charges against Carillo and therefore all related proceedings are concluded.

“In keeping with its commitment to the rule of law, Belize partially waived Ms. Carillo’s diplomatic immunity so that the Canadian authorities could carry out their investigation without impediment,” the Ministry said.

In addition, the Ministry informed that the Government of Belize has determined that Carillo will remain in her post as Belize’s State Representative to ICAO.

The Ministry expressed appreciation to the Canadian Authorities for their cooperation and support.

World.title: 20 things only a Hampton girl would know
World.content:
Hampton School business students at the third annual 20 Twenty growth marketing conference at ISRATECH's store in Kendal, Manchester.

One of the oldest boarding schools in Jamaica, the Malvern-based all-girls’ Hampton School was founded in 1858, two years after its all-boys brother school, Munro College.

With its motto Suma Virtute Et Humanitate (With Utmost Courage and Courtesy), the school is known for producing well-rounded ladies.

Observer Online spoke with members of the school’s alumni community, who shared fond memories of their time at the institution and some insights on things a person would only know if they attended Hampton.

1. The Quadrangle — While mainly used for devotions, the Quadrangle was the meeting place for the entire school, including teachers, who looked on from the staffroom balcony. Devotions became known as ‘quad’ and were mandatory for ladies to start the morning with the good word. With girls lined up in order of forms, the fifth formers would get exposed to the sun first as it rose higher, but the longer quad went on, especially if it’s a Monday or a Friday, just prepare for everyone to be hot!

2. The ‘sacred’ garden, stairs and blocks — The principal’s garden leading to the front office with its turtle pond was strictly out of bounds for students, and most would only walk through it if they returned after graduation. Similarly, no student was ever supposed to set foot on the steep teachers’ stairs leading to the staff room, and no lower school students should ever be seen on the sixth and fifth form blocks.

3. Blueprint — Blueprint is one of the only all-female steel bands in the country, and Hamptonians will tell you it’s the best! Tickets for the band’s annual show, Echoes, sell out quickly. Founded by the school’s long-time music teacher Alison Morris, Blueprint often performs alongside the school’s celebrated choir.

4. Seniors rule the seats — Hampton was one of the few schools in the country with a fully functional private bus system decades before the new Rural School Bus Programme, and seating charts were no joke. As an informal rule, only seniors were allowed at the back of the bus, and girls would sit in descending order.

5. Late-bugs walk! — Hampton ladies who were late to school would not have the privilege of getting dropped off near the quadrangle; rather, they would have to walk up the long hill leading to the quad in the early morning sun as penance.

6. The green tables — The green (now blue) tables and benches set up across the school grounds hold a special spot in every Hamptonian’s heart; from laughs to trading ‘sus’, they remain a cherished meeting spot for students.

7. Flaming black cake and carolling – This blazing dessert was a speciality afforded to boarding students each year during Christmas celebrations. Students would also be expected to dress warmly and go out carolling in the quiet town of Malvern where the school is situated.

8. Hamptonia — The school’s song, a celebration of its location, creation, ethos and students with its notoriously difficult high notes is learned quickly by all new students if only because it is sung so often at ‘quad’. ‘Vivat floreat Hamtonia, Crescat floreat, Hamptonia, In saecula, per multa Floreat Hamptonia.’

9. Tuck — For boarders, who would only go home every three weeks, tuck boxes were where food and snacks were stored, and students would get access to them on Wednesday evenings and weekends. Opening tuck boxes to trade cup soups, banana chips and Tiggaz was always an exciting prospect.

10.‘Substance’ and cheese/ Sugarbun and cheese — Some older Hamptonians describe it as a cornbread-like cake while other younger ladies remember a brown spiral bun, but whether you called it ‘substance’ or ‘sugarbun ’, the baked good sold with a slice of cheese was always in high demand at ‘bottom caf’ or ‘top caf’.

11. ‘Country’ side and ‘city’ side dorms – Dormitories are split down the middle with a ‘country’ side and a ‘city’ side; the city side consists of the newer pink, green and blue buildings, while the country side consists of older, more traditional dwellings including Villa, Cottage and Ivy Rota.

12. Prizegiving — Held every November, this ceremony is based on academic performance. Only girls with an average of over 75 per cent were allowed to attend along with their families, to be awarded a silver pin (for averages 75 to 84 per cent) or a gold pin (85 per cent and above) to be worn on uniforms or ties.

13. “It’s not Hampton High” (sigh) — Every Hampton girl has, at some point, had to correct someone about the name of the institution, which is Hampton School (for Girls), not Hampton High or Hampton High School, an oft-repeated mistake.

14. The Hampton Clap — Five rounds of five successive claps, a sound distinctive to Hampton and instantly recognisable to anyone who attended the institution.

15. With utmost courage and courtesy — Poise and courtesy are an important part of life at Hampton. Grace, dignity, and composure are emphasised, even after leaving school, you’re unlikely to find a Hamptonian eating while walking or walking with their hands in their pockets. Chewing gum is also not allowed and would never be found for sale in the school’s cafeteria.

16. Dear Munro… — Hampton’s brother school is a 15-minute drive away, and phones are not allowed for lower school students. In order to communicate with their friends (and beaus!) boarders would send specially folded letters delivered by the ‘day-girls’. Written on a single ‘book-leaf ’, the letters would be folded so that the paper became the envelope too, concealing the contents prior to delivery. Aside from letters, the two schools share an intrinsic bond, from excitement about supporting the all-boys school at football and track meets and Schools Challenge Quiz, shared bus routes and pandemonium when they came to visit; Hampton without Munro is like sugarbun without cheese.

17. Chapel — Religion is important for Hampton ladies, and boarders attend services in the school’s historic chapel every Sunday. The attire for these sessions is the same for all students: their bright white chapel gowns.

18. Poui trees — Gracing the grounds of Hampton School are several poui trees, the largest in front of the Information Technology labs. Once these started to bloom with their distinctive yellow flowers, it’s said it would be too late to start studying, as exams are around the corner!

19. Names we can’t forget – The people make the place, and there are some names beloved by students that have been passed down through generations: Mr Singh (hello, get away!), Mr Hall (Biology and Quiz), Ms Reid (History), Ms Quest (Art), Ms Green (Housemother), Ms King (Law), Mrs Taylor (lunch matron), Mr Dwight (cook), Maxine (ancillary staff), Mickey (groundskeeper) and of course Mr Fabian Letman (Security and logistics).

20. Finish the sentence — “Hampton Ladies are…”, “Heads up shoulders back…”, “Hampton ladies don’t set trends…” “If Gold rusts…”

– Dana Malcolm

World.title: Caribbean Cup success showcases strides in local club football, says Ricketts
World.content:
JFF President, Michael Ricketts (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Kingston, Jamaica — Portmore United and Mount Pleasant Football Academy will contest the Concacaf Caribbean Cup final in December, ensuring that the regional crown will remain in Jamaican hands for the third time in four years.

It follows Portmore’s triumph in 2019 and the successes of fellow Jamaican clubs Cavalier in 2024 and Mount Pleasant in 2025.

Portmore and Mount Pleasant, having progressed to the final, also qualified for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.

It is the first time since 2004, when Harbour View faced Tivoli Gardens, that two Jamaican teams will meet in the final of the Caribbean club competition.

The Jamaica Football Federation (JFF), in congratulating both clubs, hailed their achievements as further evidence of the progress being made by local teams on the regional stage.

JFF President Michael Ricketts said the qualification of Portmore United and Mount Pleasant was a significant accomplishment for Jamaican football.

“I would like to wholeheartedly congratulate Mount Pleasant Football Academy and Portmore United for qualifying for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup and also for getting to the final of the Caribbean Cup,” Ricketts said.

“This is the fourth year in a row that at least one Jamaican club is in the final of the Caribbean Cup, so we are very pleased by the strides made by our clubs on the island,” he noted.

“This guarantees that just like in 2024 and in 2025, we will have a Jamaican club lift the Caribbean crown come December 5,” Ricketts added

The 2026 Caribbean Cup champions will receive a bye to the Round of 16 of the 2027 Champions Cup, while the runners-up and third-place team will begin their campaigns in the first round.

The official draw for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup is scheduled for Monday, December 21, 2026.

World.title: Shift in policy
World.content:
Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith explains to individuals attending Wednesday’s post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House in St Andrew the country’s decision to abstain from voting on the United Nations resolution calling for an end to the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States against Cuba.The resolution was passed on Wednesday but with the lowest level of support in 30 years with 130 countries voting in favor, 17 against, and 25 abstentions. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

THE Opposition People’s National Party (PNP) on Wednesday flayed the Government for its decision to abstain from voting on the United Nations resolution calling for an end to the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States against Cuba, insisting that the Administration’s sudden shift in policy was an “inconsistency” which has left Jamaicans in the dark.



The outcry followed on indications by Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith during Wednesday’s post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House in St Andrew that the island was one of 25 countries that abstained on the resolution on the Cuban embargo, entitled the ‘Necessity of Ending the Economic, Commercial and Financial Embargo’, imposed by the United States against Cuba, when the vote was taken in the UN General Assembly.

Johnson Smith, who admitted that the decision was “a shift in policy”, said, “We did not vote ‘against’ because we do not support unilateral actions in accordance with the UN Charter, and we did not vote ‘for’ because it is clear that continuing to do the same thing each year to support the resolution simpliciter with no improvement in the circumstances is but in fact a deepening of the humanitarian crisis and suffering. This does not serve the benefit of the Cuban people.”

She further said the position taken is also consistent with the country’s broader perspective on multilateralism as stated in the national policy statement.

“We cannot simply continue to defend it and do the same things and believe that in a changing world it will somehow magically manifest Agenda 2030 and the systems be deemed to be fully effective. We believe that the systems need reform, and this requires us to act differently,” she said adding that an explanation of vote was also presented by Jamaica’s ambassador to the United Nations on Wednesday morning.

The vote marked a titanic shift, as historically Jamaica has been voting “yes” in favour of ending the US embargo against Cuba for over 30 years since the annual UN resolution began.

The resolution was passed with the lowest level of support in 30 years with 130 countries voting in favour, 17 against, and the 25 abstentions.

Wednesday, Opposition spokesperson on foreign, regional and diaspora affairs Senator Donna Scott-Mottley, in a statement to the media, expressed grave concern over Jamaica’s decision to abstain.

“For decades, Jamaica has joined the overwhelming majority of the international community in calling for an end to the embargo against Cuba. That position has transcended changes of Administration and has reflected our commitment to sovereignty, self-determination, and the right of nations to pursue their development free from external coercion. It is therefore deeply concerning that Jamaica should now depart from that position without any explanation to the Jamaican people,” she said.

The Opposition spokesperson pinpointed what she described as an apparent inconsistency between Jamaica’s abstention at the UN and the proceedings in the House of Representatives on Tuesday when a motion concerning Cuba, brought by the Government, was passed without objection.

“It is difficult to reconcile the position taken in our Parliament yesterday with the decision made at the United Nations today. What has changed in the space of 24 hours? If the Government has determined that Jamaica’s position on this matter should change, then it has a responsibility to explain the basis for that decision. Foreign policy cannot be conducted in a manner that leaves the Jamaican people uncertain about where their country stands,” Scott-Mottley stated.

The Opposition spokesperson, in emphasising that Jamaica’s relationship with Cuba has been characterised by decades of friendship, mutual respect, and meaningful cooperation, particularly in health and education, said the principles of sovereignty, non-interference, and respect for international law remain especially important to small states such as Jamaica.

“Jamaica is a small State, but we have never regarded that as a reason to surrender our independent voice in international affairs. Indeed, it is precisely because we are a small State that the principles of sovereignty, non-interference, and respect for international law must remain central to our foreign policy,” Scott-Mottley declared.

She said Johnson Smith must provide an immediate explanation of Jamaica’s abstention and clarify whether it signals a change in the Government’s policy towards Cuba.

“The Jamaican people are entitled to know whether this decision reflects a considered change in national policy and, if so, what circumstances have brought it about. Our international positions must be guided by principle, consistency, and the national interest,” Scott-Mottley added.

Johnson Smith on Wednesday in referencing the motion entitled, ‘Motion on the Economic and Humanitarian Situation in Cuba’, which was passed by Parliament, said it was “consistent with the perspective that a broader view of the complex situation in Cuba is needed”.

“Rather than simply calling for an end to the embargo as has been done in previous years, the motion called on the Parliament to express its deep concerns regarding the economic and humanitarian challenges confronting the Cuban people and affirms that their welfare and aspirations must remain central to efforts to address these challenges; recognise the importance of intensified economic and institutional reforms as well as respect for fundamental human rights and freedoms as well as other essential elements of sustainable development; and support constructive engagement between Cuba and the United States grounded in mutual respect and peaceful dialogue aimed at reducing economic restrictions and other barriers to international trade, finance and investment while facilitating Cuba’s progressive integration into the international economic system, rather than its isolation under the blockade,” she stated.

“These broader contexts are not included in the resolution before the United Nations and there is no scope to adjust the language of the resolution, so we therefore abstained,” the foreign affairs minister told the briefing.

She further pointed to remarks by Prime Minister Andrew Holness at the opening ceremony for Caricom heads meeting in St Kitts Nevis in July of this year, at which he expressed concern at the worsening humanitarian suffering, the impact on Cuba’s circumstances on the region, and affirmed solidarity with Cuba, but also called for US-Cuba dialogue aimed at stability and improving the circumstances of the people. Speaking then, Holness called for reform and suggested that, if, possible Caricom member states could play a constructive role in engagement and cooperation.

World.title: ‘A who mi murder?’
World.content:
Ruddock is on trial in the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston in relation to the October 17, 2021 human sacrifice-type killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James. He is accused of cutting the woman’s throat on instructions from his now deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith, seen here

A former detective testified on Wednesday that when he informed Andre Ruddock that he would be charged for murder, he inquired of the cop who the victim of that murder was, and when told he would be charged for conspiracy to murder, he demanded a lawyer.

This happened three days after he had already confessed during a caution statement at the Freeport Police Station in Montego Bay, St James, on October 18, 2021. The confession was recorded on a video in which Ruddock appeared calm while telling detectives that he was guilty of killing a woman at a church. After he gave that caution statement, detectives then proceeded to conduct a question-and-answer session to get more information out of him about the incident. The question-and-answer session was also video-recorded and Ruddock was in fact heard confessing. He then signed to written versions of the said statement as well as the answers he gave to the detectives.

Ruddock is on trial in the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston in relation to the October 17, 2021 human sacrifice-type killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James. He is accused of cutting the woman’s throat on instructions from his now deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith.

On Wednesday, the witness, who was the lead detective in the matter, told the court that Ruddock was transported from Montego Bay to Kingston on October 21, 2021 and was housed at the headquarters of the Major Investigations Division.

“I approached him whilst in custody and informed him of the charge of murder and conspiracy to murder. I cautioned him for the offence of murder and when cautioned he then said, ‘A who mi murder?’ I then charged him with murder. I cautioned him for conspiracy to murder and he said, ‘Call mi lawyer, please.’”

During the caution statement and question-and-answer session in Montego Bay, no attorney was present. However, in that interview room were two justices of the peace along with two detectives and Ruddock. The accused was not heard requesting an attorney at any point during those sessions.

Prosecutor Latoya Bernard asked the witness on Wednesday if prior to Ruddock being taken to Kingston to be charged, if the accused had complained to him about being beaten, threatened, or harmed in any way by a detective constable. The witness said no.

“He did not have any injuries on him. He did not make any complaints about being assaulted by him or any other officers,” the witness said.

The trial resumes on Friday, when the last witness for the prosecution, a pathologist, will begin testifying.

World.title: Andrew Tosh, Anthony B lead musical salute to Peter Tosh
World.content:
Son of Peter Tosh, Andrew Tosh, performs one of his father’s most famous hits during the recent staging of Tosh Fest 2026.

“I am moved by the turnout of patrons who came out to pay tribute to the legacy of my father despite the rains,” said Niambe McIntosh, head of the Peter Tosh Foundation, reflecting on a celebration that underscored the enduring power of Peter Tosh’s music and message.

That spirit of devotion was on full display at Woodstock Beach in Negril, Westmoreland, on Saturday, October 17, as artistes, cultural enthusiasts, and music lovers turned out in droves for Tosh Fest 2026, despite the inclement weather. They gathered with one purpose in mind: To honour the reggae icon while celebrating 50 years since the release of his landmark album Legalize It.

From the spiritual grounding of Nyabinghi drumming to the impassioned performances of established and emerging acts, the celebration brought Peter Tosh’s revolutionary catalogue and uncompromising principles into focus, reminding those gathered that his legacy extends far beyond the music.

Among the evening’s most moving moments was the appearance of Peter Tosh’s son, Andrew, whose striking vocal resemblance to his father lent added poignancy to renditions of some of the reggae legend’s hits.

As he delivered the familiar songs, patrons joined in, transforming the performances into a collective expression of remembrance for a man whose voice continues to resonate across generations.

Anthony B brought his own intensity to the tribute, combining high-energy delivery with the conscious messaging that has long defined his artistry. For the artiste, following in Peter Tosh’s ideological footsteps was a deliberate choice rather than a passing musical influence.

“While others were doing other things, I chose not to follow the crowd; I chose to follow Peter Tosh,” he remarked, underscoring the enduring influence of the late singer’s fearlessness and willingness to challenge convention.

The evening also featured performances and selections from poet Mutabaruka, Grammy Award-winning songwriter Medisun, conscious music act Karbon, young artistes Dahvid Slur and Aza Lineage, and selector Rory Stone Love, whose selections contributed to a programme rooted in reggae’s cultural and revolutionary traditions.

The celebration opened with a Nyabinghi drumming ceremony, paying homage to the spiritual traditions that helped shape reggae music, followed by a screening highlighting Peter Tosh’s musical legacy before the stage came alive with performances.

Yet, at the heart of the celebration was the message behind the music.

Released in 1976, Legalize It became one of the artiste’s career-defining works, boldly confronting the stigma surrounding cannabis while speaking to broader themes of personal freedom, human rights, and political advocacy. Fifty years later, its message remains inseparable from the legacy of an artiste who used his platform to challenge injustice and demand equality.

McIntosh said the anniversary provided an opportunity to revisit the album not simply as a landmark in reggae history, but as a powerful statement of freedom and human rights.

Despite the rain delaying the start of the festivities, the turnout in Peter Tosh’s home parish held particular significance for the foundation, reinforcing the importance of keeping his legacy alive in the community most closely associated with his roots.

“We made the intentional commitment to hosting the celebrations in the parish he loved,” McIntosh said, adding that the foundation anticipates Tosh Fest growing in local and international patronage, bringing economic benefits to Westmoreland residents while establishing the event as a fixture on Jamaica’s cultural and entertainment calendar.

Tosh Fest formed part of a wider week of activities celebrating the singer’s life and work. Taste of Tosh, held at the Peter Tosh Museum on October 14, brought members of the music fraternity together in tribute to the legend.

Tosh Talks, staged on October 15 and 16 at Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts and The University of the West Indies, respectively, featured academic presentations on Tosh’s life, legacy, and Legalize It, alongside panel discussions.

The commemorations continued on October 19, National Heroes’ Day and Peter Tosh’s earthstrong, with dawn Nyabinghi drumming and a blessing by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church at his resting place in Belmont, Westmoreland.

World.title: JCF calls for review of ganja law amid tensions with Rastas
World.content:
Senior Superintendent of Police Arielle Brown Blake (left), head of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Legal Affairs branch, speaks as JCF Legal Officer Jamie Brown-Bailey looks on during Wednesday’s meeting of the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Green Paper on the National Policy for Culture, Entertainment and the Creative Economy 2025–2035..

THE Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) is calling for a comprehensive review of the Dangerous Drugs Act, saying gaps and ambiguities in the law governing sacramental ganja use by Rastafarians must be addressed to clarify the community’s religious protections and guide police enforcement.

The force says uncertainty over how officers should verify religious authorisation, identify approved cultivation sites and recognise places of worship has contributed to tensions with Rastafari adherents, whose use of ganja is recognised under Jamaican law for sacramental purposes.

Head of Legal Affairs at the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), Senior Superintendent of Police Arielle Brown Blake, told the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Green Paper on the National Policy for Culture, Entertainment and the Creative Economy 2025–2035 on Wednesday that the law governing sacramental ganja use by Rastafarians should be reviewed to address ambiguities that have contributed to tensions between the community and the police.

Responding to questions from Opposition Senator Allan Bernard following the JCF’s presentation to the committee, who asked whether Jamaica should move away from criminalising ganja towards a broader legislative framework that better recognises Rastafari’s religious and cultural rights, Brown Blake said the JCF supports a comprehensive review of the legislation and a shift towards an approach that better protects the community’s constitutional rights.

“In supporting our citizens’ rights and freedoms under the constitution, I do think that it is something that we can consider moving away from, and not just can consider, should consider, instead of moving away from a criminalisation framework into a framework that allows them to take hold of the rights that the constitution enshrines them with,” Brown Blake said.

She said the force recognised that the current system had created difficulties for both police officers and members of the Rastafari community, adding that the law’s gaps and the lack of updated information on authorised spaces had contributed to disputes.

Brown Blake said the JCF had already been discussing a review of the legislation with its parent ministry, the Ministry of National Security and Peace, and the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

She added that the force supported reform that would improve Rastafari adherents’ ability to practise their religion, while allowing police to enforce the law with greater certainty.

The JCF’s submission also focused on the practical challenges officers face when determining whether ganja-related activities fall within the law’s sacramental exemptions. It called for clear guidance covering possession, cultivation, storage, transportation, smoking and events where ganja is used as a sacrament.

The force recommended that the policy explain when authorisation is required, what conditions apply and how officers should verify relevant information. It also called for clarity on identification letters or other documents issued by recognised Rastafari priests, elders and leaders, including how their authenticity should be checked.

JCF Legal Officer Jamie Brown-Bailey said the proposed policy should establish clear procedures for transferring responsibility for sacramental ganja matters from the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs to the ministry responsible for culture.

She said the transfer should identify the functions being moved, explain how decisions and authorisations would be communicated to police, and ensure that existing authorisations remain valid while outstanding applications are addressed.

The force also recommended that the responsible ministry maintain current records of designated cultivation lands, authorised individuals and organisations, and events exempted under the law.

Brown Bailey noted that the Dangerous Drugs (Designation of Land for Cultivation of Ganja for Sacramental Purposes) Order, 2023, came into operation on July 20, 2023, and was amended on August 3 that year.

She said the policy should also clarify how places of Rastafari worship are identified and registered for relevant legal purposes, with accessible procedures and clear criteria.

The debate comes amid ongoing Government consultations on Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis framework, which were announced in July following recommendations from the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce. The consultations are aimed at clarifying the rules governing sacramental organisations, approved cultivation sites, possession and transportation, as well as enforcement procedures.

The earlier discussions also followed reports of Rastafarians facing prosecution despite legal provisions for sacramental ganja use. In the case of Westmoreland resident Troy Harrison, the Crown offered no evidence on possession and dealing charges, which were subsequently dropped in the parish court. Harrison’s attorney, Marcus Goffe, told the Jamaica Observer that some police officers continued to interpret the law as they saw fit, arguing that members of the community were being unfairly targeted despite the 2015 amendments to the Dangerous Drugs Act.

On Wednesday, Committee chair and Culture Minister Olivia Grange acknowledged that practical difficulties remained and said the policy must allow Rastafari adherents to exercise their rights with certainty while enabling the police to enforce the law fairly.

“The regime, which is put in place, is defined so that Rastafari, the community, who it’s meant to be, they are meant to be the beneficiaries of this regime, can exercise their rights with certainty. And equally, the JCF can enforce with certainty,” Grange said.

Senator Bernard also questioned, during the sitting, whether the difficulties identified by the JCF pointed to a deeper problem with the continued criminalisation of ganja, rather than administrative shortcomings alone.

He asked whether the policy should address the historical relationship between the Jamaican state, the police and Rastafari, including decades of discrimination and criminalisation alleged by members of the community.

Bernard also asked whether Jamaica should consider replacing the existing prohibition-based approach with modern legislation that distinguishes ganja from more harmful controlled substances.

Brown Blake said she believed the policy should focus on protecting Rastafari’s identity and rights and look towards the future, rather than detailing past tensions.

“I am not of the view that the tensions need to be articulated in that paper, just their identity and their rights, and that those rights should be preserved. And the policy looks towards the future rather than taking a backward view. That is my personal and professional opinion,” she said.

Government Senator Kavan Gayle said the JCF’s participation would be valuable when Rastafari representatives appear before the committee, arguing that engagement could help address perceptions of conflict between the community and the police.

The committee is reviewing the Green Paper on the National Policy for Culture, Entertainment and the Creative Economy 2025–2035, which proposes transferring specific responsibilities relating to sacramental ganja use from the justice ministry to the ministry responsible for culture.

World.title: HIGHER HEIGHTS
World.content:
Australia forward Samantha Kerr (fourth left) vies for the ball with Jamaica forward Khadija Shaw (fourth right) during their France Women’s World Cup Group C match at the Alpes Stadium Grenoble, central-eastern France, on June 18, 2019. (Photo: AFP)

WITH Khadijah “Bunny” Shaw now recognised as a top three player in women’s football, former Reggae Girlz Head Coach Charlie Edwards believes the national senior women’s team should reach another level and move closer to being a serious contender at the FIFA World Cup.

Manchester City striker Shaw is still celebrating her third-place finish in the Ballon d’Or Féminin rankings on Monday at the awards ceremony in London. The achievement adds to her Women’s Super League Player of the Season, Professional Footballers Association Player of the Year and Football Writers’ Association Footballer of the Year recognition, which she claimed over the past few months for her impressive 2025/2026 season.

Shaw won her third-consecutive WSL golden boot after scoring 21 goals in 22 games, leading City to their second-ever league title. Her 35 goal contributions across all competitions were also pivotal in City’s FA Cup title win.

Along with her club objectives, Shaw is looking to lead Jamaica to a third-consecutive FIFA Women’s World Cup in November, as the Reggae Girlz takeonCostaRicaintheConcacaf W Championship quarterfinals in Texas, USA.

Edwards, who led the national team from 2007 to 2008, told the Jamaica Observer that Shaw’s Ballon d’Or ranking must be used as a stepping stone for the Reggae Girlz to better their finishes at previousWorldCupappearances.

After failing to advance from the group stage on their debut in France in 2019, Jamaica made history by reaching the round of 16 in 2023 in Australia and New Zealand, where they were narrowly beaten by Colombia.

“Now that [teams] are realising that we have a top-class player, it is going to force coaches now to start sitting down, putting game plans together to play against Jamaica,” Edwards said. “But what I’d love to see it do, though, is motivate the rest of the players in the squad to step their game up and propel Jamaica to another level.”

“The last time [at the World Cup] we made the final cut for the round of 16. I’d love to see us get back to the round of 16 and win a game or two and I really don’t think it’s far-fetched. I think we have the quality in the squad that can perform and do well, so let’s hope that this becomes the momentum or the drive behind us performing even better in the World Cup, once we get to the World Cup.”

Shawhasanincredible67goals in 49 caps for the national team and Reggae Girlz Head Coach Hubert Busby says their success in future tournaments depends heavily on their captain.

“If you look at the stats of what shemeanstoManCitywhenshe’s intheline-upandwhatshemeans for us when she’s in the line-up, they’re almost the same — they’re about a 75 win percentage, she averages a goal a game per programme. So, there’s no getting away from the impact that she has, both at Man City and with the national team,” he told the Observer.

“We’re a different team when she’s in there, there’s no doubt about it. Teams have to play us differently, we can play differently. When you have one of the best players in the world, it’s only natural that she lifts the ability, or not so much the ability, but she lifts the confidence of the group. Also, she inspires a group both on and off the pitch so she’s our leader and when she’s with us, you can see what an impact she has on the team.”

Edwards, who also won 12 women’s league titles with Barbican FC, says Shaw’s Ballon d’Or ranking shouldn’t only have animpactonthepitch.Hesaysthe Jamaica Football Federation and other stakeholders must use the accolade as a springboard to help boost women’s football locally.

“This is a momentum that Jamaica could use in a very significant way in the sense of motivating the young, talented female players in Jamaica. You’re looking at the Women’s Premier League, you’re looking at the high school [level] — this is mileage that we need to capitalise on and utilise it in a very significant way to help develop and grow what we are working so hard to accomplish,” he said.

“I personally think her accomplishment should create a lot more inspiration for the young players in Jamaica and maybe evenaroundtheCaribbean.What she has done is shine a light where nobody else in the Caribbean has ever shone light. I really hope that they capitalise on it and realise that if we can produce a Ballon d’Or third-place finisher, young girls will say if I work hard enough,IcouldbethenextBunny Shaw and that is a mentality that I want the young players to start adopting.”

World.title: ‘They are not criminals’
World.content:
An image shared by US White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt depicting people boarding a deportation flight in January 2025. (Photo: @PressSec / via X)

FOREIGN Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith has reiterated that individuals sent to Jamaica under the third-country national (TCN) agreement with the United States (US) have zero criminal antecedents other than breaching that country’s immigration laws.

Speaking during Wednesday’s Post Cabinet Press briefing at Jamaica House in St Andrew, Johnson Smith said that detail was worth repeating given apparent confusion in some quarters about the individuals transiting the country under the arrangement.

“There are countries which have agreed to receive criminals. They exist; when the United States speaks about sending criminals under TCN agreements they send them to those countries. Jamaica is not one of them. Our country has negotiated arrangements whereby persons with criminal antecedents will not be sent to Jamaica,” the foreign affairs minister stressed.

“Other than having broken the United States immigration laws, that is having illegally entered the US, they are not criminals, those are the persons who are sent to transit Jamaica. So, when the US says that under TCN agreements criminals are being sent, they are not including Jamaica,” she emphasised.

On Tuesday, United States Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin shared on social media that “through engaging in fully legal third-country removals, [and] thanks to TCN agreements with various countries, we have been able to deport some of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the US, including those who are so barbaric that even their home countries won’t take them back“.

According to Johnson Smith, the individuals are “vetted on the US side and they are vetted on the Jamaica side before they enter Jamaica”.

“Our arrangement does not agree to receive any criminals… so I just wanted to make that clear,” she added.

In the meantime, in providing an update on the 22 third country nationals sent here, Johnson Smith said compared to Tuesday when she reported that one person returned home and 21 continue to be in country with one requesting to stay, nine have since departed while departure arrangements are at various stages of processing for the remaining 11.

The first 22 TCNs – 15 males and seven females – arrived at the Norman Manley International Airport in Kingston on October 13. They are under the care of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) while arrangements are made to facilitate their return to their respective home countries.

The governments of Jamaica and the US, earlier this year, signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to facilitate the temporary reception of individuals in Jamaica before return to their countries of origin. The MOU was inked amidst US efforts to manage regional structured migration. The MOU provides for its suspension if 10 third country nationals apply to remain in Jamaica through asylum applications or other humanitarian processes. The full details of that MOU are yet to be made public.

The Jamaican Government has previously stated that under the agreement the country will not accept more than 25 individuals per fortnight.

World.title: Left-wing Berlin mayor candidate’s private Hamas remarks complicate coalition talks
World.content:
Der Spiegel asked Eralp about antisemitism within her party. Eralp acknowledged that boundaries had been crossed at some campaign events. The journalists then asked whether she was referring to Ibrahim Ibrahim, a pro-Palestinian agitator who attended the Left Party’s election-night celebration. Eralp answered “yes,” according to Der Spiegel, but later sought to remove the exchange from the interview transcript.



In private comments apparently to her assistants, inadvertently included in the returned transcript, Eralp referred to advice she said she had previously received from Berlin’s State Criminal Police Office (LKA) about publicly naming individuals linked to organized crime: “The LKA said at the time that they recommend never naming specific individuals. Back then, it was about organized crime. Now it’s about people with connections to Hamas.”

She added: “I cannot put myself and my family in danger for SPIEGEL. What do we do now? Cancel the entire interview?”

In a statement through his lawyers earlier this month, Ibrahim said he was not a member of the Left Party and said he rejected antisemitism. “I categorically reject the accusation of supporting terrorism,” his statement said.

In another private comment on the Ibrahim Ibrahim question, Eralp referred to an unidentified man by his first name, saying he “does not want to name specific individuals, neither does my husband, nor do I. He is afraid of these people, and so am I.” Der Spiegel did not identify the unknown man or explain his relationship to Eralp.

The CDU’s mayoral candidate, Stefan Evers, who placed second in the vote, said the remarks exposed a contradiction between Eralp’s concerns and her party’s position. The Left Party has called for reducing police numbers, while Evers alleged that members were working with the people Eralp feared.

“If the woman who is supposed to govern Berlin in the future is so afraid for herself and her family that she hesitates to publicly name terrorist sympathizers, while parts of her own party are working hand in hand with those very circles, then reasonable voices within the Greens and [Social Democrats] must finally pull the emergency brake,” Evers told POLITICO.

Former Berlin Mayor Michael Müller, a Social Democrat, warned that Eralp could be vulnerable to blackmail.

Eralp said Thursday she still wants to become Berlin’s mayor. Asked about the report, she told journalists: “I will not comment because private, internal information has been published. But what I can say very clearly is that, as governing mayor, I will ensure the safety of all Berliners.”

World.title: EU governments helpless as energy prices soar to four-year highs
World.content:
But at the Thursday summit, EU energy ministers broadly acknowledged that both Brussels and national capitals had run out of ideas to contain price pressures.

“We’ve exhausted most of our short-term options,” said one senior European energy official, granted anonymity to offer a candid perspective. “What’s left is really crisis management.”

For the past year, government attempts to cushion price rises with renewables schemes, windfall taxes and costly fuel subsidies have ultimately failed to contain anxieties that have since boiled over into widespread protests across the continent.

“The EU and member states don't have a magic wand to make the price increases go away,” Irish Energy Minister Darragh O’Brien, whose government holds the EU's six-month rotating presidency, told reporters. “There's a lot of measures that have been taken already in the short term. What today is about is actually seeing how we can move to more sustainable measures.”

But even crisis management is proving politically difficult. Despite calls by EU energy chief Dan Jørgensen earlier this year to encourage consumers and businesses to cut energy use, European ministers are reluctant to make such a move official policy.

“I don't want to see that we will limit people,” said Mika Nykänen, the state secretary to Finland's energy ministry. Instead, he called for policy designed to “change behavior” and reduce energy consumption less painfully. “Industry does it naturally. Normal households, normal families — they sometimes need encouragement,” he said. “For instance, subsidies to invest in the energy efficiency of houses, windows.”

World.title: Carney frames C$1.6B AI investment as national security imperative
World.content:
“Sovereignty now requires secure access to semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technology, vaccines, space-based communications and artificial intelligence,” Carney said. “Canada is taking a major step forward in artificial intelligence.”

In a pre-summit speech earlier Thursday in Montreal, von der Leyen cited April’s multi-billion dollar merger between Cohere and German counterpart Aleph Alpha as a key piece of the deepening Canada-EU cooperation that is set to unfold at Friday’s talks on AI.

“Both Canada and Europe believe this technology should serve people. So we will work together to tackle head-on the safety and security issues of runaway AI. We will develop together rules and standards and strong global governance,” she said.

Carney said Canada was making a commercial investment alongside private investors including Nvidia, Bell and Germany’s Schwarz Group.

Cohere co-founder and CEO Aidan Gomez announced the initial close of its Series E funding round on Thursday, which is targeting up to C$7 billion at a C$35.7 billion valuation.

Gomez joined Carney at Mila, the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, for the Canadian portion of the funding announcement.

World.title: Meet the front-runners to replace Lagarde
World.content:
The choices will also be influenced by horse trading over what will likely be a package deal with the opportunity to fill the two executive board seats that will be vacant in January and May.

Softly spoken de Cos

An economist with a Ph.D. from the University of Madrid, de Cos joined the Bank of Spain in 1997, moved to Frankfurt in 2004 to be an adviser to the ECB’s executive board, before returning to the Spanish central bank. He rose through the ranks to become governor, serving from 2018 to 2024. In this role he restored the Bank of Spain’s reputation after a series of missteps before and during the financial crisis.

His achievement was implicitly acknowledged by his appointment to two terms as chair of the Basel Committee for Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for bank regulation. He now runs the Bank for International Settlements, the institution often described as the central bankers’ central bank.

His style is low-key: a modest dove, meaning that he is more attentive than hawks to growth and employment alongside inflation. Still, when inflation surged in 2022, de Cos backed the ECB’s shift toward higher rates. Equally, he has little time for governments that put off essential pension system reforms, having published a sharp critique of the Pedro Sanchez government while at the Bank of Spain.

His case

De Cos has long been groomed by Lagarde’s predecessor Mario Draghi, whose voice continues to carry a heavy weight in European economic debates and may influence the preference of some countries as they mull who to place at the top of the Frankfurt institution.

As France faces mounting debt pressures, de Cos’ experience as a senior Bank of Spain economist during the eurozone crisis could convince EU governments that he is the best fit. Galo Nuño, vice dean and professor of economics at IE University and a former alternate member of the ECB governing council, called it “a huge advantage.”

World.title: Britain’s spy agency doesn’t know where thousands of its memory sticks are
World.content:
He noted that the devices “may contain IPA-related data” — which has a high level of sensitivity.

IPA-related data refers to information collected or held under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. That could include intercepted communications such as emails, texts and telephone calls, as well as information extracted from people’s computers or phones.

The report added that GCHQ currently estimates the number of devices “to be in the thousands” and is currently undergoing work so it can report how many of the devices have been confirmed as lost.

“We remain very concerned about this issue and are disappointed with the time it has taken GCHQ to investigate,” the report notes.

Last year IPCO disclosed that GCHQ and fellow intelligence agency MI5 had been unable to locate considerable numbers of storage devices, some of which potentially containing information classified as "TOP SECRET."

A GCHQ spokesperson said: “As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations.

"We recognise the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken."

World.title: Von der Leyen touts ‘associate member’ status for Canada over objections of EU capitals
World.content:
The Commission president said in her speech that talks about associate membership would focus on deeper cooperation across AI, climate and energy policy, as well as bolstering shared work between the European Commission and the Canadian government as well as “Parliament to Parliament” and “Court to Court,” a reference to the European Court of Justice and Canada’s Supreme Court.

Such a status, she said, would be open “only to our closest partners outside of Europe, who are ready to open a new frontier together — and to chart the course together, to think beyond the terms of our partnership today, toward the most ambitious vision we can build.”

Von der Leyen’s use of the term associate membership — which she first mentioned in September — is likely to rub some EU capitals the wrong way after a group of countries led by Germany objected to including a reference to the term in a joint EU-Canada statement that was seen by POLITICO and is due to be published on Friday.

After days of talks, EU countries opted for softer language to describe the two sides’ future relations, including the “Alliance for the Future” — the term used by the Canadian side — as well as an “even closer association ... short of full membership.”

EU diplomats have told POLITICO that while capitals support the broader aim of closer ties with Canada, they are wary of offering a status that has never been proposed before and whose legal contours remain undefined. Berlin had previously floated associate member status for Ukraine, including specific privileges such as observer status in the European Commission, but that effort was rejected.

Reacting to reports that EU countries would drop the “associate member” term, Carney said on Tuesday: “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature. What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians … and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose.”

World.title: Canada to join EU network of supercomputers
World.content:
The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an €8.2 billion budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers.

The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of €30 billion.

Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start.

“Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term ‘middle power’ cooperation plays in AI,” said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

But he added that for now “it doesn’t put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S.

“As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn’t result in massive buildouts will help,” he said.

World.title: Former Spanish employment minister died in train crash
World.content:
Báñez served in center-right Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy’s government from 2011 to 2018 and played a central role in Spain’s response to the eurozone crisis. During that period, she developed a warm personal relationship with Ursula von der Leyen, now European Commission president, who was then her counterpart in Germany’s labor ministry.

As employment minister, Báñez oversaw the conservative government’s controversial 2012 labor-market reform, which made it easier for companies to dismiss workers and drew fierce opposition from trade unions. The administration argued the changes would make hiring more flexible and accelerate the country’s economic recovery.

Speaking from the crash site Wednesday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared three days of national mourning. “All of Spain is mourning,” he said.

“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” Sánchez added. “We are going to get to the bottom of this, and if there has been negligence, it will be revealed, and if there have been failures in the system, we will act decisively.”

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the initial investigation suggested the collision was caused by an official at the national railway control center in Madrid who “inexplicably” instructed one high-speed train to proceed along a track where another had stalled.

Puente insisted Spain has “a safe transport system,” but acknowledged that “human action plays a role” and that, despite extensive safety regulations and protocols, “failures can occur.”

World.title: Ukraine: Russian strike kills two teenage girls in Chernihiv
World.content:
Firefighters rushed to extinguish burning cars and tackle flames and smoke pouring from damaged buildings, while emergency crews attended to victims amid scattered debris. Footage shows rescuers carrying a person into an ambulance and a body lying under a blanket near the scene.

 

The local military administration said the attack involved a Banderol cruise missile, a relatively inexpensive jet-powered weapon capable of loitering before striking its target. Businesses, homes and vehicles were damaged in the attack.
