World.title: Political analyst: ‘If Aliyev has to choose between Russia and Turkey, he will choose Russia’
World.content:
Tensions between Azerbaijan and Turkey

Political analyst Arastun Orujlu has discussed the reasons for the recent tensions between Azerbaijan and Turkey, as well as their possible consequences, in an interview with Meydan TV.

In his view, one of the main reasons for the disagreement between Baku and Ankara is Azerbaijan’s growing closeness to Israel.

– Mr Orujlu, what do you think is the main reason for the tensions that have emerged between Turkey and Azerbaijan in recent days?

– The tensions between Turkey and Azerbaijan have nothing to do with Islam or religious values. These factors serve merely as a pretext, primarily for official Baku, which uses them to provoke conflict. However, I do not rule out personal motives either. Experience shows that personal considerations often lie behind the Azerbaijani authorities’ strong reactions to the actions of other countries.

Ilham Aliyev views every issue through the prism of his personal interests. Nevertheless, I believe the current tensions are primarily political. They reflect Azerbaijan’s desire to distance itself from neighbouring countries and pursue a foreign policy oriented towards Tel Aviv and Washington. This trend is now clearly visible.

– You link these tensions to Azerbaijan’s foreign policy. In Turkey, however, people have criticised the Azerbaijani authorities both over their policies on the hijab and over their relations with Israel. To what extent does this criticism reflect political considerations? Are there genuine disagreements between Ankara and Baku on these issues?

– These are separate issues, so let me address them one by one. The hijab has always been a matter of principle for Turkey’s Justice and Development Party (AKP). For a long time, it sparked heated political debates in Turkey. The country experienced serious upheaval and a painful period over this issue. Therefore, if the current Turkish government, led by the AKP, had failed to respond to what was happening, it would undoubtedly have damaged its standing among its own voters.

In fact, the first reaction did not come from the AKP leadership. It began on Turkish social media, where journalists and individual users started protesting. Only later did the AKP leadership respond, and not at government level. The response came from Oktay Saral, an adviser to Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on party affairs.

As for Israel, the problems here are genuinely serious and entirely political. Turkey and Israel are engaged in an intense struggle for influence in the South Caucasus, the Middle East and the eastern Mediterranean. Israel is effectively seeking regional dominance. Turkey, meanwhile, believes it should take the leading role because it has stronger moral and historical claims to it, as well as greater military capabilities than Israel. Turkey’s strong reaction to the genocide unfolding in Gaza also plays an important role.

We know these problems have existed for quite some time. There is no doubt that Israel is trying to expand its influence in Central Asia through Azerbaijan and the South Caucasus. Central Asia is one of Turkey’s key foreign policy priorities, and Israel has already begun strengthening its position there. The two sides have very sharp disagreements over this issue.

It is also well known that the Azerbaijani authorities maintain exceptionally close relations with Israel. After the United States, Azerbaijan may well be Israel’s closest partner.

– In this context, how do you assess Azerbaijan’s decision to declare 31 Turkish citizens persona non grata? How might this decision affect relations between the two countries?

– As far as I can tell, Ilham Aliyev is trying to weaken Turkey’s influence in Azerbaijan. I do not mean its influence over the government, but rather Turkey’s role in Azerbaijani society. Although no opinion polls have been conducted, the situation clearly suggests that Turkey became the most popular country among Azerbaijanis after the 44-day war. Deep historical, cultural and ethnic ties explain this. Perhaps this is precisely what worries Ilham Aliyev.

He effectively signalled that a conflict was brewing at the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) congress. For some reason, many observers overlooked his remarks. In his speech, Ilham Aliyev addressed not only economic and social problems but also put forward three political arguments with an underlying message.

First, he stated directly that nobody had provided Azerbaijan with free support, and that even weapons and ammunition had been sold at global market prices. Azerbaijanis immediately thought of Turkey when they heard these words. Yet Ilham Aliyev himself has repeatedly said that Azerbaijan would have found itself in a difficult position without Turkish support. At the Victory Parade following the 44-day war, he stood alongside Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on the main podium. Now, suddenly, he has made this statement. It is quite clear that he directed it specifically at Turkey.

Second, in the same speech, he stressed the need to improve the quality of education. But if Ilham Aliyev genuinely wants to improve education, he should appoint professionals to senior positions in the sector. Today, Azerbaijan’s education system is run entirely by brokers, shopkeepers and traders who have nothing to do with education.

The third point concerned strengthening patriotic sentiment. Aliyev was effectively saying: “I will fight against Turkey, and your first homeland is Azerbaijan.” That was the message behind his words.

Look at who took part in all the disputes and conflicts that followed. They included media outlets linked to the Azerbaijani authorities, individuals, influencers, media platforms, experts and even people who call themselves opposition party leaders. They all joined the campaign. It was carefully planned.

Let me repeat: it appears that Ilham Aliyev has set himself the task of weakening Turkey’s standing and influence in Azerbaijani society. Alternatively, someone may have assigned him that task.

– We have previously seen the Azerbaijani authorities use similar rhetoric and pressure tactics when relations with other countries deteriorated. For example, when relations with Europe worsened, independent NGOs and media representatives became targets. When tensions with Russia escalated, authorities targeted the Sputnik news agency and several politicians. During tensions with Iran, they put pressure on religious believers. Now we see a similar approach towards Turkey. Which specific issue, in your view, lies at the heart of the disagreement between Azerbaijan and Turkey?

– I believe the issue concerns foreign policy alone. As I have already said, Azerbaijan is moving closer to Israel, and this process is advancing very rapidly. Moreover, Azerbaijani media have featured not merely people who support Israel, but individuals with direct links to Israeli organisations. They have accused Turkey of wrongdoing while defending the Azerbaijani authorities’ position.

For example, the English-language Azerbaijani website News.Az published an article by a certain Roman Gurevich. After reading it, I noticed that subsequent events in Azerbaijan unfolded according to the scenario described in that article. This shows that Israel has considerable influence over Azerbaijani media.

All the websites and media outlets that belong to Global Media Group also have links to Israel. People in Turkey can see this and understand that Azerbaijan is moving away from them. Relations between Israel and Turkey have deteriorated to such an extent that Azerbaijan has effectively found itself having to choose a side. Ankara can clearly see that Azerbaijan — or, more precisely, Ilham Aliyev and his family — are choosing Israel. I believe this is the main reason for the current conflict.

But what measures can they take against Turkey? Turkey has no levers of influence within Azerbaijan. Western countries, for example, once had some influence over certain NGOs and media outlets. The authorities arrested their representatives on fabricated charges. When relations with Iran deteriorated, they arrested religious believers. During tensions with Russia, they detained IT specialists whom the Azerbaijani authorities themselves had invited into the country.

Turkey has no comparable resources in Azerbaijan. Taking such steps against Turkey would also carry serious risks. Azerbaijan itself has considerable leverage in Turkey, including a network of lobbyists it funds and media resources. In addition, Azerbaijani investments in Turkey amount to around $20 billion.

Nevertheless, I do not think relations will deteriorate to the point of a complete break. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s phone call was more than an invitation. It was also a warning with a clear message: “Stop this process.” The Azerbaijani authorities had been orchestrating an extremely dirty campaign against Turkey, including at the military leadership level. Perhaps even Russia and Iran have not faced attacks this harsh.

– How might the current tensions affect the future of relations between the two countries?

– These tensions have already affected relations. The relationship between Azerbaijan and Turkey rests on several distinct foundations, unlike Azerbaijan’s ties with other countries.

The first is the relationship between the two states. The second is the personal relationship between Ilham Aliyev and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, which brings together various interests. For example, companies close to the AKP operate in Azerbaijan. The third foundation is the connection between the two societies. This is the most reliable pillar of their relationship.

The concept of “One nation, two states” is more than a slogan. The relationship between the two peoples has deep historical roots stretching back at least 120 to 130 years. This third pillar has suffered the damage.

Various groups hostile to Turkey have become more active in Azerbaijan and taken advantage of the situation. They have effectively received a signal that they can now criticise, insult and accuse Turkey. As a result, they have dealt a significant blow to the most important foundation of relations between the two countries.

– At what level will the two countries maintain their political and strategic alliance after this?

– That will depend on many external factors. The results of elections in Israel and the political situation in the United States will play an important role, for example. Recently, an American researcher published a book alleging that large sums of money had been transferred to Donald Trump’s son-in-law through Azerbaijan. This should not surprise us, because Azerbaijan conducts much of its foreign policy through lobbying and financial mechanisms.

Future developments will depend on these factors. For example, if the Republican Party loses the US midterm elections and Trump’s influence weakens, Ilham Aliyev will have to realign himself with either Russia or Turkey.

I say this with full responsibility: if Aliyev has to choose between Russia and Turkey, he will choose Russia. Around 70% of people in Azerbaijan’s current leadership have ties to Russia, while 30% have ties to Israel. There are virtually no people in the Azerbaijani leadership who look to Turkey.

Tensions between Azerbaijan and Turkey

World.title: Georgia’s new gambling tournament law raises ombudsman concerns, draws Patriarchate response
World.content:
International gambling tournaments in Georgia

Georgia‘s parliament has passed a bill in its second reading that would allow casinos to organise international gambling tournaments. The initiative provides for permits to hold such tournaments, the introduction of relevant fees and fines for violating permit conditions.

Under the bill, an “international gambling tournament” is defined as a competition organised by a casino in which the prize fund is guaranteed in advance by the organiser and at least 80% of participants are foreign nationals.

Georgian government representatives have justified the move by citing its potential to boost tourism and economic activity. However, the country’s ombudsman has criticised the fast-tracked legislative process and the lack of a proper assessment of potential social harm.

Metropolitan Anton of Vani and Baghdati said the Georgian Patriarchate would discuss the issue on 30 October and present its unified position to the public following the meeting.

What will change?

Under the bill, organisers will be exempt from paying fees for the use of gaming tables used exclusively for international gambling tournaments if the prize fund exceeds 3 million lari. Organisers will also be allowed to generate revenue from holding such tournaments.

International gambling tournaments may be held both at licensed casino premises and at other venues.

The annual permit fee for organising such tournaments will be 100,000 lari (approximately $39,000). Violating permit conditions will carry a fine of 50,000 lari, while organising or holding an international gambling tournament without the required permit will result in a fine of 150,000 lari.

According to the bill’s authors, the amendments aim to improve the legal framework governing gambling and establish clear regulations for organising international gambling tournaments.

The bill’s sponsors note that existing legislation neither defines the term “international tournament” nor contains provisions regulating such events. They argue that this creates uncertainty for businesses and regulatory authorities.

What does the ombudsman say?

Following the bill’s first reading, Georgia’s ombudsman called on parliament to halt its further consideration and adoption.

According to the ombudsman, the fast-tracked consideration of an issue affecting the public interest is particularly problematic, especially without a proper expert assessment or comprehensive analysis of potential human rights risks.

The ombudsman argues that the bill lacks an assessment of its impact on public health and a proper analysis of potential social harm and the costs of preventing it. Furthermore, relevant experts and organisations were not involved in drafting the legislation, while international experience was not taken into account.

The ombudsman also notes that the bill’s explanatory memorandum claims the proposed changes will not affect children’s rights but provides no justification for this conclusion.

“When considering bills of this kind, it is crucial to conduct a comprehensive and thorough examination of the issue, including by ensuring broad participation of experts in the relevant field,” the ombudsman stressed.

The ombudsman emphasises that discussions of the proposed amendments should not focus solely on potential economic benefits. Instead, their impact on public health and social well-being, as well as the associated risks, must be given due consideration.

What does the Patriarchate say?

According to Archpriest Andria Jaghmaidze, head of the Georgian Patriarchate’s public relations department, no prior discussions were held on the issue, and the Patriarchate itself has not yet examined the bill in detail.

Jaghmaidze noted that the Patriarchate has been actively involved in developing regulations governing gambling since 2017. He also said that the Patriarchate had reviewed the ombudsman’s position and largely shared the arguments presented.

“The Patriarchate cannot remain on the sidelines of such a process. We hope that dialogue with the bill’s sponsors will lead to a positive outcome,” Jaghmaidze said.

Metropolitan Anton of Vani and Baghdati said the Georgian Patriarchate was examining the legislative initiative concerning international gambling tournaments and preparing its official position on the matter.

According to the metropolitan, the Patriarchate will hold a discussion on 30 October to examine potential risks associated with the bill, after which it will formulate and publicly announce its unified position.

“Judging by what is apparent so far, I see certain risks. We have not yet fully examined the details — I have only heard some discussions about the issue on television. Of course, we will study the details and express our opinion. Frankly, much remains unclear, although we may still receive further explanations,” Metropolitan Anton said in an interview with InterPressNews.

He added that the Patriarchate intended to discuss the issue with government representatives and formulate its position on the bill in consultation with other senior clergy.

“Of course, we cannot remain indifferent,” the metropolitan said.

How has government policy on gambling changed?

In recent years, the Georgian Dream party’s gambling policy has primarily focused on tightening restrictions and limiting the number of people allowed to gamble.

During the early years of Georgian Dream’s rule, parliament twice rejected legislative initiatives aimed at banning gambling s and tightening regulations, in 2013 and 2019. In 2013, one of the arguments against such measures was the potential damage to the advertising industry, while Bidzina Ivanishvili warned of the risk of creating an unfavourable investment climate.

The situation changed significantly in late 2021, when parliament adopted a comprehensive package of gambling regulations. According to the government, the measures were intended to restrict access to gambling and limit its advertising.

Major restrictions came into force in March 2022:

The minimum gambling age for Georgian citizens was raised to 25.

Socially vulnerable individuals, public officials and people included in a designated register were banned from gambling.

Gambling s were banned on television, outdoors and on Georgian websites, with limited exceptions for certain forms of sponsorship.

Taxation and regulatory oversight were tightened.

The minimum gambling age for foreign nationals remained 18.

Subsequent changes revealed a distinct approach: maintaining strict restrictions for the local population while encouraging the development of the gambling industry targeting foreign customers.

According to an industry review published in June 2026, the government introduced a bill to establish preferential licensing and tax arrangements for online gambling companies targeting overseas customers.

The initiative proposed incentives for operators serving foreign markets, while maintaining a higher tax burden on the segment of the industry catering to Georgian citizens.

World.title: Armenian parliament ratifies framework agreement on Trump Route (TRIPP) project
World.content:
Armenia ratifies agreement on TRIPP project

The parliament of Armenia has ratified a framework agreement on strategic co-operation under the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project. The parties initialled the document during Marco Rubio’s visit to Yerevan on 26 May 2026 and signed the final version remotely just a few days later.

TRIPP (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) is a road that will connect Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory. The project also aims to reopen regional transport links. As a result, Armenia will gain access to third countries via Azerbaijan. For several years, Yerevan and Baku could not agree on this issue. Azerbaijan demanded a road that it called the “Zangezur corridor”. Armenia’s authorities said they were ready to reopen all transport routes but rejected the term “corridor”, arguing that it implied a loss of Armenian control and sovereign rights over the territory. The two sides reached an agreement only on 8 August in Washington. Under the deal, the road will remain under Armenia’s sovereign control, while the US will join the project as a business partner. The initiative took the name “Trump Route” after the US president, who mediated the agreement.

Parliament ratified the agreement with 63 votes in favour and 32 against. Only MPs from the ruling faction supported it.

The parliamentary opposition had announced in advance that it would vote against ratification of the framework agreement. Opposition MPs argued that the document took US and Azerbaijani interests into account but failed to protect Armenia’s interests.

MPs from the ruling faction, by contrast, believe the project will reopen regional transport links on the basis of reciprocity. In their view, this would benefit Armenia economically. The opposition disagrees, pointing to the lack of any financial assessments.

Debates on ratifying the TRIPP project began in parliament the previous day. MPs had only two hours for the discussion. However, opposition lawmakers managed to raise all their concerns and put forward several proposals.

Opposition MP on the interests of the US, Armenia and Azerbaijan

Anna Grigoryan, head of the opposition Armenia faction, noted that Armenia and the United States had signed a bilateral document concerning the implementation of TRIPP. However, she said, the document also refers to a third party — Azerbaijan.

“Azerbaijan’s interests are actually reflected in this document more directly and clearly than the interests of the Republic of Armenia.”

Grigoryan also outlined what she believes each side stands to gain from the project.

“The US gains a direct presence in the region, particularly along the border with Iran, in a strategically crucial area. Azerbaijan secures a link between Nakhchivan and the rest of the country — a goal that both Azerbaijan and Turkey have long pursued.”

When asked what Armenia stands to gain, she said the question was harder to answer.

“When the political majority tries to answer this question, the first word they use is ‘unblocking’. But on the ground, no transport links are being reopened and no borders are opening. So that part of the answer does not reflect reality.”

Should the launch of TRIPP be linked to the signing of a peace treaty?

Narek Karapetyan, leader of the opposition Strong Armenia faction, is concerned that Azerbaijan may lose its incentive to sign a peace treaty once the Trump Route begins operating.

“Azerbaijan gets what it set out to achieve, while what we are supposed to get — peace — could be postponed for five to ten years. Why would they sign a peace treaty with Armenia if they are already getting a link to Nakhchivan?”

Official Yerevan has not ruled out the possibility that the Trump Route could begin operating before Armenia and Azerbaijan sign a peace treaty.

The MP argues that the two important issues should not be treated separately. He proposes linking the implementation of the Trump Route to the signing of a peace treaty.

Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Ruben Rubinyan disagreed. In his view, it is a positive development that TRIPP can proceed without depending on the signing of a peace treaty.

“If you argue that we should not implement this project in order to secure the signing of a peace treaty, you are saying that TRIPP is a bad initiative for Armenia. But TRIPP is by no means a bad initiative for Armenia.”

The ruling party representative welcomed the prospect of “elements of peace taking shape on the ground” independently of the peace treaty. By “elements of peace”, Rubinyan means both the launch of the Trump Route and the ongoing process of delimiting and demarcating the border between the two countries.

Background to the Trump Route project

The Trump Route offers Armenia a real opportunity to reopen regional transport links. For Azerbaijan, it provides the shortest route connecting the country with Nakhchivan.

The project envisages using the railway along a stretch of about 43km through Armenian territory. A motorway, energy infrastructure and digital communications links will also run through the area.

All infrastructure located on Armenian territory will remain under Armenia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction.

The ratified framework agreement provides for the establishment of TRIPP Development Company, which will oversee the project’s development and implementation.

Initially, the US will own 74% of the company’s shares and Armenia will hold 26%. After 49 years, if the parties extend their co-operation for a further 50 years, Armenia’s stake will rise to 49%. Armenia will grant TRIPP Development Company exclusive rights to use and develop land, along with other necessary powers within the areas allocated to the project, for 49 years.

Armenia and the US still need to agree on and adopt the company’s charter and shareholder agreement.

It also remains unclear what border-crossing arrangements will apply to Armenian citizens travelling through Nakhchivan.

Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said the two sides had yet to agree on the technical details of travel through Azerbaijani territory.

“We still need to discuss these issues with Azerbaijan. They fall within the framework of Armenia–Azerbaijan relations.” Armenia–Azerbaijan relations.”

Armenia ratifies agreement on TRIPP project

World.title: ‘Like a black cat in a dark room’: Georgia’s opposition ban case enters sixth day of hearings
World.content:
What happened at Georgia’s opposition ban hearing

On 28 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the sixth day of hearings on a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties. The court is currently hearing submissions from the parties involved. On Tuesday, it heard arguments from representatives of the Coalition for Change.

The lawsuit names the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that these parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties whose aims include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments is that the parties refuse to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The United National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining Georgia’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The lawsuit holds the party responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia over South Ossetia, when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the accusations. Hearings are scheduled to continue through 30 October. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the claim, meaning at least four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

The Coalition for Change is represented in court by Nika Gvaramia, Tengo Tevzadze, Maia Kopaleishvili, Giga Lemonjava and Marika Arevadze. None of their motions was granted.

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia clashed twice with the coalition’s representatives, over their citation of a European Parliament resolution and their reference to the “Russian doctrine”.

The hearings will resume on 29 October at 11 a.m.

Judge Nadaraia: “European Parliament resolution is irrelevant to this case”

Giga Lemonjava presented an 8 October 2026 European Parliament resolution at the hearing. The resolution compared the Georgian ruling party’s bid to ban opposition parties with the Russian and Belarusian models, describing it as part of a strategy to eliminate political pluralism and turn Georgia into a one-party state.

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia interrupted the presentation and asked how the resolution was relevant to the proceedings. Lemonjava replied that it was not directly relevant to the case but that the public should be informed about it.

Nika Gvaramia commented: “Public hearings mean that participants are speaking not only to the court but also to the public.”

Nadarაიa responded: “Public hearings mean that everyone can follow the proceedings, not that someone can make political statements here.” He also reprimanded Gvaramia, saying: “You are interrupting me and disrupting the proceedings.”

Judge Nadaraia says comparison with Russia’s new doctrine is irrelevant to court proceedings

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia raised a similar objection for a second time during Giga Lemonjava’s address.

The opposition representative drew attention to two claims in the lawsuit against the opposition: that the previous government, when the United National Movement was in power, artificially restored the borders of the former South Ossetian Autonomous Region in 2007 and started the war with Russia in 2008.

Lemonjava argued that these claims closely matched Russia’s new foreign policy and security doctrine. If the court accepted them, he said, a Georgian state institution would be giving legal legitimacy to Russia’s version of events for the first time. “You need to be aware of this danger,” he told the judges.

Lemonjava also argued that giving legal force to these claims would contradict Article 78 of Georgia’s Constitution, which obliges state institutions to take all measures to ensure the country’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

Nadaraia did not allow Lemonjava to continue with this line of argument, describing his remarks as “demagoguery” and saying he had gone beyond the scope of the proceedings. The judge again told him not to interrupt.

Judge Gotsiridze: “Do not look for a black cat where there is none”

Maia Kopaleishvili, representing the Coalition for Change, and Constitutional Court judge Eva Gotsiridze previously served together on the court’s panel. At the hearing, they clashed over a section of the lawsuit concerning an alleged attempt to enter parliament.

Kopaleishvili questioned whether Gotsiridze had studied the ruling party’s lawsuit thoroughly enough. The judge called the remark inappropriate.

“Perhaps this issue simply needs clarification. Do not look for a black cat where there is none,” Gotsiridze replied.

Opposition representative Kopaleishvili tells ruling party lawyers: “You were my students”

Maia Kopaleishvili addressed Archil Gorduladze and Tornike Cheishvili, who are representing the ruling party in court.

“You said opposition parties should be banned to protect future generations from a threat. You were my students. What threat do my colleagues and I pose to the country’s future?” Kopaleishvili asked.

Gvaramia warns of return to Soviet-style one-party elections

Nika Gvaramia noted that 28 October marked 36 years since Georgia held its first multiparty elections in 1990, as the Soviet Union was breaking apart.

“And now we are going back to where we started,” he said.

Gvaramia also described as a “distorted reality” the attempt to remove Lelo opposition party leader Badri Japaridze from politics, despite his being one of the signatories of Georgia’s 1991 Act of Restoration of State Independence.

Opposition assesses court hearing

Tornike Artkmeladze, a member of Lelo, said after the hearing that banning opposition parties in a single move would destroy what had been painstakingly built over the past 35 years.

“This is preparation for the first stage of clearing the political field — first of parties, and then they will move on to banning any active political activity. Georgian Dream wants to be the only force on the political scene. But they fail to understand that there are at least a million people in this country who will not give up their freedom,” Artkmeladze said.

News in Georgia

World.title: Germany-to-Kazakhstan money transfers rise 1.92% to $2.68M in August
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 30. The total value of money transfers sent from Germany to Kazakhstan via international money transfer systems (IMTS) increased by 1.92% in August 2026 compared to July.

This is according to Trend’s calculations based on data from the National Bank of Kazakhstan (NBK).

A total of 5,760 transfers were sent from Germany to Kazakhstan in August, compared with 5,830 in July, representing a 1.20% decrease. The total value of these transfers rose to 1.209 billion tenge ($2.68 million), from 1.187 billion tenge ($2.63 million) in July.

Transfers from Germany accounted for 10% of the total value of international money transfers received in Kazakhstan in August, up from 7.4% in July.

In August 2026, Kazakhstan received a total of 31,420 inbound transfers from abroad via IMTS. The number of transfers decreased by 18.6%, while their total value declined by 23.8% compared to July. The total value of inbound transfers amounted to 12.152 billion tenge ($26.96 million).

"The main share of inbound transfers from abroad via IMTS was conducted in US dollars (accounting for 65.3% of the total number and 81.7% of the total volume of received transfers) and in Kazakh tenge (15.5% and 7.2%, respectively)," the bank’s report states.

Currency conversions are based on the National Bank of Kazakhstan exchange rate: $1 = 450.69 tenge.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 30, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 30. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 34-th day of the second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev made a post on his official Twitter account that the Azerbaijani Army liberated several villages in Jabrayil, Zangilan and Gubadli districts from the occupiers.

- President Ilham Aliyev called Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry released information on the latest situation in the frontline. The battles continued mainly in the direction of Aghdara, Khojavand and Gubadli. A list of destroyed military equipment of the Armenian Armed Forces was announced.

- A number of Azerbaijani settlements were shelled in the morning. A video of the destruction of Smerch, from which the Armenian Armed Forces shelled Barda, was released.

- Another high-ranking Armenian serviceman who committed a war crime was killed.

- Gubadli was subjected to artillery fire from the territory of Armenia.

- A video of the destruction of the missile-artillery depot of the Armenian Armed Forces was released.

- A video report from the liberated Khudafarin village of Jabrayil district was released.

- A video of the destruction of two more 'Smerch' missile systems, from which Armenian troops shelled the cities of Barda and Tartar, was released.

- Armenian armed forces launched 'Smerch' missile at Alasgarli village of Tartar.

- A video of exact strikes on the Armenian troops, as well as video of the destruction of another 'Osa' anti-aircraft missile system of Armenian troops were released.

World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 29. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and U.S. President Donald Trump held a telephone conversation.

This was stated in a press release issued by the Turkish Presidency.

According to the statement, Trump called Erdogan during a dinner attended by heads of state, organized on October 29 to mark Republic Day and the summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS).

During the conversation, Erdogan conveyed to the US president the greetings of the OTS member states’ leaders who attended the dinner. World.title: First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva attended performance of “The Seagull” (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 29. On October 29, the Maly Drama Theatre – Theatre of Europe from St. Petersburg, Russia, presented its interpretation of Anton Chekhov’s play The Seagull at the Azerbaijan State Academic Musical Theatre as part of the Baku International Arts Festival (BIAF 2026).

First Vice-President of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva attended the performance alongside her daughter Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva.

Directed by Lev Dodin, a recipient of major Russian theatre awards, including the Golden Mask, the production is regarded as one of the most acclaimed interpretations of the classic play.

The set and costume designer is Alexander Borovsky.

The cast includes Sergey Kuryshev, People’s Artist of Russia, and Honored Artists Elizaveta Boyarskaya and Igor Chernevich, among others.

This is the second edition of the Baku International Arts Festival. Running until November 8, the festival is organized with the support of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Culture. BIAF 2026 features more than 20 events, including concerts, ballet and theatre performances, film screenings, meet-and-greet sessions with artists, and masterclasses.

The festival brings together artists and creative ensembles from Azerbaijan, the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada, Russia, the United States, France and other countries.

World.title: Player prepares for World Cup after career reshaped by injury
World.content:
There are many things to prepare for when playing a game of rugby league. How to break a line, gain an edge or pick a way through a defence.

You don't prepare for one unfortunate tackle to alter the course of your life forever.

In 2020, at the age of 18, while playing for the Narellan Jets in south-west Sydney, Bryce Crane was on the wrong end of a tackle and suffered permanent nerve damage and paralysis of his right arm.

Yet, there was only one thing on his mind.

"You don't really quite understand how much something means to you until it is ripped away," Crane said.

"It's weird to think about but I didn't think about my life, I just thought that I lost the game that I loved growing up playing."

For the love of the game

Crane was told not to worry about the sport. Now, he is preparing for a home World Cup as Australia's Physical Disability Rugby League (PDRL) star fullback.

Australia will host New Zealand and England in the three-team round-robin tournament which runs from October 30 to November 8 in Sydney.

Crane (left) says it will mean a lot to once again represent Australia at the tournament. (Getty Images: Ashley Allen)

"It's really exciting to get into the World Cup; we have had a few camps with the squad, so we are getting around knowing each other," Crane said.

It will be his second PDRL World Cup after he starred for Australia in the inaugural edition in 2022.

Despite Australia failing to win a game, Crane's performances earned him a spot in the Rugby League World Cup Dream Team, which also contained players from the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.

He was the only PDRL player in the team, and was named alongside fellow Australian internationals Josh Addo-Carr, Cameron Murray and Tarryn Aiken.

Bryce Crane was a stand-out for Australia at the 2022 World Cup. (Getty Images: Ashley Allen)

In the eyes of his teammates though, he does not just contribute to the team through his talismanic play.

Luke Vella, who is also an NRL assistant coach at the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, knows the hallmarks of a top-quality player.

"He is obviously very skilful and has a great ability to play the game, but he is very humble," Vella said.

"He is also very encouraging, there is times I know Bryce can make a break or make a tackle, but he puts others before himself quite often and encourages them and supports them along with their game."

Full circle moment

The final of the tournament will be held at the Sydney Football Stadium before one of the men's semifinals, the biggest stage the game has been played on so far.

Vella was injured at the ground while playing for the Bulldogs' under-20 side in 2014, and should Australia qualify for the decider, he will step onto that field for the first time in a playing role since then.

Luke Vella is part of the Australian PDRL team. (Supplied: Lainey Gaudron)

"It's funny, I haven't really thought about it too much to be honest," Vella said.

"Obviously the stadium got knocked down and rebuilt, it is a little bit different.

"I can't really describe what the emotions would be if we get there and I get the opportunity to play on the field again."

Vella's passion for the game quickly returned after his career-ending injury, and in 2019, he was named head coach of the Bulldogs' under-20s team, giving him a chance to push players to achieve dreams of making the NRL.

After coaching the team to the Jersey Flegg Cup in 2023, he earned his promotion to the first grade coaching ranks for the 2024 season, while balancing his return to playing.

He made his international debut for Australia against New Zealand in November 2024 in Auckland.

"When I got injured at 20, I fell back in love with it because it got taken away from me," Vella said.

"I love it because my thing for coaching is to develop players and help them achieve their goals, but then the competitive side, running around, throwing the ball around, a bit of contact too.

"All things rugby league, all come back to love."

For Crane and Vella, the pride in representing their country is palpable.

"At the end of the day, I'm not just representing myself, my family, my country, but I'm also representing people with all different types of disabilities," Crane said.

"I feel like that is a pretty cool thing to do."

This content was produced for the ABC's International Day of People with Disability coverage, which runs from November 19 to December 25, 2026.

The ABC is partnering with International Day of People with Disability to recognise the contributions and achievements of the 5.5 million Australians with disability.

World.title: Is it time the CLP stops blaming Labor for the NT's problems?
World.content:
Four-hundred and forty-three.

That's how many times Country Liberal Party (CLP) politicians referred to former Territory Labor governments over the six sitting days of NT parliament this month.

Over those same six days, the current Labor opposition was mentioned by the CLP a further 137 times.

It didn't go unnoticed by Opposition Leader Selena Uibo.

"This constant rhetoric of Labor, Labor, Labor," she told parliament.

"It is like an obsession now with the CLP, to … act like it is not in government.

" There are constant excuses — ask a minister a question: 'Oh, Labor did this two years ago' — ask a minister a question: 'Oh, Labor did this four years ago'. "

Selena Uibo has been critical of the CLP government for its frequent references to Labor. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The CLP is now more than halfway through its first term of government in the NT, having trounced Territory Labor at the 2024 election.

After eight years and three chief ministers, voters not only decided a change was needed — they gave Labor a walloping.

An escalating crime problem, weak economy and a series of integrity scandals were among the reasons the party was completely wiped out in Darwin, leaving it with just four remote-based seats in a 25-member parliament.

But while Labor might reasonably be blamed for many of the Territory's problems, including record debt, gas shortages and botched major projects, is it time the CLP starts taking responsibility?

Gerard Maley referred to Labor almost 50 times during a single speech in parliament. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Remote Territorians left behind

While NT governments of both persuasions have failed to fix long-standing issues in remote communities, under the CLP's current term, violence in the bush has been a recurring theme.

So far this year, NT Police have responded to community unrest or large-scale disturbances in Maningrida, Wadeye, Tennant Creek, Palumpa, Yuendumu, Santa Teresa, Ngukurr, Numbulwar and Elliott.

The CLP is yet to properly roll out its key election promise of restoring local control to community councils, while federal parliament has heard claims the NT's remote housing target is off track.

Since June, two teenage girls, including a 16-year-old girl in Alpurrurulam, have allegedly been murdered by their older, adult partners in remote communities.

While in opposition, Aboriginal Affairs Minister Steve Edgington called for Alpurrurulam's police station to be reopened, but the CLP government now says that will not be happening.

The Alpurrurulam police station was closed during Labor's time in power. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

The nation was devastated in April when Kumanjayi Little Baby was allegedly abducted and murdered in Alice Springs, following failures in the child protection system.

Last week's report into the Department of Children and Families' conduct relating to the little girl made several similar recommendations to a coroner's report from November 2024, which minister Robyn Cahill dismissed at the time.

The North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency later criticised Ms Cahill for not listening to the coroner's recommendations.

During her speech in parliament last week on the new report, Ms Cahill said the department "could have stepped in" to remove the little girl on several occasions, but that did not occur "due to the focus and policies of the previous Labor government".

That was despite eight child protection notifications being made about Kumanjayi Little Baby while Ms Cahill was in office.

Robyn Cahill has criticised a coroner's report into the deaths of four Aboriginal women. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

Work to do on crime, health and economy

While the CLP may be credited with driving down crime statistics in most parts of the Territory, and particularly in Alice Springs, some have questioned the sustainability of its tough law-and-order approach.

Some Territorians are suspicious of the positive crime stats, saying people have stopped reporting offences.

And in some cases, the numbers are rising, with property offending around the Top End higher this August than when the CLP was elected.

Despite crime still being a key focus for the government, CLP members regularly refer to Labor’s record in parliament.

“[Victims] will not forget what it was like under Labor,” Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby said this month.

" Labor let crime go through the roof. There was a crime crisis every [parliamentary] sittings. "

Having lowered the age of criminal responsibility from 12 to 10, legislated tougher bail laws, expanded police powers and commissioned new prisons, the CLP has little room to move on the issue, with the NT the second-most imprisoned jurisdiction in the world behind El Salvador.

The territory's run down health system is another frequent problem for the government.

Youth crime has dominated the news cycle in Katherine during recent months. (Supplied: NT Police Force)

NT Health this week bungled its response to a privacy breach, while the Health Services Union said the smell of decomposing bodies at the crumbling Royal Darwin Hospital was leaving staff feeling "physically sick".

After Ms Uibo called on Mr Edgington to resign as Health Minister on Thursday, he responded through a social media post saying "we will not take lectures from a failed Territory Labor health minister".

"Labor had years to improve the Territory’s health system but had no plan and genuinely no idea," he said.

Meanwhile, the CLP likes to trumpet successes on the economic front, with the Beetaloo Basin gas field and Arafura Rare Earths mining project underway, but overall private investment is at COVID-era levels.

Arrogance creeping in, speaker says

Having previously served as a CLP deputy chief minister over a decade ago, Robyn Lambley now watches the debate in NT parliament from the speaker's chair.

The Alice Springs-based independent believes her old party is "partly justified" in hammering Labor due to the "pile of unresolved and unfunded legacy issues" it left behind.

But she said the mudslinging had just about reached its expiry date.

"It's what governments do, but after a while it becomes boring and it becomes a way to deflect from them just getting on with it and doing what Territorians want them to do," Ms Lambley said.

" It's something that they need to resolve, for the most part, and just get on with it. "

Robyn Lambley is a former CLP deputy chief minister and current independent speaker of the NT parliament. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Throughout its eight years in power, Labor were just as guilty of blaming the CLP for the NT's woes and Ms Lambley said it could be a slippery slope for the current government.

"At times I see this government behaving in quite an arrogant way, as I saw the arrogance creeping very quickly with the former Labor government," she said.

"Territorians do not like arrogant politicians."

With just one parliamentary sitting week to go in 2026, the CLP has its final opportunity this year to show it can stand on its own two feet.

World.title: Perth man, 22, charged with planning terrorist attack
World.content:
A 22-year-old Perth man has been charged with preparing for a terrorist attack.

The man, who is expected to appear in court today, was initially arrested and charged with nine offences in December.

But following further investigations by Western Australia's Joint Counter Terrorism Team, he has now been charged with one count of "acts done in preparation for, or planning, terrorist act".

Police allege the man sought help on a messaging platform about "explosive devices, military and tactical training, education, weapons manufacturing, combat techniques and fake documents" as part of planning for a terrorist attack.

World.title: Ex-Sydney childcare worker charged with 200 more abuse offences
World.content:
Notorious childcare paedophile Ashley Paul Griffith has been charged with more than 200 additional child abuse offences, allegedly committed against nearly two dozen children in NSW.

NSW Police allege Griffith sexually abused 23 children while he was working in Sydney's inner west between July 2014 and December 2017.

Griffith was extradited from Queensland to NSW on Wednesday and was arrested at Silverwater Correctional Facility on Friday morning.

The Queensland man is facing 202 offences in NSW relating to allegations of child sex abuse committed against children between the ages of one and five.

The charges include 68 counts of sexual intercourse with a child under the age of 10 and 42 counts of aggravated sexual intercourse with a child under the age of 10.

He has also been charged with 23 counts of producing child abuse material and aggravated indecent assault relating to children.

The 48-year-old has been sentenced to life in jail in Queensland after admitting to offences against 69 girls at early learning centres in Brisbane and Italy over two decades.

'Horrific' allegations

Superintendent Linda Howlett said police hope "closure" comes to the victims. (ABC News)

Child Sex Abuse Squad Commander Detective Superintendent Linda Howlett said the allegations were "horrific".

"There's no other word for it, It's actually horrific," Superintendent Howlett told reporters on Friday morning.

"We're talking about the sexual abuse of small children over an extended period of time. As you can appreciate we're charging with over 200 offences and it is quite horrific.

"Not [just] horrific for the victims, but also their families as well. So hopefully today this charging will mean that they will be able to have some sort of closure."

'Lengthy and complex investigation'

NSW Police said its State Crime Command's Child Abuse Squad and the Australian Federal Police had been investigating the Sydney-based allegations since November 2022.

It said the "lengthy and complex investigation" involved forensically examining thousands of digital files and extensive victim identification inquiries.

After his extradition earlier this week, Queensland Corrective Services said Griffith would remain in NSW until the conclusion of the legal process and would go on to serve his jail term in the state that imposed the harsher sentence.

Griffith was sentenced for his Queensland offences in 2024, where the judge ordered Griffith to serve 27 years before being eligible for parole, almost double the state's statutory minimum sentence.

The matter was heard in a in NSW bail court on Friday morning, where legal aid lawyer Bethany Burns did not apply for bail on Griffith's behalf and it was formally refused.

Griffith was not required to appear, and Judge Daniel Covington adjourned the matter until January.

World.title: Free hearing bus helping 2,000 kids faces closure as funding ends
World.content:
Jody Wright knows just how lucky he is to have a healthy teenager at home.

His son Eli had chronic middle ear problems as a child, and Mr Wright said a chance screening by a mobile hearing service in Dubbo, in western NSW, saved the boy's life.

Eli Wright has had three surgeries to remove a growth from his middle ear. (ABC Western Plains: Jen McCutcheon)

Eli was diagnosed with a cholesteatoma, a cyst that grows behind the eardrum in the middle ear, which can be fatal if left untreated.

"With his third operation … they cleaned the growth out, but it was millimetres from his brain," Mr Wright said.

"We thought we were going to lose him at times, but he's pulled through.

" If we didn't have the hearing bus, we'd have never known he had it. "

But the free service is at risk of closing.

The charity behind it has lost its main sponsor and needs to find up to $400,000 a year to keep running.

The Hear Our Heart Ear Bus Project offers free hearing tests in the western region. (ABC Western Plains: Jen McCutcheon)

Servicing the bush

The Hear Our Heart Ear Bus Project began in late 2011 as part of the Dubbo District Deaf Club.

The makeshift mobile children's ear clinic travels about 9,000 kilometres each year to more than 40 stops in Dubbo and western NSW, providing free hearing tests to pre-school and school-aged children.

Project director Donna Rees said in the past five years, "over 10,000 tests have been conducted, and half of those have been Aboriginal children within the region".

The tests have led to 310 children being referred to ear, nose and throat specialists, and 51 being fitted with a hearing device.

Previously, the allied health service had significant philanthropic backing through bequests.

The Hear Our Heart Ear Bus Project makes 40 stops a year around western NSW. (Supplied)

The Hall Foundation has been the principal sponsor since 2018, but made its last contribution in July.

The project is looking for new supporters to cover running costs of up to $400,000 a year or it risks closing by the middle of next year.

"The funding is desperately needed to continue funding the staff," Ms Rees said.

"We've literally got 10 fingers in 10 pies or more."

The Western NSW Local Health District declined to comment on the service.

Without the service, many families would have to travel to Dubbo for private screening.

"We'd never have been able to afford help, there's no way," Mr Wright said.

" It would be devastating; it would be a great loss to this community. "

The Hear Our Heart Ear Bus Project only has funding secured until mid-next year. (ABC Western Plains: Jen McCutcheon)

Closing the gap

The aim of the bus is to reduce rates of middle ear infection, or otitis media, and hearing loss among Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal children.

The condition is a major cause of long-term ear and hearing problems in Aboriginal children, with about 8,800 children affected in 2022-23, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

University of Newcastle professor and Worimi man Kelvin Kong is one of Australia's leading ear, nose and throat specialists.

He has spent his career improving access to culturally safe health care for Indigenous communities and said services like the ear bus were vital to help close the gap.

"Hearing loss is a developmental emergency," he said.

"It is so crucial that our children are hearing because if they're not hearing, they aren't learning.

"Hear Our Hearts do such an invaluable service to the community and they've been doing it for such a long time … they are incredible."

Kelvin Kong has a particular interest in treating ear diseases in Indigenous children. (Supplied)

In the case of the Wright family, it was not just Eli who received help.

"Sebby, my 7-year-old, he's got grommets through the bus and not only them two but my wife as well; she's got grommets and hearing aids from them," Mr Wright said.

"We probably would never have gotten it without the bus, we are very grateful."

Mr Wright said since the screenings, both Eli and Sebby were making inroads at school.

"They were having trouble in school, but now they are actually learning and they're coming home happy that they've gone to school so we're getting on with life now," he said.

Ms Rees said without the bus, there would be a lot of children sitting in school with hidden hearing loss undetected and undiagnosed and not meeting their potential with educational outcomes.

World.title: Patterson's failed appeal leaves few legal avenues for the mushroom killer
World.content:
Victoria's Court of Appeal has rejected Erin Patterson's appeal against her convictions, leaving the 52-year-old with few remaining legal options in her bid for freedom.

Patterson was convicted last year of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder after serving a deadly beef Wellington lunch laced with death cap mushrooms to her relatives in 2023.

A Victorian Supreme Court jury found her guilty of murdering in-laws Don and Gail Patterson, along with Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson. Mrs Wilkinson's husband, Ian Wilkinson, was gravely ill following the lunch, but survived.

Erin Patterson appeal live updates: For the latest on the court's decision to impose a harsher sentence, read our blog.

The Leongatha mother has always maintained her innocence and claimed she did not know the mushrooms in the beef Wellington were poisonous.

In August, Patterson appealed against the three life sentences handed down over the crime, but her lawyers were unsuccessful in having her conviction quashed.

Today, the Court of Appeal not only dismissed Patterson's appeal, but increased her sentence to life in prison without parole.

Could Victorian courts hear another appeal?

Former criminal barrister and legal researcher Christopher Corns said the Court of Appeal's decision meant there were very few options for Patterson to plead her case moving forward.

"The general principle in Victoria is that an appellant can only have one appeal, at least under the section that Patterson has used to appeal the conviction," Dr Corns said.

"However in 2019, reforms were introduced to permit a second appeal against conviction in very rare circumstances."

He said a second appeal could only be launched in the case of "fresh and compelling" evidence coming to light that would exonerate a convicted person.

A court sketch of convicted murderer Erin Patterson during her appeal hearing in August. (Supplied: Anita Lester)

Dr Corns said examples could be seen in the case of Nicola Gobbo, where several of her former clients were able to go to the Court of Appeal for a second time.

However, Dr Corns said in this particular case, it was unlikely to be an option.

"It seems to me that it is most unlikely that in Erin Patterson's case that she would be able to utilise that avenue, because if there was any significant evidence it would have been turned up by now by her," he said.

Could Patterson appeal to the High Court?

With that legal avenue unlikely, Dr Corns said Patterson's "only hope" was the High Court of Australia, which is able to overrule Victoria's Court of Appeal.

But Dr Corns warned the High Court of Australia was not simply another court where those convicted could "have a second go" at appealing.

"There are very strict criteria that the High Court applies to determine which cases they will hear or not," he said.

One high-profile example is Cardinal George Pell, who in 2020 had his convictions quashed by the High Court of Australia after his appeal was first rejected by the Victorian Court of Appeal.

Cardinal George Pell fought a high-profile legal battle in the High Court of Australia. (Reuters: Mark Dadswell)

Criminal law barrister Nick Papas KC said while the case of Cardinal Pell was a strong example of such an appeal, in reality it was "generally very difficult" for those appeals to be successful.

He said there needed to be a "fundamental failure" with the way Court of Appeal judges had interpreted the law for a person to have their appeal heard.

"You can't just think there was a mistake," Mr Papas said.

"It's got to be a clear-cut error that justifies an intervention over the decision of the Court of Appeal."

World.title: Dream shakes off scheduling controversy to force WNBA Finals decider
World.content:
Izzy Borlase's dream of winning a WNBA championship ring with Atlanta remains alive and kicking after the Australian rookie helped the Dream drag the finals series into a winner-takes-all decider against the Golden State Valkyries in San Francisco.

Game seven in San Francisco on Sunday (AEDT) should be a Halloween spine-tingler, with 22-year-old Borlase dreaming of joining 11 previous Australian winners of WNBA championships.

Opals ace Borlase was one of only seven players picked by Atlanta coach Karl Smesko as the Dream powered its way to an emphatic series-levelling 80-69 victory in front of a noisy near sellout crowd.

The Dream brushed aside the irritation and indignity of having to play the pivotal game six at lunchtime, rescheduled to accommodate a regular season home game for men's counterparts the Atlanta Hawks.

Izzy Borlase was used sparingly as the Dream leaned on the starting five. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

Increased interest in the Dream's finals run saw a number of games shifted to the home of the NBA's Hawks, which can accommodate 17,000 people, but game six was initially scheduled to be played at the Dream's regular-season home arena, with a 3,500-seat capacity.

After an outcry about the sixth game of the Hawks' 82-game regular season taking precedence over the Dream's push for their first title, the contest was moved to the bigger venue but forced into a 12:30pm (local time) slot to allow the Hawks to face the Cavaliers in prime time.

Borlase played very much a support role in her 12 minutes of court action as Atlanta's powerful starting line-up took control in an opening blitz and never looked back after holding a 17--point advantage at the end of the first quarter.

The Dream was sparked by Allisha Gray (23 points), Rhyne Howard (21) and another double-double from star Angel Reese, who had 14 rebounds and six assists to go with her 15 points.

Atlanta, shooting hot, only ever looked remotely rattled in the final quarter as the visitors, seeking to seal the win that would have brought them the title for the first time in just their second season, got to within eight points going into the final minute.

But there was no cause for alarm as Gray sank a three-pointer under pressure to get the home crowd roaring.

This marks the first time the WNBA Finals has gone to a decider since 2019, when the Washington Mystics beat the Connecticut Sun 3-2 in a best-of-five series.

This season marks the second time the championship has been decided in a best-of-seven format, with last year's victory by the Las Vegas Aces over the Phoenix Mercury coming via a 4-0 sweep.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP/ABC

World.title: 'Cold and calculating' Erin Patterson has sentence increased
World.content:
Erin Patterson has lost her appeal against her murder convictions over the deaths of three relatives who ate beef Wellingtons that contained death cap mushrooms.

A separate appeal by the prosecution to impose a harsher sentence was upheld and Patterson will be re-sentenced.

Erin Patterson appeal live updates: For the latest on the court's decision to impose a harsher sentence, read our blog.

The decision today by the Court of Appeal means it is likely Patterson will die in jail.

Patterson was last year sentenced to life in prison with a non-parole period of 33 years for the murders of Don and Gail Patterson, and Heather Wilkinson, along with the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian.

She had mounted an appeal on seven grounds, all but two of which were dismissed by the Court of Appeal judges.

The appeal was heard on the remaining two grounds, but was dismissed.

Patterson, who watched the proceedings on a video link from a women's prison, sat back in her seat and appeared to stare blankly when the decision was announced.

It is unclear whether her legal team will mount a challenge in the High Court.

She is being held in the maximum security wing of the Dame Phyllis Frost women's prison.

Offending was 'careful and deliberate'

The Court of Appeal judges upheld prosecutors' appeal against the non-parole period that was included in her original sentence.

Delivering the court's judgment, Justice Stephen McLeish said the crimes involved "shocking criminality" and Patterson's conduct deserved to be "denounced in the strongest terms".

It is unclear whether Patterson's legal team will mount a challenge in the High Court. (ABC News: Anita Lester)

He said Patterson's decision to plan and then poison her relatives with a beef Wellington laced with poisonous mushrooms involved an "elaborate series of deceptions".

"The offending was carefully planned and deliberate," he said.

Justice McLeish described Patterson's crimes as "extraordinarily cold and calculating."

"The applicant's intent to murder all four victims was sustained for nearly three weeks from when she invited them to lunch, through to preparing and serving the poisoned meal and then throughout the protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted," he said.

It was therefore inappropriate for parole to be an option, he said.

What happens next in Erin Patterson's case? Victoria's highest court has upheld Erin Patterson's convictions for the murder of three relatives and the attempted murder of a fourth. Few legal options now remain for the killer.

The decision to reject Patterson's appeal leaves her with few legal options, including appealing to the High Court of Australia.

Patterson's leave to appeal was granted by the judges on two of the seven grounds her lawyers put forward in arguments.

The first of those grounds related to a mistake that meant the jury hearing her case stayed at the same hotel as a police witness.

However, the appeal judges said today there was no reason to think the jury wouldn't have carried out its sworn duty.

The second related to the use of expert evidence derived from Patterson's mobile phone data used by the prosecution to show she had visited areas identified in internet posts as death cap mushroom sites.

The court decided that this evidence was admissible as part of the wider circumstantial case put forward by the prosecution.

World.title: Sam Wood’s ‘party lifestyle, drug use’ aired as he makes fresh bid for bail
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Sam Wood’s ‘party lifestyle, drug use’ aired as he makes fresh bid for bail Cloe Read October 30, 2026 — 1:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Former reality television star Sam Wood, accused of strangling and assaulting his wife Snezana, has made a fresh bid for bail, with a court hearing of his alleged drug use and “party lifestyle”. The former The Bachelor contestant allegedly attacked Ms Wood during a holiday in Noosa on Queensland’s Sunshine Coast earlier this month. Sam Wood met his future wife Snezana on The Bachelor Australia in 2015. Channel Ten Wood, 46, was charged with strangulation and assault occasioning bodily harm and has been in custody since his arrest on October 3, with his first bail application denied days later. The fitness guru, who dropped his lawyer Mathew Cuskelly in favour of barrister Paula Morreau KC, has made a new bail application in the higher Supreme Court.



In a hearing on Friday, Morreau detailed the pair’s relationship, saying it had been “suffering with significant stressors and more frequent confrontations”. She referred to material before the court that detailed Wood’s alleged drug and alcohol use, and a “party lifestyle”, but there was no suggestion he suffered from addiction. Andrew Wood (centre), the father of Sam Wood, is seen arriving at the Brisbane Supreme Court on Friday. AAPIMAGE She said Wood, who had struggled with anger, would usually leave to avoid confrontation, and that willingness was an important component to assess his risk for his release. “He is a man who has never before faced a charge,” Morreau said, adding he had no history of domestic violence.



She conceded the offences were serious, but there was no unacceptable risk to his release. She said there was a prospect that denying his release would mean he would serve longer in remand than he would if convicted. Morreau told the court Wood’s trial would probably not be until as early as late 2027. Sam Wood has been behind bars since October 3 on domestic violence charges. The barrister pointed to an earlier complaint by Ms Wood in 2021 referenced in prosecution documents. She said the allegations were untested, and they did not have the same support of a witness or medical attention. Putting forward his proposed addresses if released on bail, Morreau said Wood could reside in Tasmania, where his children would be able to visit him.



She also said there could be an alternative address in Queensland if the prosecution preferred. Morreau said Wood was a recognisable man, and the risk he would travel to Melbourne undetected was remote. Proposed bail conditions included that Wood would report to police three times a week, and he would attend a men’s behavioural change program. Wood’s charges have a maximum term of imprisonment of seven years, Morreau told the court. But, she added, Wood would probably face a two-year sentence if convicted, which the prosecution had also agreed. In opposing Wood’s release, Crown prosecutor Jessica Guy said the force to Ms Wood’s neck was for an extended period of time, and she had been unable to breathe or speak. Wood did not stop when she tried to free herself, and her head was banged on the floor, Guy said.



She said Wood’s conduct had escalated since the 2021 incident in Victoria. She pointed to choking being a predictive indicator of escalation in domestic violence offending. Details of the allegations were revealed in court earlier this month during the unsuccessful bail hearing. The court heard Wood pushed his wife into a wardrobe, before the argument spilled into the hallway, where Wood’s stepdaughter, Eve Markoski-Wood, told him to stop yelling. He then allegedly approached Eve aggressively, prompting Ms Wood to intervene, placing herself in Wood’s path, telling him to leave her daughter alone. He allegedly grabbed his wife by the throat with one hand, throwing her against the wall and striking her head. The court was told Wood then threw her to the floor, holding her throat, gripping tighter and preventing her from breathing.



Ms Wood tried to free herself, the court heard, but was unable to do so, telling police she thought her husband was “going to kill her”. The court heard Wood had denied strangling or causing bodily harm to his wife. The hearing continues.
