World.title: This is a show for anyone who has experienced loss of any kind
World.content:
CultureLive reviewsMelbourne live reviews This is a show for anyone who has experienced loss of any kind Thuy On and Andrew Fuhrmann October 30, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Key points THEATRE: Before I Forget by Kamarra Bell-Wykes is centred on early-onset dementia

DANCE: Orbit at Dancehouse kicks off with Agitato and Charcoal

THEATRE

Before I Forget ★★★★

Melbourne Theatre Company, Fairfax Studio - Arts Centre Melbourne, until November 28 The debilitating creep of early-onset dementia is the focus of this new play, developed through MTC’s Next Stage writers’ program, a commissioning and residency initiative that seeks to foster emerging theatre-makers. Loosely based on lived experiences, Before I Forget is the work of Kamarra Bell-Wykes, whose capacity here is as both the playwright and the director. Melodie Reynolds-Diarra, Roxanne McDonald and Tyallah Bullock (left to right). Pia Johnson It paints a portrait of a woman, once vital and vibrant, who’s losing the contours of her days. Faith Wells (Roxanne McDonald), a renowned First Nations academic and linguist, once had a wicked tongue and a fierce intellect, but her language – and indeed her life skills – are now mired in forgetfulness and confusion. While Faith is in the middle of giving a lecture, she becomes disoriented and hears voices. The play begins with her losing her keys and handbag, and as the disease takes a firmer grip, she fails to recognise her own grandchild Hope (Tyallah Bullock) and mistakes her son Jet (Nathan Wright) for her own father.



But when plans are discussed to relocate her into an aged care home, Faith rages and refuses to go gently into that institution, much to the chagrin of her daughter Karma (Melodie Reynolds-Diarra). McDonald is brilliantly convincing as the erstwhile leader, activist and trailblazer who now needs round-the-clock care for basic daily tasks. There is a mischievousness and playfulness to her even as she battles both memory fog and her daughter’s and granddaughter’s ministrations, and it’s this humour that leavens the otherwise serious intent of the play. Before I Forget explores loss of all kinds. Pia Johnson Also funny in a feckless way is Wright, who makes a brief appearance as the son Jet, who loves but leaves, and is unable to do any actual caring for his mother. We’re reminded of how much caregiving is relegated to the domain of women. To afford the fees for residential care, Faith’s home has been sold – its new owners are days away from moving in. The set features two beds on either side of a couch, with an ominous “For Sale” sign in the far corner. There are documents and folders in disarray on the floor as Karma and Hope try to pack away Faith’s research papers.



What’s particularly egregious is that for a linguist whose job and passion was to reclaim and restore Indigenous languages, Faith’s memory loss means aspects of her own life have disappeared – her own cultural legacy compromised. Editor's pick Visual art Whistleblowers, children and stateless men: The artist telling stories one image at a time Before I Forget explores three generations of women grappling with change and transition. As the dutiful daughter trying to manage the household, Reynolds-Diarra is a tightly coiled ball of anger and frustration, while Bullock is sweetly earnest as she teases and plays with her grandmother, hoping for connection. Sometimes she’s rewarded by moments of lucidity. Tonally, the play’s emotional arc moves back and forth from fear, hurt, outrage, and tenderness. The play is all about loss – not just of identity, but of a home, independence, and dignity. But Bell-Wykes has a broader reach in her remit than just the interpersonal interactions of one family – one that reaches back into the annals. The living wake, a eulogy that the three women conduct to acknowledge each other’s strengths and to celebrate each other, is a balm to counter the fact that, as Faith points out, there were no burials for ancestors massacred by colonialists. Before I Forget is as much a story about remembrance and honouring the Indigenous matrilineal line as it is about ageing, illness and death. The set opens up to reveal the luminous skyline and a scattering of stars, offering us a greater sense of spirituality and transcendence that goes beyond earthly mortality.

Reviewed by Thuy On



DANCE

Orbit Week 1: Charcoal and Agitato ★★★★

Dancehouse, Carlton, until October 31 It’s a familiar lament: contemporary dance rarely travels in Australia. We almost never get the chance to see the work of independent dance artists based in other cities. For that reason, a new national touring initiative called Orbit should be welcomed. Charcoal by Keia McGrady Gregory Lorenzutti The program comprises two double bills, which tour through five venues across Victoria, South Australia and NSW. The first program opens with Charcoal by emerging choreographer Keia McGrady, from south-east Queensland. This delicate, sensitively shaped duet responds to the regenerative power of cultural burning: the First Nations practice of using low fires to manage Country.



Crouched on a large sheet, the dancers crush sticks of charcoal and scrawl loose forms, suggesting a landscape viewed from above. As if rising from the ashes, they gradually stretch and unfold, then quicken, with fleeting animal imagery emerging as the work reaches its climax. McGrady and Amelia Jean O’Leary give earnest, attentive performances, sustaining the duet’s gentle, nurturing atmosphere as its movement slowly gathers intensity. Agitato by Jo Lloyd Gregory Lorenzutti The progression from quiet beginnings to fuller activity is straightforward but handled with assurance. McGrady focuses on developing her theme, allowing the simple image of regeneration to progress with clarity. The second piece, Jo Lloyd’s Agitato, a standout work from last year, responds to a short, rackety piano piece by Fanny Mendelssohn, as remixed by Duane Morrison, with whirling, spasming figures.



Yet it also opens chasms within the music. The four dancers seem to enter these fissures, discovering strange little scenes and fleeting, almost painterly arrangements amid the tumult. Related Article Melbourne live reviews Betrayal and good-intentions gone wrong: Eliza tells the story of the world’s first chatbot With two new dancers in the quartet, Agitato seems an even greater achievement on second viewing: an epic of churning anxieties. This is the sort of gripping theatre that I think vindicates Orbit’s ambitions. It’s fascinating to think what audiences elsewhere make of it.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: I first met Patrick Stewart in 1988 and many times since. I was dazzled by him
World.content:
CultureTV & radioVale I first met Patrick Stewart in 1988 and many times since. I was dazzled by him Michael Idato October 30, 2026 — 12:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Living as we do, roughly an adult human’s lifespan since the invention of modern celebrity, the daily headlines invariably include the death of someone famous. In the last few days alone, we have lost German actor Elke Sommer, American actor Susan Saint James and Star Trek actor Walter Koenig. But fans of Star Trek have taken a double hit; Sir Patrick Stewart, who played the debonair Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation, has also died. And while it’s difficult to unpick why one death affects some people more than another, that Picard’s Star Trek was technically a generation younger than Koenig’s seems to tap close to why Stewart’s death is so deeply felt. Actor Patrick Stewart. AP In one sense, Stewart’s life is easily captured: a dashing science fiction hero, lent a natural elegance by his perfect British baritone voice. He ran contrary to Hollywood convention – a bald, foreign replacement for his 1960s counterpart, the blonder, easier-on-the-eye Captain Kirk – but he had natural cinematic magnetism. He was an actor’s actor. And the camera loved him.



Related Article Updated

Vale ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86 But the truth of Stewart’s life is so much more complex. Indeed, the depth of his accomplishments on the stage eclipse his television fame, even though the latter will always dominate discussion of his career. And his background - surviving poverty, and a shockingly violent upbringing - gave him an emotional complexity that he could never quite resolve. Born and raised in Mirfield, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, in England, his father was an army veteran who suffered from PTSD, and returned from combat prone to fits of violence. The difficulties of his childhood, and his inability to protect his mother, would haunt Stewart in later years. He devoted time, energy and money to domestic violence organisations. But resolution for his own feelings would elude him. And though he came to the television screen later in his career – he was 47 when he signed on to Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1987 – he seemed somehow ageless. Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. Paramount Pictures



“Actors live in a world of make believe,” he told me, in one of our many conversations over the years. “We live in a giant nursery where we get to play very expensive games. But although they’re games, our objective is to make them appear real and truthful. So, ageing in the conventional sense, I don’t think, quite applies to us because our job is becoming other people, taking on another life. “There are times for me when ageing, believe me, I know how it feels,” he added. “Look at these fingers, I was told by a rheumatologist the other day I have poster boy arthritic hands. I could become the poster boy for arthritis.” We both laughed. “But at times, it feels like a role that I’m playing. A lifetime’s role.” I first met Patrick Stewart on the set of the 1988 made-for-television adaptation of Moby Dick. He was playing Captain Ahab, a man consumed by a destructive obsession with an elusive whale, whose choice brought the safety of his crew, and his self-destruction, into conflict. Curiously, like the enduring internal pain of his powerlessness as a child in the face of paternal violence, these were characters whose characteristics he managed to twist into later performances. Captain Picard would channel Captain Ahab, in a later Star Trek film. And Stewart’s powerlessness as a child, and unspoken grief over the loss of his mother, would resurface in sequel series, Picard. Old soldiers never die … Stewart’s Picard with Riker (Jonathan Frakes) and Seven of Nine (Jeri Ryan) in the sequel, Picard. Paramount+



I was dazzled by him. And he, I suspect, was charmed by a journalist whose first questions were not about either Moby Dick or Star Trek, but who went straight to a beloved childhood classic, Little Lord Fauntleroy (1980), with Sir Alec Guinness, and Excalibur (1981), John Boorman’s spectacular Arthurian masterpiece, in which Stewart played Guinevere’s father, Leodegrance of Cameliard. The most enduring role of his career, was doubtless the diplomatic and debonair Captain Picard. The Next Generation was a reboot, but its characters, and their storied lives, would build an expanded universe far more complex than their 1960s predecessors. Editor's pick Review How Patrick Stewart went from the Bard to where no man has gone before Actor and character aged together like a fine wine, I suggested to him once, and he agreed. “It’s a good analogy, the wine analogy,” he said. “It does feel like that. There came a point quite early in the seven years when we were shooting the series when I didn’t have to sit in my trailer and think myself into the role. I was him. So it became second nature and I didn’t have to examine, necessarily, his background to determine how to play a scene. It was spontaneous and instinctive.” Of his upbringing, Stewart always seemed both unsentimental and deeply affected. Nor was he ever complacent about either what Hollywood offered him, or what he might achieve in it. Indeed, he began his career with the lowest of expectation.



“I think my background and what I’d learned about being a professional actor had prepared me for the fact that there was no promise, there was only possibility,” Stewart told me. “And the odds were very bad for it being a successful career. At that time, I was content to just be working.” Graduating from drama school, he landed neither a manager, nor an agent. “I was firmly convinced that my career was over before it had begun,” he recalled. “I actually went back to my parents’ home, I had no money and I thought, ‘well, I had my shot and that was it’. It didn’t quite turn out like that, and one of the reasons it didn’t was pure good fortune and quite a lot of hard work.” Patrick Stewart with his wife, Sunny Ozell, in 2020. Getty Images In 2001, Stewart was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE). In 2010, he was made a Knight Bachelor by Queen Elizabeth II for services to drama. In a richly storied career, he was nominated for Emmy, Tony and Golden Globe awards. He won a Grammy, for the spoken word album Prokofiev: Peter and the Wolf. He won Olivier awards for his stage performances in Antony and Cleopatra and Hamlet. And he won a Drama Desk award for his one-man stage adaptation of A Christmas Carol, which he wrote, and starred in.



Related Article Vale Star Trek actor Walter Koenig dies aged 90 In a curious footnote, Stewart’s relationship with Charles Dickens’ iconic work would become almost as all-consuming as his Star Trek fame. It was later staged at the Old Vic in London and the Marquis Theatre on Broadway, but in a powerful demonstration of the ties that bind, and his connection to his childhood, complex as it was, the play opened with a single performance, in the parish church of Stewart’s birthplace, Mirfield, West Yorkshire. Acting, he later said to me, “is a job I have always loved. I’ve loved it passionately and been, and felt, lucky and very happy to be doing it under any circumstances. That I was acting at all, wherever I was, whether I was being paid well or poorly for it, didn’t matter. I was doing the work. Don’t tell the studios this, or my agent, but I would’ve done it without being paid for a long period of time.” Stewart is survived by his wife, American singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell, whom he married in 2013, and again in 2020, and two children, a son, Daniel, and a daughter, Sophia, from his first marriage, to British theatre actor and dancer Sheila Falconer. World.title: ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86
World.content:
Updated CultureCelebrityVale ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86 Kayla Olaya and Nell Geraets Updated October 30, 2026 — 12:50pm ,first published October 30, 2026 — 7:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Patrick Stewart, the classically trained stage actor who scaled the Shakespearean canon and added gravitas to a Star Trek franchise and X-Men films, has died. He was 86. Stewart, who was knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his Los Angeles home after being diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, according to a statement on his X account. Patrick Stewart, best known for his Star Trek performances and pictured in the backyard of his Los Angeles home in 2023, died on Wednesday (Thursday AEDT). “We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife, Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” it said. His death comes just days after Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, in the original Star Trek series and seven subsequent feature films, died at the age of 90.



While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the X-Men and Star Trek: The Next Generation series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career on stage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of A Christmas Carol and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land and Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot in repertoire with his good friend Sir Ian McKellen. Patrick Stewart and Ian McKellen worked together for more than 50 years and were fast friends. Ilya S. Savenok/Getty McKellen became close to Stewart while working on 2000 release X-Men, eventually officiating his wedding to Sunny Ozell in 2013. He shared a moving tribute to his long-time friend on Instagram, reflecting on the Yorkshire-born performer’s journey from stage to screen and his wide-ranging impact on the arts. “We first met as ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago, but we weren’t in the same productions. My first strong memory was a few years later, meeting him in the street in central London when he told me about an offer to take over a leading part in Star Trek,” McKellen wrote.



“ ‘But Patrick think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk – getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?’ Well, he took the risk, and thank goodness for us all that he did, for not just his devoted Trekkies but film and theatre audiences who marvelled at his using international celebrity to star in a string of cinema successes (X-Men of course) and in great classical plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Peter Shaffer, Pinter and Beckett at Stratford-upon-Avon, in London’s West End and on Broadway. “America was his adopted home, where he met his adored Sunny who has cared for him through sickness and health, through thick and thin. But he never forsook his origins: and the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as Chancellor of Huddersfield University in Yorkshire … He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.” McKellen ended his tribute by noting that Stewart’s “farewell performance” would be seen in December upon the release of Avengers: Doomsday, in which he plays Professor X. Stewart became an actor at 18, gaining acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company beginning in the 1960s. He spent decades working on stage and performing various roles in UK TV productions.



But it wasn’t until he was cast in Star Trek: The Next Generation from 1987 to 1994 that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s. He leaves behind his wife Sunny Ozell and two adult children – son Daniel Stewart and daughter Sophie Stewart, whom he shares with his first wife, Sheila Falconer. Patrick Stewart (front row, second from left) with the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation. William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk alongside Stewart in Star Trek: Generations (1994), honoured the renowned performer on social media as “a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor”. “What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote on Facebook. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.”



Fellow Star Trek actor George Takei, who played Sulu in the original 1960s TV series, paid tribute on social media dedicated to fans across the world, “mourning the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend”. “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before,” Takei wrote on Bluesky. “He inspired a whole next generation of stargazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.” Australian star Hugh Jackman also paid tribute to Stewart, noting the time they had spent together filming the X-Men films. “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days,” the Wolverine star wrote on Instagram, paired with two photos of the actors arm-in-arm.



Born in 1940 in the Yorkshire town of Mirfield in England’s north in coal-mining country, Stewart grew up in the era of ration ­coupons, lamplighters in the streets and once-a-week baths in a zinc tub in front of the coal stove, he told Good Weekend in 2023. His father was demobbed from the army following the end of World War II when he was five. Stewart recalls him returning hardened and abusive towards his wife after bouts of drinking. Books and then films became an escape for the young Stewart. Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation. MEDIANET In his teenage years, he took acting courses, threw himself into amateur theatre and, at 17, won a place at the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. The local council gave him a full scholarship. Stewart went on to marry choreographer Sheila Falconer, have two ­children and a 20-year stage, film and TV career – until he was randomly summoned to the United States to meet Gene Roddenberry, the creator of Star Trek.



Related Article Good Weekend ‘I am just sad a lot of the time’: A former Star Trek captain on his life on earth A producer had spotted Stewart lecturing American students on William Shakespeare and suggested him for a role in a new series of the ­franchise, The Next Generation. According to Stewart, the meeting didn’t go well, and Roddenberry was not a fan. So it came as a shock when he was recalled to audition for Star Trek: The Next Generation and then cast as captain of the Enterprise. “During ­filming [Roddenberry] would come down from his comfortable ­office and sit in his director’s chair, arms folded, ­frowning at me and clearly thinking, ‘But I didn’t want him; what’s he doing in my show?’ ” Stewart told Good Weekend. The network salary also changed things for him.



“The cast were all buying cars: Mercedes and Audis. I bought a Honda Prelude, to the dismay of my fellow ­actors. [Co-star] Jonathan Frakes accused me of having a ­poverty mentality.” Head of Marvel Studios Kevin Feige reminisced on the first time he met Stewart while on the set of the first X-Men film, describing it as a moment he will never forget. Actors James McAvoy, Patrick Stewart, and Hugh Jackman from X-Men: Days Of Future Past, in 2014. Getty “After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe – and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas. Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humour,” the studio head said in a statement shared with The Hollywood Reporter. “It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him … His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.”



Seth MacFarlane, who worked with Stewart on comedy productions like Family Guy, Ted and American Dad!, said he was a rare actor who “could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful”. “I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day one of a new film,” MacFarlane wrote on Instagram. “He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, ‘Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed.’ We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet.” Stewart also acted in Star Trek: Picard, a sequel to The Next Generation, featuring Picard in his post-Starfleet retirement and drawing in characters from other Star Trek shows, notably Seven of Nine (Jeri Ryan) from Star Trek: Voyager. “I will never say goodbye to Jean-Luc Picard, to his ideals, to his struggles to create an honest world, an unprejudiced world. That will always remain inside me in the same way that other roles have,” Stewart told this masthead in 2022.



With Reuters, AP Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: Annie Cannon-Brookes’ paddock-to-plate precinct under investigation
World.content:
BusinessEntrepreneurshipDevelopment Annie Cannon-Brookes’ paddock-to-plate precinct under investigation Lucy Macken and Patrick Begley Updated October 30, 2026 — 12:49pm ,first published 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Billionaire Annie Cannon-Brookes’ bid to more than double the capacity of her highly successful farm gate and restaurant precinct in the NSW Southern Highlands has hit a major snag. The tourist destination is already facing dozens of submissions from residents citing heavy traffic on country roads, parking problems and safety risks around the nearby rail line since it opened at Easter. Three Blue Ducks founders Darren Robertson, Annie Cannon-Brookes and Andy Allen at Burradoo. Locals have dubbed the traffic monitors and signage around the farm as Burradoo’s “Checkpoint Charlie”. Now the venture is under investigation by the local council after using “farm gate” laws introduced in 2022 to obtain fast-tracked development consent.



Wingecarribee Shire Council confirmed the investigation into Burradoo Park Farm’s compliance in a statement to this masthead on Thursday, adding “no further comment will be provided”. The 250-hectare property just outside Bowral is home to the award-winning Three Blue Ducks restaurant, plus a Three Blue Ducks bakery and cafe, an orchard, a market garden, and cattle and sheep grazing, making it arguably the premier tourist venue in the sleepy township. The Three Blue Ducks restaurant won the New Restaurant of the Year award before a 500-strong crowd on Monday at the Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide awards on Monday. The Burradoo Farm precinct. Wolter Peeters The site was consolidated from a handful of separate properties five years ago, and reimagined by Cannon-Brookes after she separated from her husband, Atlassian co-founder Mike Cannon-Brookes, in 2023. Their divorce settlement is yet to be finalised.



Burradoo Park Farm took advantage of new planning laws passed by the NSW government that made it easier for commercial farmers to earn extra income through various forms of agritourism, by-passing the need for development approval from council. Consent was granted to the farm-gate operation, which lies within 250 metres of both neighbouring homes and a rail line, raising questions as to whether it complied with the legislation. “It’s such a joke to call this a farm-gate operation,” said local David Coulthard. “It’s so much bigger than that. This is a farm gate on an industrial scale.” Local councillor Rachel Russell said: “Theoretically this fast-tracked farm-gate legislation was to help struggling farmers. How is it actually being used? Could we need just a couple more checks and balances to get it right for everyone?”



A private certifier granted Burradoo Park Farm complying development consent to become a farm gate in 2024, with a proposed gelato shop, market-garden cooking area, bakery and restaurant. The precinct has proven to be an unmitigated success for its billionaire owner. Related Article Good Food Guide ‘This is very special to us’: Three Blue Ducks wins historic first Good Food Guide award Since the day it opened in April, the crowds have exceeded expectations, prompting management to introduce a ticketing system to try to stagger visitors over the day, traffic control wardens on weekends, and additional parking. Many locals stressed they were not against the existing farm-gate operation, but were taken by surprise by the impact it has had on the local area.



“We feel invaded every weekend,” resident Peter Morris said. “It’s kind of cool to have this venue on your [back] step, and it’s certainly become a major destination for people across NSW, but there’s also been a fair amount of resentment from locals when they discovered it had already opened, and brought significantly increased traffic with it.” Three Blue Ducks in Burradoo, NSW. Jennifer Soo For Morris, the “traffic nightmare” began in April. He logged 804 traffic movements from 8am to 10am one Sunday, whereas previously he would have registered 20 passing cars, he said. Other objections raised the safety of accessing the venue via a railway crossing.



“At Burradoo Station there are barriers preventing direct pedestrian access across the railway lines with appropriate warning signs, as well as automatic gates preventing any crossings if a train is approaching,” resident Robert Johns said in his submission. Johns said the number of pedestrians accessing the property on any given day would far exceed those at Burradoo Station. A spokesperson for the Australian Rail Track Corporation said it was not consulted during the original approval process for Burradoo Park Farm. Burradoo Park Farm and its Three Blue Ducks restaurant are a huge success, but this quiet country town has turned into major tourism drawcard as well as a traffic nightmare. Sam Mooy The original application argued that existing commercial premises were exempt from setback rules preventing farm gate approvals within 250 metres of neighbouring homes or rail lines.



Burradoo Park Farm did not answer detailed questions from this masthead about the setback rules. The Department of Planning issued a one-line response directing inquiries to council. The application said the nearest homes on neighbouring land were more than 600 metres away, although maps show there are others within a 250-metre radius. The application calculated the distance to the rail line at 250.7 metres when using the “shortest walking distance” along a route through the farm, down a road and out to the rail line. Three Blue Ducks in Burradoo has its own vegetable patch and green house. Louise Kennerley A Burradoo Park Farm spokesperson said: “When council raised concerns regarding the approval pathway, we responded constructively and moved into the development application process as quickly as possible.”



The spokesperson said since opening, the farm had worked to address concerns raised by council and the community. “This has included implementing visitor management measures, traffic controls, shuttle bus services, parking arrangements, pedestrian safety initiatives and a range of specialist studies to support the assessment process.” Related Article Celebrity relationships ‘Focused on their children’: Mike Cannon-Brookes and wife Annie separate In submissions, locals said they feared conditions would worsen given the development application before council was hoping to expand the operation from 100 visitors at any one time to 250. “The idea that hundreds more cars will be speeding down our street each day, putting people at risk and ruining the area is frightening,” stated one of the more than 50 objections on the council website.



“There are no footpaths to walk on so anyone trying to walk their dog, a baby in a pram or just themselves is taking their life in their hands, not to mention the school children walking to and from school.” Of the more than 100 submissions before council, almost half are in support of the development application, citing the significant private investment in the local economy, employment opportunities and the kitchen garden facilities. Among those vouching for the expansion are the head of Cannon-Brookes’ SMART Collective, which operates the park, Three Blue Ducks’ group executive chef Troy Crisante, as well as other chefs and support staff at the venue, contractors involved in the development of the operation, the director of the local traffic control company. Another supporter is the Stephanie Alexander Kitchen Garden Foundation, a charity that has partnered with Cannon-Brookes’ philanthropic SMART Collective to create an immersive food education hub at the farm gate. World.title: ASX climbs, banks jump; Binance freezes $3.5b in assets after suspected hack
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX climbs, banks jump; Binance freezes $3.5b in assets after suspected hack Staff writers Updated October 30, 2026 — 12:41pm ,first published October 30, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Australian sharemarket has opened higher after a volatile night on overseas markets, as Google parent Alphabet’s historic plunge weighed down Wall Street, while crypto company Binance has frozen billions in assets after a suspected hack. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 52.5 points, or 0.6 per cent, in early trade. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Thursday. Alphabet’s drop sent Wall Street’s benchmark index into the red. AP Mining giant Rio Tinto slumped 2.6 per cent after an incident at its Oyu Tolgoi copper mine in Mongolia. A rockfall triggered by a seismic event on Thursday caused three workers to be injured, the company said in a statement on Friday. The company did not comment on the status of operations at the mine, but Bloomberg reported they had been suspended. The mining sector was mixed in early trade. BHP edged up 0.1 per cent, while Fortescue slid 0.7 per cent. Gold stocks slipped as the price of the precious metal retreated. Northern Star was down 0.2 per cent and Evolution Mining retreated 0.6 per cent in early trade.



Financial stocks advanced as Commonwealth Bank and National Australia Bank each added 0.8 per cent while Westpac and ANZ Bank both climbed 0.8 per cent. Shares in supermarket giant Coles plunged 11.7 per cent after the company’s first quarter sales result revealed that growth had slowed in October, and it highlighted customers were shopping around for value. It also said high fuel costs would add to its expenses, and it expected first-half supermarket profits to be flat compared with the prior period. Energy stocks advanced after oil prices rose on signs the US might resume military strikes against Iran, risking fresh turbulence in the region that might affect energy flows. West Texas Intermediate rose towards $US103 a barrel, after swinging more than $US3 in the previous session, while Brent settled near $US115. A top commander briefed US President Donald Trump on military options on Thursday, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump has repeatedly given signals he might restart airstrikes against Tehran after midterm elections next week. Woodside Energy rose 2.2 per cent and Santos added 1.5 per cent while, among the refiners, Ampol advanced 0.9 per cent and Viva Energy was up 0.5 per cent. Technology stocks were higher as WiseTech rose 1.3 per cent, Xero 1.7 per cent, Technology One 0.6 per cent and Codan 0.5 per cent. Data centre operator NEXTDC slipped 1.6 per cent.



The Australian dollar was 0.3 per cent lower at US70.34¢. Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, suspended all deposits and withdrawals as it investigates a security incident that has so far resulted in the freezing of more than $US2.54 billion ($3.6 billion) in assets. The suspected hack sent digital tokens tumbling. “We are working non-stop to resolve this issue. Binance will cover all losses,” the company said in a post on X. “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds, and works with law enforcement.” Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao said the exchange may have been hacked but he expects all user funds will be fully covered. Zhao, who goes by CZ, no longer runs the company but remains its largest shareholder. Online forums were rife with loss estimates and theories of how the attack was designed, none of them confirmed. Blockchain tracker Arkham has identified wallets associated with the suspected hacker holding about $US5.9 billion in digital assets, though the figure does not necessarily represent the amount stolen from Binance.



Bitcoin slumped, falling below $US77,000 to its lowest level since September, with other tokens also selling off. Overnight, the historic drop for Alphabet’s stock dragged the US market lower after the company behind Google and YouTube reported weaker growth for the summer than analysts expected. The report underscored worries about whether all its huge investments in artificial-intelligence technology would pay off. Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve ‘Politics played no role’: Fed hits pause button ahead of midterms Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent for its first loss in four days, even though the wide majority of stocks rose within the index and across Wall Street. The Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.4 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132 points, or 0.3 per cent. Alphabet is one of the most influential stocks on Wall Street because it’s one of the largest, and the Class A shares of its stock fell 12.6 per cent for their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago. The tech giant had been under pressure to at least meet analysts’ expectations for growth amid concerns about how much it’s spending to invest in AI.



Alphabet said that it burnt through more cash during the latest quarter, according to a measure called free cash flow, after its purchases of property and equipment topped $US51 billion ($73 billion). Worries are weighing on the entire AI industry following a frenzy to build data centres and fill them with AI chips. Not only are concerns high that the AI revolution might not produce as much profit and productivity as hoped, future spending on data centres is also under pressure because of how expensive it has become to borrow money to buy more chips. Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results after the closing bell that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations. However, the company posted strong sales growth in its prominent cloud computing unit. Sales in its so-called Amazon Web Services rose 39.3 per cent during the latest quarter ended September 30, higher than the 37 per cent clip in the previous quarter. It marked the fastest growth rate in nearly five years, the company said. Still, shares were down more than 7 per cent in after-market trading when the results were released as investors focused on the core business.



Alphabet’s drop overshadowed what would have otherwise been a good day for the US sharemarket. Four out of every five stocks within the S&P 500 climbed, and the index would have been higher if not for Alphabet. Many companies rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected, including KLA Corp. The company, whose equipment helps make semiconductors, rose 5.5 per cent. ECB chief Christine Lagarde will resign in February, nine months before the end of her term. AP Eli Lilly climbed 6.6 per cent, Mastercard rose 4.2 per cent and Merck added 3.8 per cent. Expectations are high for profit growth broadly across US companies. That’s what allowed the S&P 500 to set its record earlier this month despite high interest rates and other worries weighing on the sharemarket.



Related Article Opinion

Oil The oil market should brace for a forever stalemate in Iran In the bond market, Treasury yields eased following several mixed reports on the US economy. The overall economy’s growth may have accelerated more during the summer than economists expected, thanks to spending by US consumers and businesses investing in AI, according to a preliminary report. But Americans’ growth in incomes was weaker in September than economists expected, while a measure of inflation worsened. Meanwhile, fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could indicate few layoffs across the country. Following the jumble of reports, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94 per cent from 5.05 per cent late on Wednesday. It’s been generally pulling back since it topped 5.3 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002.



In sharemarkets abroad, indexes rose in Europe after the European Central Bank held interest rates steady on the continent. The bank’s president, Christine Lagarde, also said she will resign in February, nine months before the end of her term. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: Sam Wood’s ‘party lifestyle, drug use’ aired as he makes fresh bid for bail
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Sam Wood’s ‘party lifestyle, drug use’ aired as he makes fresh bid for bail Cloe Read October 30, 2026 — 1:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Former reality television star Sam Wood, accused of strangling and assaulting his wife Snezana, has made a fresh bid for bail, with a court hearing of his alleged drug use and “party lifestyle”. The former The Bachelor contestant allegedly attacked Ms Wood during a holiday in Noosa on Queensland’s Sunshine Coast earlier this month. Sam Wood met his future wife Snezana on The Bachelor Australia in 2015. Channel Ten Wood, 46, was charged with strangulation and assault occasioning bodily harm and has been in custody since his arrest on October 3, with his first bail application denied days later. The fitness guru, who dropped his lawyer Mathew Cuskelly in favour of barrister Paula Morreau KC, has made a new bail application in the higher Supreme Court.



In a hearing on Friday, Morreau detailed the pair’s relationship, saying it had been “suffering with significant stressors and more frequent confrontations”. She referred to material before the court that detailed Wood’s alleged drug and alcohol use, and a “party lifestyle”, but there was no suggestion he suffered from addiction. Andrew Wood (centre), the father of Sam Wood, is seen arriving at the Brisbane Supreme Court on Friday. AAPIMAGE She said Wood, who had struggled with anger, would usually leave to avoid confrontation, and that willingness was an important component to assess his risk for his release. “He is a man who has never before faced a charge,” Morreau said, adding he had no history of domestic violence.



She conceded the offences were serious, but there was no unacceptable risk to his release. She said there was a prospect that denying his release would mean he would serve longer in remand than he would if convicted. Morreau told the court Wood’s trial would probably not be until as early as late 2027. Sam Wood has been behind bars since October 3 on domestic violence charges. The barrister pointed to an earlier complaint by Ms Wood in 2021 referenced in prosecution documents. She said the allegations were untested, and they did not have the same support of a witness or medical attention. Putting forward his proposed addresses if released on bail, Morreau said Wood could reside in Tasmania, where his children would be able to visit him.



She also said there could be an alternative address in Queensland if the prosecution preferred. Morreau said Wood was a recognisable man, and the risk he would travel to Melbourne undetected was remote. Proposed bail conditions included that Wood would report to police three times a week, and he would attend a men’s behavioural change program. Wood’s charges have a maximum term of imprisonment of seven years, Morreau told the court. But, she added, Wood would probably face a two-year sentence if convicted, which the prosecution had also agreed. In opposing Wood’s release, Crown prosecutor Jessica Guy said the force to Ms Wood’s neck was for an extended period of time, and she had been unable to breathe or speak. Wood did not stop when she tried to free herself, and her head was banged on the floor, Guy said.



She said Wood’s conduct had escalated since the 2021 incident in Victoria. She pointed to choking being a predictive indicator of escalation in domestic violence offending. Details of the allegations were revealed in court earlier this month during the unsuccessful bail hearing. The court heard Wood pushed his wife into a wardrobe, before the argument spilled into the hallway, where Wood’s stepdaughter, Eve Markoski-Wood, told him to stop yelling. He then allegedly approached Eve aggressively, prompting Ms Wood to intervene, placing herself in Wood’s path, telling him to leave her daughter alone. He allegedly grabbed his wife by the throat with one hand, throwing her against the wall and striking her head. The court was told Wood then threw her to the floor, holding her throat, gripping tighter and preventing her from breathing.



Ms Wood tried to free herself, the court heard, but was unable to do so, telling police she thought her husband was “going to kill her”. The court heard Wood had denied strangling or causing bodily harm to his wife. The hearing continues. World.title: This is a show for anyone who has experienced loss of any kind
World.content:
CultureLive reviewsMelbourne live reviews This is a show for anyone who has experienced loss of any kind Thuy On and Andrew Fuhrmann October 30, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Key points THEATRE: Before I Forget by Kamarra Bell-Wykes is centred on early-onset dementia

DANCE: Orbit at Dancehouse kicks off with Agitato and Charcoal

THEATRE

Before I Forget ★★★★

Melbourne Theatre Company, Fairfax Studio - Arts Centre Melbourne, until November 28 The debilitating creep of early-onset dementia is the focus of this new play, developed through MTC’s Next Stage writers’ program, a commissioning and residency initiative that seeks to foster emerging theatre-makers. Loosely based on lived experiences, Before I Forget is the work of Kamarra Bell-Wykes, whose capacity here is as both the playwright and the director. Melodie Reynolds-Diarra, Roxanne McDonald and Tyallah Bullock (left to right). Pia Johnson It paints a portrait of a woman, once vital and vibrant, who’s losing the contours of her days. Faith Wells (Roxanne McDonald), a renowned First Nations academic and linguist, once had a wicked tongue and a fierce intellect, but her language – and indeed her life skills – are now mired in forgetfulness and confusion. While Faith is in the middle of giving a lecture, she becomes disoriented and hears voices. The play begins with her losing her keys and handbag, and as the disease takes a firmer grip, she fails to recognise her own grandchild Hope (Tyallah Bullock) and mistakes her son Jet (Nathan Wright) for her own father.



But when plans are discussed to relocate her into an aged care home, Faith rages and refuses to go gently into that institution, much to the chagrin of her daughter Karma (Melodie Reynolds-Diarra). McDonald is brilliantly convincing as the erstwhile leader, activist and trailblazer who now needs round-the-clock care for basic daily tasks. There is a mischievousness and playfulness to her even as she battles both memory fog and her daughter’s and granddaughter’s ministrations, and it’s this humour that leavens the otherwise serious intent of the play. Before I Forget explores loss of all kinds. Pia Johnson Also funny in a feckless way is Wright, who makes a brief appearance as the son Jet, who loves but leaves, and is unable to do any actual caring for his mother. We’re reminded of how much caregiving is relegated to the domain of women. To afford the fees for residential care, Faith’s home has been sold – its new owners are days away from moving in. The set features two beds on either side of a couch, with an ominous “For Sale” sign in the far corner. There are documents and folders in disarray on the floor as Karma and Hope try to pack away Faith’s research papers.



What’s particularly egregious is that for a linguist whose job and passion was to reclaim and restore Indigenous languages, Faith’s memory loss means aspects of her own life have disappeared – her own cultural legacy compromised. Editor's pick Visual art Whistleblowers, children and stateless men: The artist telling stories one image at a time Before I Forget explores three generations of women grappling with change and transition. As the dutiful daughter trying to manage the household, Reynolds-Diarra is a tightly coiled ball of anger and frustration, while Bullock is sweetly earnest as she teases and plays with her grandmother, hoping for connection. Sometimes she’s rewarded by moments of lucidity. Tonally, the play’s emotional arc moves back and forth from fear, hurt, outrage, and tenderness. The play is all about loss – not just of identity, but of a home, independence, and dignity. But Bell-Wykes has a broader reach in her remit than just the interpersonal interactions of one family – one that reaches back into the annals. The living wake, a eulogy that the three women conduct to acknowledge each other’s strengths and to celebrate each other, is a balm to counter the fact that, as Faith points out, there were no burials for ancestors massacred by colonialists. Before I Forget is as much a story about remembrance and honouring the Indigenous matrilineal line as it is about ageing, illness and death. The set opens up to reveal the luminous skyline and a scattering of stars, offering us a greater sense of spirituality and transcendence that goes beyond earthly mortality.

Reviewed by Thuy On



DANCE

Orbit Week 1: Charcoal and Agitato ★★★★

Dancehouse, Carlton, until October 31 It’s a familiar lament: contemporary dance rarely travels in Australia. We almost never get the chance to see the work of independent dance artists based in other cities. For that reason, a new national touring initiative called Orbit should be welcomed. Charcoal by Keia McGrady Gregory Lorenzutti The program comprises two double bills, which tour through five venues across Victoria, South Australia and NSW. The first program opens with Charcoal by emerging choreographer Keia McGrady, from south-east Queensland. This delicate, sensitively shaped duet responds to the regenerative power of cultural burning: the First Nations practice of using low fires to manage Country.



Crouched on a large sheet, the dancers crush sticks of charcoal and scrawl loose forms, suggesting a landscape viewed from above. As if rising from the ashes, they gradually stretch and unfold, then quicken, with fleeting animal imagery emerging as the work reaches its climax. McGrady and Amelia Jean O’Leary give earnest, attentive performances, sustaining the duet’s gentle, nurturing atmosphere as its movement slowly gathers intensity. Agitato by Jo Lloyd Gregory Lorenzutti The progression from quiet beginnings to fuller activity is straightforward but handled with assurance. McGrady focuses on developing her theme, allowing the simple image of regeneration to progress with clarity. The second piece, Jo Lloyd’s Agitato, a standout work from last year, responds to a short, rackety piano piece by Fanny Mendelssohn, as remixed by Duane Morrison, with whirling, spasming figures.



Yet it also opens chasms within the music. The four dancers seem to enter these fissures, discovering strange little scenes and fleeting, almost painterly arrangements amid the tumult. Related Article Melbourne live reviews Betrayal and good-intentions gone wrong: Eliza tells the story of the world’s first chatbot With two new dancers in the quartet, Agitato seems an even greater achievement on second viewing: an epic of churning anxieties. This is the sort of gripping theatre that I think vindicates Orbit’s ambitions. It’s fascinating to think what audiences elsewhere make of it.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: I first met Patrick Stewart in 1988 and many times since. I was dazzled by him
World.content:
CultureTV & radioVale I first met Patrick Stewart in 1988 and many times since. I was dazzled by him Michael Idato October 30, 2026 — 12:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Living as we do, roughly an adult human’s lifespan since the invention of modern celebrity, the daily headlines invariably include the death of someone famous. In the last few days alone, we have lost German actor Elke Sommer, American actor Susan Saint James and Star Trek actor Walter Koenig. But fans of Star Trek have taken a double hit; Sir Patrick Stewart, who played the debonair Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation, has also died. And while it’s difficult to unpick why one death affects some people more than another, that Picard’s Star Trek was technically a generation younger than Koenig’s seems to tap close to why Stewart’s death is so deeply felt. Actor Patrick Stewart. AP In one sense, Stewart’s life is easily captured: a dashing science fiction hero, lent a natural elegance by his perfect British baritone voice. He ran contrary to Hollywood convention – a bald, foreign replacement for his 1960s counterpart, the blonder, easier-on-the-eye Captain Kirk – but he had natural cinematic magnetism. He was an actor’s actor. And the camera loved him.



Related Article Updated

Vale ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86 But the truth of Stewart’s life is so much more complex. Indeed, the depth of his accomplishments on the stage eclipse his television fame, even though the latter will always dominate discussion of his career. And his background - surviving poverty, and a shockingly violent upbringing - gave him an emotional complexity that he could never quite resolve. Born and raised in Mirfield, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, in England, his father was an army veteran who suffered from PTSD, and returned from combat prone to fits of violence. The difficulties of his childhood, and his inability to protect his mother, would haunt Stewart in later years. He devoted time, energy and money to domestic violence organisations. But resolution for his own feelings would elude him. And though he came to the television screen later in his career – he was 47 when he signed on to Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1987 – he seemed somehow ageless. Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. Paramount Pictures



“Actors live in a world of make believe,” he told me, in one of our many conversations over the years. “We live in a giant nursery where we get to play very expensive games. But although they’re games, our objective is to make them appear real and truthful. So, ageing in the conventional sense, I don’t think, quite applies to us because our job is becoming other people, taking on another life. “There are times for me when ageing, believe me, I know how it feels,” he added. “Look at these fingers, I was told by a rheumatologist the other day I have poster boy arthritic hands. I could become the poster boy for arthritis.” We both laughed. “But at times, it feels like a role that I’m playing. A lifetime’s role.” I first met Patrick Stewart on the set of the 1988 made-for-television adaptation of Moby Dick. He was playing Captain Ahab, a man consumed by a destructive obsession with an elusive whale, whose choice brought the safety of his crew, and his self-destruction, into conflict. Curiously, like the enduring internal pain of his powerlessness as a child in the face of paternal violence, these were characters whose characteristics he managed to twist into later performances. Captain Picard would channel Captain Ahab, in a later Star Trek film. And Stewart’s powerlessness as a child, and unspoken grief over the loss of his mother, would resurface in sequel series, Picard. Old soldiers never die … Stewart’s Picard with Riker (Jonathan Frakes) and Seven of Nine (Jeri Ryan) in the sequel, Picard. Paramount+



I was dazzled by him. And he, I suspect, was charmed by a journalist whose first questions were not about either Moby Dick or Star Trek, but who went straight to a beloved childhood classic, Little Lord Fauntleroy (1980), with Sir Alec Guinness, and Excalibur (1981), John Boorman’s spectacular Arthurian masterpiece, in which Stewart played Guinevere’s father, Leodegrance of Cameliard. The most enduring role of his career, was doubtless the diplomatic and debonair Captain Picard. The Next Generation was a reboot, but its characters, and their storied lives, would build an expanded universe far more complex than their 1960s predecessors. Editor's pick Review How Patrick Stewart went from the Bard to where no man has gone before Actor and character aged together like a fine wine, I suggested to him once, and he agreed. “It’s a good analogy, the wine analogy,” he said. “It does feel like that. There came a point quite early in the seven years when we were shooting the series when I didn’t have to sit in my trailer and think myself into the role. I was him. So it became second nature and I didn’t have to examine, necessarily, his background to determine how to play a scene. It was spontaneous and instinctive.” Of his upbringing, Stewart always seemed both unsentimental and deeply affected. Nor was he ever complacent about either what Hollywood offered him, or what he might achieve in it. Indeed, he began his career with the lowest of expectation.



“I think my background and what I’d learned about being a professional actor had prepared me for the fact that there was no promise, there was only possibility,” Stewart told me. “And the odds were very bad for it being a successful career. At that time, I was content to just be working.” Graduating from drama school, he landed neither a manager, nor an agent. “I was firmly convinced that my career was over before it had begun,” he recalled. “I actually went back to my parents’ home, I had no money and I thought, ‘well, I had my shot and that was it’. It didn’t quite turn out like that, and one of the reasons it didn’t was pure good fortune and quite a lot of hard work.” Patrick Stewart with his wife, Sunny Ozell, in 2020. Getty Images In 2001, Stewart was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE). In 2010, he was made a Knight Bachelor by Queen Elizabeth II for services to drama. In a richly storied career, he was nominated for Emmy, Tony and Golden Globe awards. He won a Grammy, for the spoken word album Prokofiev: Peter and the Wolf. He won Olivier awards for his stage performances in Antony and Cleopatra and Hamlet. And he won a Drama Desk award for his one-man stage adaptation of A Christmas Carol, which he wrote, and starred in.



Related Article Vale Star Trek actor Walter Koenig dies aged 90 In a curious footnote, Stewart’s relationship with Charles Dickens’ iconic work would become almost as all-consuming as his Star Trek fame. It was later staged at the Old Vic in London and the Marquis Theatre on Broadway, but in a powerful demonstration of the ties that bind, and his connection to his childhood, complex as it was, the play opened with a single performance, in the parish church of Stewart’s birthplace, Mirfield, West Yorkshire. Acting, he later said to me, “is a job I have always loved. I’ve loved it passionately and been, and felt, lucky and very happy to be doing it under any circumstances. That I was acting at all, wherever I was, whether I was being paid well or poorly for it, didn’t matter. I was doing the work. Don’t tell the studios this, or my agent, but I would’ve done it without being paid for a long period of time.” Stewart is survived by his wife, American singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell, whom he married in 2013, and again in 2020, and two children, a son, Daniel, and a daughter, Sophia, from his first marriage, to British theatre actor and dancer Sheila Falconer. World.title: ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86
World.content:
Updated CultureCelebrityVale ‘Rest in the heavens, Captain’: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86 Kayla Olaya and Nell Geraets Updated October 30, 2026 — 12:50pm ,first published October 30, 2026 — 7:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Patrick Stewart, the classically trained stage actor who scaled the Shakespearean canon and added gravitas to a Star Trek franchise and X-Men films, has died. He was 86. Stewart, who was knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his Los Angeles home after being diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, according to a statement on his X account. Patrick Stewart, best known for his Star Trek performances and pictured in the backyard of his Los Angeles home in 2023, died on Wednesday (Thursday AEDT). “We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife, Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” it said. His death comes just days after Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, in the original Star Trek series and seven subsequent feature films, died at the age of 90.



While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the X-Men and Star Trek: The Next Generation series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career on stage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of A Christmas Carol and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land and Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot in repertoire with his good friend Sir Ian McKellen. Patrick Stewart and Ian McKellen worked together for more than 50 years and were fast friends. Ilya S. Savenok/Getty McKellen became close to Stewart while working on 2000 release X-Men, eventually officiating his wedding to Sunny Ozell in 2013. He shared a moving tribute to his long-time friend on Instagram, reflecting on the Yorkshire-born performer’s journey from stage to screen and his wide-ranging impact on the arts. “We first met as ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago, but we weren’t in the same productions. My first strong memory was a few years later, meeting him in the street in central London when he told me about an offer to take over a leading part in Star Trek,” McKellen wrote.



“ ‘But Patrick think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk – getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?’ Well, he took the risk, and thank goodness for us all that he did, for not just his devoted Trekkies but film and theatre audiences who marvelled at his using international celebrity to star in a string of cinema successes (X-Men of course) and in great classical plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Peter Shaffer, Pinter and Beckett at Stratford-upon-Avon, in London’s West End and on Broadway. “America was his adopted home, where he met his adored Sunny who has cared for him through sickness and health, through thick and thin. But he never forsook his origins: and the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as Chancellor of Huddersfield University in Yorkshire … He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.” McKellen ended his tribute by noting that Stewart’s “farewell performance” would be seen in December upon the release of Avengers: Doomsday, in which he plays Professor X. Stewart became an actor at 18, gaining acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company beginning in the 1960s. He spent decades working on stage and performing various roles in UK TV productions.



But it wasn’t until he was cast in Star Trek: The Next Generation from 1987 to 1994 that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s. He leaves behind his wife Sunny Ozell and two adult children – son Daniel Stewart and daughter Sophie Stewart, whom he shares with his first wife, Sheila Falconer. Patrick Stewart (front row, second from left) with the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation. William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk alongside Stewart in Star Trek: Generations (1994), honoured the renowned performer on social media as “a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor”. “What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote on Facebook. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.”



Fellow Star Trek actor George Takei, who played Sulu in the original 1960s TV series, paid tribute on social media dedicated to fans across the world, “mourning the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend”. “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before,” Takei wrote on Bluesky. “He inspired a whole next generation of stargazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.” Australian star Hugh Jackman also paid tribute to Stewart, noting the time they had spent together filming the X-Men films. “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days,” the Wolverine star wrote on Instagram, paired with two photos of the actors arm-in-arm.



Born in 1940 in the Yorkshire town of Mirfield in England’s north in coal-mining country, Stewart grew up in the era of ration ­coupons, lamplighters in the streets and once-a-week baths in a zinc tub in front of the coal stove, he told Good Weekend in 2023. His father was demobbed from the army following the end of World War II when he was five. Stewart recalls him returning hardened and abusive towards his wife after bouts of drinking. Books and then films became an escape for the young Stewart. Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation. MEDIANET In his teenage years, he took acting courses, threw himself into amateur theatre and, at 17, won a place at the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. The local council gave him a full scholarship. Stewart went on to marry choreographer Sheila Falconer, have two ­children and a 20-year stage, film and TV career – until he was randomly summoned to the United States to meet Gene Roddenberry, the creator of Star Trek.



Related Article Good Weekend ‘I am just sad a lot of the time’: A former Star Trek captain on his life on earth A producer had spotted Stewart lecturing American students on William Shakespeare and suggested him for a role in a new series of the ­franchise, The Next Generation. According to Stewart, the meeting didn’t go well, and Roddenberry was not a fan. So it came as a shock when he was recalled to audition for Star Trek: The Next Generation and then cast as captain of the Enterprise. “During ­filming [Roddenberry] would come down from his comfortable ­office and sit in his director’s chair, arms folded, ­frowning at me and clearly thinking, ‘But I didn’t want him; what’s he doing in my show?’ ” Stewart told Good Weekend. The network salary also changed things for him.



“The cast were all buying cars: Mercedes and Audis. I bought a Honda Prelude, to the dismay of my fellow ­actors. [Co-star] Jonathan Frakes accused me of having a ­poverty mentality.” Head of Marvel Studios Kevin Feige reminisced on the first time he met Stewart while on the set of the first X-Men film, describing it as a moment he will never forget. Actors James McAvoy, Patrick Stewart, and Hugh Jackman from X-Men: Days Of Future Past, in 2014. Getty “After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe – and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas. Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humour,” the studio head said in a statement shared with The Hollywood Reporter. “It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him … His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.”



Seth MacFarlane, who worked with Stewart on comedy productions like Family Guy, Ted and American Dad!, said he was a rare actor who “could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful”. “I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day one of a new film,” MacFarlane wrote on Instagram. “He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, ‘Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed.’ We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet.” Stewart also acted in Star Trek: Picard, a sequel to The Next Generation, featuring Picard in his post-Starfleet retirement and drawing in characters from other Star Trek shows, notably Seven of Nine (Jeri Ryan) from Star Trek: Voyager. “I will never say goodbye to Jean-Luc Picard, to his ideals, to his struggles to create an honest world, an unprejudiced world. That will always remain inside me in the same way that other roles have,” Stewart told this masthead in 2022.



With Reuters, AP Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.
