World.title: Annie Cannon-Brookes’ paddock-to-plate precinct under investigation
World.content:
BusinessEntrepreneurshipDevelopment Annie Cannon-Brookes’ paddock-to-plate precinct under investigation Lucy Macken and Patrick Begley Updated October 30, 2026 — 12:49pm ,first published 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Billionaire Annie Cannon-Brookes’ bid to more than double the capacity of her highly successful farm gate and restaurant precinct in the NSW Southern Highlands has hit a major snag. The tourist destination is already facing dozens of submissions from residents citing heavy traffic on country roads, parking problems and safety risks around the nearby rail line since it opened at Easter. Three Blue Ducks founders Darren Robertson, Annie Cannon-Brookes and Andy Allen at Burradoo. Locals have dubbed the traffic monitors and signage around the farm as Burradoo’s “Checkpoint Charlie”. Now the venture is under investigation by the local council after using “farm gate” laws introduced in 2022 to obtain fast-tracked development consent.



Wingecarribee Shire Council confirmed the investigation into Burradoo Park Farm’s compliance in a statement to this masthead on Thursday, adding “no further comment will be provided”. The 250-hectare property just outside Bowral is home to the award-winning Three Blue Ducks restaurant, plus a Three Blue Ducks bakery and cafe, an orchard, a market garden, and cattle and sheep grazing, making it arguably the premier tourist venue in the sleepy township. The Three Blue Ducks restaurant won the New Restaurant of the Year award before a 500-strong crowd on Monday at the Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide awards on Monday. The Burradoo Farm precinct. Wolter Peeters The site was consolidated from a handful of separate properties five years ago, and reimagined by Cannon-Brookes after she separated from her husband, Atlassian co-founder Mike Cannon-Brookes, in 2023. Their divorce settlement is yet to be finalised.



Burradoo Park Farm took advantage of new planning laws passed by the NSW government that made it easier for commercial farmers to earn extra income through various forms of agritourism, by-passing the need for development approval from council. Consent was granted to the farm-gate operation, which lies within 250 metres of both neighbouring homes and a rail line, raising questions as to whether it complied with the legislation. “It’s such a joke to call this a farm-gate operation,” said local David Coulthard. “It’s so much bigger than that. This is a farm gate on an industrial scale.” Local councillor Rachel Russell said: “Theoretically this fast-tracked farm-gate legislation was to help struggling farmers. How is it actually being used? Could we need just a couple more checks and balances to get it right for everyone?”



A private certifier granted Burradoo Park Farm complying development consent to become a farm gate in 2024, with a proposed gelato shop, market-garden cooking area, bakery and restaurant. The precinct has proven to be an unmitigated success for its billionaire owner. Related Article Good Food Guide ‘This is very special to us’: Three Blue Ducks wins historic first Good Food Guide award Since the day it opened in April, the crowds have exceeded expectations, prompting management to introduce a ticketing system to try to stagger visitors over the day, traffic control wardens on weekends, and additional parking. Many locals stressed they were not against the existing farm-gate operation, but were taken by surprise by the impact it has had on the local area.



“We feel invaded every weekend,” resident Peter Morris said. “It’s kind of cool to have this venue on your [back] step, and it’s certainly become a major destination for people across NSW, but there’s also been a fair amount of resentment from locals when they discovered it had already opened, and brought significantly increased traffic with it.” Three Blue Ducks in Burradoo, NSW. Jennifer Soo For Morris, the “traffic nightmare” began in April. He logged 804 traffic movements from 8am to 10am one Sunday, whereas previously he would have registered 20 passing cars, he said. Other objections raised the safety of accessing the venue via a railway crossing.



“At Burradoo Station there are barriers preventing direct pedestrian access across the railway lines with appropriate warning signs, as well as automatic gates preventing any crossings if a train is approaching,” resident Robert Johns said in his submission. Johns said the number of pedestrians accessing the property on any given day would far exceed those at Burradoo Station. A spokesperson for the Australian Rail Track Corporation said it was not consulted during the original approval process for Burradoo Park Farm. Burradoo Park Farm and its Three Blue Ducks restaurant are a huge success, but this quiet country town has turned into major tourism drawcard as well as a traffic nightmare. Sam Mooy The original application argued that existing commercial premises were exempt from setback rules preventing farm gate approvals within 250 metres of neighbouring homes or rail lines.



Burradoo Park Farm did not answer detailed questions from this masthead about the setback rules. The Department of Planning issued a one-line response directing inquiries to council. The application said the nearest homes on neighbouring land were more than 600 metres away, although maps show there are others within a 250-metre radius. The application calculated the distance to the rail line at 250.7 metres when using the “shortest walking distance” along a route through the farm, down a road and out to the rail line. Three Blue Ducks in Burradoo has its own vegetable patch and green house. Louise Kennerley A Burradoo Park Farm spokesperson said: “When council raised concerns regarding the approval pathway, we responded constructively and moved into the development application process as quickly as possible.”



The spokesperson said since opening, the farm had worked to address concerns raised by council and the community. “This has included implementing visitor management measures, traffic controls, shuttle bus services, parking arrangements, pedestrian safety initiatives and a range of specialist studies to support the assessment process.” Related Article Celebrity relationships ‘Focused on their children’: Mike Cannon-Brookes and wife Annie separate In submissions, locals said they feared conditions would worsen given the development application before council was hoping to expand the operation from 100 visitors at any one time to 250. “The idea that hundreds more cars will be speeding down our street each day, putting people at risk and ruining the area is frightening,” stated one of the more than 50 objections on the council website.



“There are no footpaths to walk on so anyone trying to walk their dog, a baby in a pram or just themselves is taking their life in their hands, not to mention the school children walking to and from school.” Of the more than 100 submissions before council, almost half are in support of the development application, citing the significant private investment in the local economy, employment opportunities and the kitchen garden facilities. Among those vouching for the expansion are the head of Cannon-Brookes’ SMART Collective, which operates the park, Three Blue Ducks’ group executive chef Troy Crisante, as well as other chefs and support staff at the venue, contractors involved in the development of the operation, the director of the local traffic control company. Another supporter is the Stephanie Alexander Kitchen Garden Foundation, a charity that has partnered with Cannon-Brookes’ philanthropic SMART Collective to create an immersive food education hub at the farm gate. World.title: ASX climbs, banks jump; Binance freezes $3.5b in assets after suspected hack
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX climbs, banks jump; Binance freezes $3.5b in assets after suspected hack Staff writers Updated October 30, 2026 — 12:41pm ,first published October 30, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has opened higher after a volatile night on overseas markets, as Google parent Alphabet’s historic plunge weighed down Wall Street, while crypto company Binance has frozen billions in assets after a suspected hack. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 52.5 points, or 0.6 per cent, in early trade. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Thursday. Alphabet’s drop sent Wall Street’s benchmark index into the red. AP Mining giant Rio Tinto slumped 2.6 per cent after an incident at its Oyu Tolgoi copper mine in Mongolia. A rockfall triggered by a seismic event on Thursday caused three workers to be injured, the company said in a statement on Friday. The company did not comment on the status of operations at the mine, but Bloomberg reported they had been suspended. The mining sector was mixed in early trade. BHP edged up 0.1 per cent, while Fortescue slid 0.7 per cent. Gold stocks slipped as the price of the precious metal retreated. Northern Star was down 0.2 per cent and Evolution Mining retreated 0.6 per cent in early trade.



Financial stocks advanced as Commonwealth Bank and National Australia Bank each added 0.8 per cent while Westpac and ANZ Bank both climbed 0.8 per cent. Shares in supermarket giant Coles plunged 11.7 per cent after the company’s first quarter sales result revealed that growth had slowed in October, and it highlighted customers were shopping around for value. It also said high fuel costs would add to its expenses, and it expected first-half supermarket profits to be flat compared with the prior period. Energy stocks advanced after oil prices rose on signs the US might resume military strikes against Iran, risking fresh turbulence in the region that might affect energy flows. West Texas Intermediate rose towards $US103 a barrel, after swinging more than $US3 in the previous session, while Brent settled near $US115. A top commander briefed US President Donald Trump on military options on Thursday, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump has repeatedly given signals he might restart airstrikes against Tehran after midterm elections next week. Woodside Energy rose 2.2 per cent and Santos added 1.5 per cent while, among the refiners, Ampol advanced 0.9 per cent and Viva Energy was up 0.5 per cent. Technology stocks were higher as WiseTech rose 1.3 per cent, Xero 1.7 per cent, Technology One 0.6 per cent and Codan 0.5 per cent. Data centre operator NEXTDC slipped 1.6 per cent.



The Australian dollar was 0.3 per cent lower at US70.34¢. Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, suspended all deposits and withdrawals as it investigates a security incident that has so far resulted in the freezing of more than $US2.54 billion ($3.6 billion) in assets. The suspected hack sent digital tokens tumbling. “We are working non-stop to resolve this issue. Binance will cover all losses,” the company said in a post on X. “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds, and works with law enforcement.” Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao said the exchange may have been hacked but he expects all user funds will be fully covered. Zhao, who goes by CZ, no longer runs the company but remains its largest shareholder. Online forums were rife with loss estimates and theories of how the attack was designed, none of them confirmed. Blockchain tracker Arkham has identified wallets associated with the suspected hacker holding about $US5.9 billion in digital assets, though the figure does not necessarily represent the amount stolen from Binance.



Bitcoin slumped, falling below $US77,000 to its lowest level since September, with other tokens also selling off. Overnight, the historic drop for Alphabet’s stock dragged the US market lower after the company behind Google and YouTube reported weaker growth for the summer than analysts expected. The report underscored worries about whether all its huge investments in artificial-intelligence technology would pay off. Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve ‘Politics played no role’: Fed hits pause button ahead of midterms Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent for its first loss in four days, even though the wide majority of stocks rose within the index and across Wall Street. The Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.4 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132 points, or 0.3 per cent. Alphabet is one of the most influential stocks on Wall Street because it’s one of the largest, and the Class A shares of its stock fell 12.6 per cent for their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago. The tech giant had been under pressure to at least meet analysts’ expectations for growth amid concerns about how much it’s spending to invest in AI.



Alphabet said that it burnt through more cash during the latest quarter, according to a measure called free cash flow, after its purchases of property and equipment topped $US51 billion ($73 billion). Worries are weighing on the entire AI industry following a frenzy to build data centres and fill them with AI chips. Not only are concerns high that the AI revolution might not produce as much profit and productivity as hoped, future spending on data centres is also under pressure because of how expensive it has become to borrow money to buy more chips. Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results after the closing bell that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations. However, the company posted strong sales growth in its prominent cloud computing unit. Sales in its so-called Amazon Web Services rose 39.3 per cent during the latest quarter ended September 30, higher than the 37 per cent clip in the previous quarter. It marked the fastest growth rate in nearly five years, the company said. Still, shares were down more than 7 per cent in after-market trading when the results were released as investors focused on the core business.



Alphabet’s drop overshadowed what would have otherwise been a good day for the US sharemarket. Four out of every five stocks within the S&P 500 climbed, and the index would have been higher if not for Alphabet. Many companies rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected, including KLA Corp. The company, whose equipment helps make semiconductors, rose 5.5 per cent. ECB chief Christine Lagarde will resign in February, nine months before the end of her term. AP Eli Lilly climbed 6.6 per cent, Mastercard rose 4.2 per cent and Merck added 3.8 per cent. Expectations are high for profit growth broadly across US companies. That’s what allowed the S&P 500 to set its record earlier this month despite high interest rates and other worries weighing on the sharemarket.



Related Article Opinion

Oil The oil market should brace for a forever stalemate in Iran In the bond market, Treasury yields eased following several mixed reports on the US economy. The overall economy’s growth may have accelerated more during the summer than economists expected, thanks to spending by US consumers and businesses investing in AI, according to a preliminary report. But Americans’ growth in incomes was weaker in September than economists expected, while a measure of inflation worsened. Meanwhile, fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could indicate few layoffs across the country. Following the jumble of reports, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94 per cent from 5.05 per cent late on Wednesday. It’s been generally pulling back since it topped 5.3 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002.



In sharemarkets abroad, indexes rose in Europe after the European Central Bank held interest rates steady on the continent. The bank’s president, Christine Lagarde, also said she will resign in February, nine months before the end of her term. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Schools Treaty decision blindsided Māori and Crown should apologise, Waitangi Tribunal says
World.content:
The Waitangi Tribunal has found the Crown acted abruptly, unilaterally and with no consultation with Māori when it removed school boards' obligations to give effect to the Treaty.

It says the decision blindsided Māori, lacked honour and the Crown should apologise.

A tribunal report, released on Friday, addresses the November 2025 removal of the explicit statutory obligation in the Education Act requiring school boards ensure schools give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

It's the third report from the Tribunal on changes in the education sector.

The first concerned changes to Treaty provisions in the Education and Training Act.

The second report examined the Government's rewrite of the school curriculum, which the Tribunal called "ideological".

The Tribunal found the Crown's Treaty breaches have caused prejudice to Māori, including harm to the Māori-Crown relationship and the likelihood that the removal of section 127(1)(d) of the Education and Training Act 2020 would leave school boards' commitment to the Treaty to chance.

In her letter to Ministers Presiding, Officer Rachel Mullins said the Crown abruptly proposed to remove section 127(1)(d), introducing the amendment at the Committee of the Whole House stage, a process which "blindsided Māori and bypassed any engagement on the reforms".

"Despite the Act's express purpose, the Crown adopted a process that excluded its Treaty partner altogether. We found that process fell short of the standard of honour required of the Crown, breached its Treaty obligations, and harmed the Māori-Crown relationship."

Rachel Mullins Supplied

The Tribunal found the Crown lacked feedback from whānau, hapū, iwi, school board members, and the wider education sector on the implications of its specific statutory changes.

"Compounding these deficiencies, there is no evidence the Crown sought official advice regarding its proposal.

"The rushed process carried out by the Crown also left no time for a Regulatory Impact Statement to inform Cabinet's decision to introduce the amendment."

The tribunal also considered the replacement section of the Act, which it found to be "deficient in several key aspects".

It found the Crown's lack of clarity about the continued relevance of the Treaty to school boards' operations has also created confusion, which "may be the largest and most lasting form of prejudice".

"In doing this, the Crown has created unnecessary ambiguity and sends an incorrect signal to school boards that the Treaty is no longer important or relevant in their work. It introduces risk that the Crown's Treaty obligations in the everyday schooling context will not be realised," Mullins wrote.

The Tribunal recommended the Crown formally apologise to Māori for its breaches of the Treaty arising from the removal of the obligations.

"The Crown removed a significant statutory Tiriti obligation abruptly, unilaterally, and without engagement with Māori, despite knowing both the importance of the provision to Māori and its obligation to engage with its Treaty partner."

Secondly, the Tribunal recommended that the Crown restore the obligations which were formerly contained in section 127(1)(d) to the Education and Training Act 2020 in its entirety.

They further recommended that the Crown work with Māori in the education sector to determine how the provision is to be reinstated within the present statutory framework, "while preserving its full substance and effect".

World.title: Kyle Whorrall trial: Attackers left American PhD student with 'catastrophic and ultimately fatal wound', Crown lawyer says
World.content:
The only mistake an American PhD student made moments before he was fatally attacked was stopping at a bus stop, Crown lawyers say.

Kyle Whorrall, 33, was left with a "a catastrophic and ultimately fatal wound" following an attack in April 2025 at the stop in Auckland's Meadowbank.

He died in hospital shortly after.

The Crown said Whorrall was on his way back from a routine evening shopping trip when he was attacked with a machete.

Four teens have pleaded not guilty to his murder and aggravated robbery in the High Court at Auckland.

Jurors heard a fifth teenager had earlier pleaded guilty to both charges.

None of the young people involved can be named.

Crown lawyer Henry Steele was closing their case on Friday.

He told the jury the group had been driving up and down St Johns Road, coming up with a plan to rob Whorrall.

The car stopped and two people got out, Steele said.

"Two figures, one armed with a machete, both with a singular purpose, to rob," he said.

The group had seen Whorrall carrying two tote bags on his way home from the shops and made a plan to rob him, not knowing the bags only had groceries, Steele said.

He said Kyle Whorrall's only mistake that evening was stopping.

"They took his wallet and they left him with a catastrophic and ultimately fatal wound to the top of his head."

Steele said the teenagers left him dying with that wound, and "very much alone".

He told the jury using the machete was the foreseeable consequence of their plan to rob Whorrall.

"It was the one risk inherent in the possession of such a weapon," he said.

"Not that it would be used, but that it could well be used to cause serious injury in the course of the robbery."

Jurors had earlier been told the Crown did not have to prove who struck the fatal blow, only that those in the car knew what could have happened.

Defence earlier in the trial had pointed to the fact that after 18 months the Crown could not definitively say who struck the killing blow.

Four teens have pleaded not guilty to Kyle Whorrall's murder and aggravated robbery in the High Court at Auckland. Supplied

Steele told jurors he wouldn't spend his opening trying to convince them who that was.

"The question for you and the question I will address in the balance of this address is each of the four defendants' individual liability for what the Crown says was the entirely foreseeable consequence of their shared common purpose, the robbery of Mr Whorrall," he said.

The Crown prosecutor put five questions to the jury: who was in the car, why where they together, what did they know when the car stopped on St Johns Road, what did they do, and was it foreseeable.

Steele drew jurors' attention to the occupant in the car that night who had already pleaded guilty to Whorrall's robbery and murder.

The teen had an obvious and long-standing propensity for violent offending, going back to 2021, Steele said.

He turned to two other teenagers, represented by Panama Le'Au'Anae and Paul Borich KC, who he said shared those similar tendencies toward machete crime.

Steele said the three of those teens being in the car on that night was not coincidence.

"They're together to commit property crime, including the use of a machete," he said.

"We know there's a machete in the car and nobody is harvesting bananas."

He pointed to an incident roughly half an hour before the attack, where four of the teens allegedly tried to steal a motorbike from Elstree Avenue in Glen Innes.

"We know that these four or these five are not just out for a drive," he said.

"This is proof of concept when it comes to the broader intention of the group, to commit property crime, to steal."

Justice Simon Mount cautioned jurors to reserve judgement about propensity evidence given by the Crown until they had heard from all lawyers.

"I expect this will be an important topic, and I want to make sure you do not make any assumptions about how you can use that evidence until after you've heard from all counsel and from me," he said.

Justice Mount reminded jurors they had only heard one side of the story.

Steele said the remaining two teens on trial, represented by Marie Taylor-Cyphers and Annabel Maxwell-Scott, did not share the same propensity as the other three.

"But what happens at Elstree Ave tells us they're in," Steele said.

"They're not just along for the ride."

Defence lawyers are expected to give their closing addresses later on.

World.title: Solomon Islands PM Wale asks public for prayers as he recovers in Australia
World.content:
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale has spoken after being taken to Australia for urgent medical treatment earlier this week.

Wale did not provide details about his condition but called on Solomon Islanders yo "keep me and my family in your prayers" as he focuses on his recovery.

In a statement on Friday, Wale thanked his well-wishers, saying their prayers have been a source of strength and comfort to him and his family.

He also expressed gratitude to Solomon Islands opposition leader Manasseh Sogavare and the opposition for their prayers, goodwill, and show of support.

"At this time, I ask that you continue to keep me and my family in your prayers as I focus on my recovery," the statement read.

The prime minister was admitted to the National Referral Hospital last weekend and referred by doctors for further treatment in Australia on Wednesday night.

It is unclear when he will return to Honiara.

World.title: Diwali Festival 2026: Come for the dancing, stay for everything else
World.content:
When Arnav Taode attended his first Auckland Diwali Festival in 2014, he never imagined he would one day be managing the event.

He had been in New Zealand for less than six months when he joined new friends at the festival and found himself surrounded by Indian music, performers and thousands of people celebrating a culture he had grown up with.

"I couldn't believe that a country can celebrate a different community's culture so majorly, to see roads shut down, to see a stage that size with our music and our performers," Taode said.

"It was very welcoming. I felt at home immediately."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407620686112

Originally from the city of Pune in western India, Taode is now event manager for the 2026 BNZ Auckland Diwali Festival, which returns to Aotea Square and Queen Street this weekend.

Known as the "festival of lights", Diwali is celebrated by millions of people around the world and symbolises the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil, although its significance and traditions vary across religious communities.

The festival, which began in 2002, has grown into one of New Zealand's largest annual cultural celebrations, showcasing traditional and contemporary Indian music, dance, food and crafts.

This year's programme includes performances across three stages, theatre, exhibitions, art installations, light projections, yoga classes, Bollywood films and activities for families.

Arnav Taode is event manager for the 2026 BNZ Auckland Diwali Festival. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Taode brings more than two decades of experience in festivals, live events and creative productions to the role.

Having grown up across India in a military family, he said he had experienced the country's cultural diversity firsthand and wanted this year's festival to reflect this.

"India cannot be defined by a smell, taste [or] colour, so from our side, I've taken aspects of our culture and tried to give them designated spaces," he said.

A new Indian art exhibition, created especially for the Auckland Diwali Festival in partnership with India-based Baaya Design, is among new additions this year.

Taode said the exhibition featured traditional art forms and artists from Indian villages, with themes connecting India and New Zealand.

Auckland's Diwali Festival, which began in 2002, has grown into one of New Zealand's largest annual cultural celebrations, showcasing traditional and contemporary Indian music, dance, food and crafts. Supplied

He wanted the festival to go beyond Bollywood dance competitions and performances, giving people more opportunities to engage with India's diverse cultural traditions.

"We have projections on the Town Hall that's giving the essence of Diwali, good over evil, us coming together to this country and our culture, how open we are to celebrate and welcome other cultures in," he said.

The Living Arts Chillout Space at Aotea Centre also returns, offering workshops and activities focused on Indian culture.

At Auckland Town Hall, three free 45-minute concerts in the concert chamber will introduce audiences to Indian classical music.

The programme also includes Ramayan Live Stage Drama, bringing the epic story to life through acting, costumes and storytelling.

Festival favourites such as the Chalk It Up Rangoli Competition, henna artists and the festival marketplace will return, alongside activities for children and whānau.

The celebrations extend beyond the main festival site, with exhibitions, workshops and other Diwali experiences at Central City Library, Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki and Auckland War Memorial Museum.

Pritesh Raniga (left) with Arnav Taode and Indian actor Meenakshi Sheshadri (right) at the opening of the Indian Cinema Showcase during this year's Diwali Festival. Supplied

An expanded Indian Cinema Showcase is another highlight of this year's Diwali celebrations, with Indian films screening at Auckland cinemas throughout October.

Pritesh Raniga, director of Forum Films, said the showcase was another way for people to celebrate Diwali and experience Indian culture.

"Along with other festivities, going to the cinemas is also a part of celebrating Diwali in India, and we wanted to bring some great movies to Auckland this time around as well," he said.

The showcase will close with Ramayana: Part 1, a highly anticipated adaptation of the Hindu epic.

The Ramayana tells the story of Prince Rama, an avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu, whose wife Sita is kidnapped by the demon king Ravana, prompting Rama to set out to rescue her.

The ancient Sanskrit epic is traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki and has been retold through literature, theatre, dance and film across generations.

The story is closely linked to Diwali, which is widely associated with Rama's return to his kingdom of Ayodhya after defeating Ravana, symbolising the triumph of good over evil and the return of light after darkness.

A wide range of cuisine from India will be available at food stalls along Queen St over the weeekend. RNZ / Yiting Lin

Raniga said the latest adaptation aimed to bring the story to a wider audience using modern technology.

"Ramayana is the pride of every Indian, and the story has been adapted multiple times, but this time it also wants to tell that story to the world with the latest technology," he said.

Diwali celebrations have already begun across central Auckland, with light displays and projections appearing at several landmarks.

Since 24 October, Auckland Town Hall has been illuminated with Diwali-themed artworks, while Te Waihorotiu Station features a projection-mapping experience combining sound, imagery and storytelling.

The Auckland Harbour Bridge is also being lit in fuchsia and orange through the Vector Lights display until 1 November, with other city landmarks and public spaces joining the celebrations.

Gatka being performed during Bandi Chhor Divas celebrations in Auckland on Saturday. Supplied

Meanwhile, hundreds of people from the country's Sikh community gathered at Aotea Square on Saturday to celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, an occasion also known as Sikh Diwali.

According to Sikh tradition, the sixth Sikh guru, Guru Hargobind, returned to Amritsar on Diwali after securing the release of 52 Hindu kings imprisoned at Gwalior Fort by Mughal Emperor Jahangir.

"It is a big day for Sikhs," said Jaspreet Singh, one of the organisers of the Auckland celebration.

Singh said it was the first time the community had held the celebration in Auckland's CBD, with organisers wanting to make Sikh culture more visible to the wider public.

"We need to show our culture so people can connect with it," he said.

"When people understand other cultures, they can respect them. When there is a gap between communities, it becomes difficult to understand each other.

"We need to show that Sikhs live here and contribute to New Zealand's economy, history and culture. That is why we organised this gathering."

"It is very important to bridge that gap, especially now," Singh said.

Auckland's Sikh community celebrated Bandi Chhor Divas at Aotea Square last weekend. Supplied

Over the past year, Sikh and wider Indian communities have faced divisive rhetoric, while nagar kirtans, or religious processions, have been disrupted by Destiny Church on two occasions.

Singh said it was a challenging time for migrant communities and people needed to work together to ensure everyone could feel they belonged in New Zealand.

"Everyone should have the same right to belong in this country and live freely here," he said.

Singh said Sikh celebrations were sometimes overlooked in wider Diwali festivities, despite the significance of the occasion to the community.

He said the Auckland gathering was an opportunity to share Sikh traditions and help people better understand the community, particularly amid the current climate.

The celebrations included gatka (a traditional Sikh martial art), kavisheri (a form of Punjabi folk poetry) and kirtan performances by children from Sikh academies around the country.

Organisers also provided a free community langar meal that was open to everyone attending.

Singh said the community hoped to make the Sikh Diwali celebration an annual event in Aotea Square.

This year's festival over the coming weekend also coincides with a planned protest organised by Destiny Church on Saturday.

Tens of thousands of people attend Auckland's Diwali Festival each year. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Taode said organisers were aware of the protest and were working with other organisations to ensure the festival remained a safe space for visitors.

"New Zealand is a country that respects peaceful gatherings to share different points of view, and we support that," he said.

"We are very aware of this and are working along with multiple organisations to make sure Diwali, as it has always been, remains a safe space for our community to gather, and other communities as well."

Auckland Council has warned that city-centre road closures, including Queen St, would affect some bus routes during the festival.

Attendees were advised to use Te Waihorotiu Station to access the festival's main stage in Aotea Square, it said.

Taode said he hoped Aucklanders from all backgrounds would come along and experience the festival.

"Come, bring your family, let's celebrate together and be accommodating to whatever comes around."

World.title: Harry Mowbray's 'Split Your Vote' website probed by Electoral Commission
World.content:
Audio player for " Harry Mowbray discusses his 'Split Your Vote' campaign " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2235548%2Fharry-mowbray-s-split-your-vote-website-probed-by-electoral-commission

Harry Mowbray discusses his 'Split Your Vote' campaign Midday Report Download MP3 11m

Businessman Harry Mowbray, who created a website encouraging vote-splitting, says the MMP electoral system is a "complete dog".

He confirmed part of his strategy was to discredit MMP and "show people how bad it is".

Mowbray was speaking to Midday Report about the Electoral Commission looking into his website, which he says he's taken offline.

A complaint was made about it, and Mowbray has made "an assumption" that it was the National Party, which has been publicly critical of vote-splitting, responsible.

He said the letter he received from the Electoral Commission asked if he had got permission for the website content from the party secretaries of ACT and New Zealand First.

"They didn't ask if I had it from National so they obviously know the answer to that," he said.

The website is designed to give the centre-right a disproportionate number of seats to its party vote through the overhang, by telling people to give their candidate vote to National and their party vote to ACT or New Zealand First.

"It's working unbelievably. The number of people that I don't know and end up talking to and they say, 'we've heard about it and we're going to split our vote', or say they don't know what it means and then I spend five minutes explaining it, and they say 'oh we get it now'."

Mowbray says Te Pāti Māori "started it" when it comes to tinkering with MMP, "and I'm showing you how we can finish it".

He believes the current system is "completely undemocratic" in that the minor parties have a much stronger voice in Parliament than their party vote should allow.

Mowbray explained the process for setting up the website and what he believed to be allowed.

The Electoral Commission "told me I haven't had secretaries for ACT or New Zealand First give permission to promote", he said.

"I didn't realise having the website was going to get classified as a promotion, because it's in my name. You're allowed to say pretty much anything you like as an individual ... that's what I was doing."

Mowbray said he was asked by the Electoral Commission whether he paid for a domain name to set-up the website, which he did for the cost of $35.

"As soon as I pay for a domain name it becomes an . I'm allowed to spend $17,000 and I haven't done that yet."

He wasn't asked to take down the website but "if it's a problem then it's down".

Asked by RNZ to confirm or deny the allegation it was behind the complaint, a spokesperson for the National Party said it wouldn't be "commenting on this story".

The Electoral Commission told RNZ it was investigating the "advertising" and whether it was "authorised", and it wouldn't be appropriate to comment further at this stage.

Party messaging must come with an authentication statement, for transparency reasons.

Earlier this week, Mowbray said he'd been pushing the message that a centre-right government could "best be achieved" by vote splitting, "supporting the local National MP or candidate with their electorate vote but giving their party vote to NZ First or ACT as coalition partners".

"That gives their party vote some effect while giving the centre-right coalition a better chance of winning."

The complaint comes as the overhang strategy gains momentum, and National has responded in turn, with a video from former prime minister Sir John Key saying not to put the election to chance.

"It's a really close election," National leader Christopher Luxon said on Friday.

"It's going to come down to the wire. As I said yesterday, there'll be one or two points in it all."

He said if voters want National, they have to vote for it.

"In an MMP system, you party vote for it."

This is not the first time National has called on Sir John Key's services to deliver a message to voters during an election campaign.

In 2023, Key released a video 10 days before the election, urging Kiwis to give their party vote to National to avoid waking up in "limbo land" without a clear result.

He argued then that National needed enough votes to govern without "lots of moving parts", but conspicuously avoided mentioning NZ First or its leader Winston Peters by name.

Key also warned prolonged negotiations would delay action on the cost of living.

The intervention was ultimately unsuccessful in its bid to prevent National being reliant on NZ First to form a government.

The country's first three-way coalition was formed about 40 days after the 2023 election, following lengthy talks.

ACT candidate Paul Henry was asked about the Electoral Commission complaint and the implication from Mowbray it had come from the National Party.

"I would be surprised if he hadn't expected that something like this would happen," Henry responded.

Asked what he made of the vote splitting strategy gaining momentum, Henry said, "it's maths isn't it?"

"Anyone that really understands mathematics will know that most of what they're saying is correct based on assumptions.

World.title: Westpac cuts fixed home loan rate
World.content:
Westpac is cutting its 18-month home loan rate by 26 basis points.

It takes the rate to 5.19 percent.

None of its other fixed term rates will change.

When the Reserve Bank decided to leave the official cash rate on hold earlier this week, commentators said it was possible it could lead to rate cuts.

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said there were a couple of reasons for that.

"Firstly, the fact that an increase [this week] was about 90 percent priced in suggests there could be some easing in shorter-term mortgage rates, particularly for six months and, to a lesser extent, one year.

"Secondly, market pricing for future meetings is also likely to be less hawkish given the bank's failure to tighten today and the relatively dovish statement with a lot of emphasis on the global risks.

World.title: Netball NZ pulls the pin on proposed Mowbray-Williams private league
World.content:
Netball New Zealand has pulled the pin on plans for a privately run domestic league, just eight weeks after signing a term sheet with investors Anna Mowbray and Ali Williams.

It is understood the decision to abandon the proposal was made at a Netball NZ board meeting on Wednesday, throwing the future of next year's domestic competition up in the air once more.

In a statement issued to RNZ on Friday morning, Netball NZ confirmed it had ended negotiations with the high-profile couple, saying an agreement to privatise the elite domestic competition could not be reached despite "considerable efforts by both parties".

"Our communications with each other are confidential," the statement said.

Netball NZ acknowledged the news would be unsettling, particularly for players and support staff, and said it would provide further information as soon as it could.

Mowbray and Williams say they are also seeking answers, claiming they have been given no explanation for the decision.

In a statement to RNZ, the pair said they were informed by Netball NZ via email on Thursday that the national body would not be forging ahead with the proposal.

"We are devastated. Ali and I gave this everything," the statement read.

"Our time, our money and our hearts. We did it because we've seen what a team can do for a community. With Auckland FC we've watched families come together, kids find heroes and a city find its voice. This was our chance to do that for netball, for women's sport, at a scale this country has never seen.

"Yesterday that ended with an email. No reason. No call."

Over the last year, elite netball has lurched from fears for its survival to hope of a rescue - and now back into uncertainty.

With the Mowbray-Williams plan off the table, questions remain over what alternative exists for 2027, and whether New Zealand can retain a meaningful professional pathway for its leading players.

The abrupt reversal is expected to take a huge toll on the players, coaching and support staff who had been hanging out for an update on the shape of the new competition.

The collapse of the deal leaves some of New Zealand's top players, including Silver Fern midcourter Peta Toeava, in limbo. Aaron Gillions / www.photosport.nz

New Zealand Netball Players Association (NZNPA) boss Pippa Moore said the organisation has seen a significant increase in players seeking mental health support and financial assistance.

"There's a number of players that we're really concerned about and I think this will just add to it. So that will be our number one focus at the moment," said Moore.

"People have been holding out for [the new league]. We've been waiting all year, and then we deliver the good news that someone's coming in to save the day and now that's just been ripped away from them leading into Christmas. And there's no suggestion of anything else at this point."

Moore added she was disappointed that she had not been directly informed by Netball NZ's of its decision.

"We've been completely blindsided to be honest. We're absolutely devastated."

A proposed lifeline for netball

Mowbray and Williams emerged as potential saviours of the sport's elite competition earlier this year, offering a lifeline with a proposal to establish a privately owned franchise league.

Originally pitched for 2028, the plan was accelerated to allow a minimum five-team competition to launch in 2027.

The proposed league was intended to bring much-needed private investment into a competition Netball NZ could no longer afford to run in its existing form.

Netball NZ board chair Alastair Carruthers revealed in July that the national body was facing losses of up to $6 million for the financial year, $3.7 million of which could be attributed to the costs of running the ANZ Premiership.

After weighing up its options, Netball NZ announced at the beginning of last month that it had selected the Mowbray-Williams proposal as its preferred option, with the parties signing a non-binding term sheet.

Netball NZ boss Jennah Wootten at the announcement of plans for a new private league in September. RNZ / Nick Monro

At the announcement, incoming Netball NZ chief executive Jennah Wootten said the parties were working towards a long-form agreement covering franchise licences, the competition window, league format, and commercial and broadcast arrangements.

It was understood an ambitious deadline of early October had been set to finalise the agreement and allow teams to begin contracting players.

But that deadline passed without a further public update on the league, fuelling growing anxiety within the netball community about the competition's future.

"We knew that [the timeline] had been pushed out because there were issues that they were struggling to agree on," said Moore.

"But we were never given the impression from either party that these issues were like they couldn't be solved and that there was a risk that it would fall over."

Player exodus

The collapse of the deal comes after a prolonged period of uncertainty that has already seen a significant number of leading New Zealand players sign contracts with clubs overseas.

With players left in limbo while netball officials grappled with some big decisions facing the game, Netball NZ were forced to roll back its eligibility rules for the Silver Ferns, allowing players based overseas to still be eligible for the national team.

The decision has seen Kiwi players flock overseas in unprecedented numbers, with 13 players taking up contracts in Australia's Suncorp Super Netball competition, including 10 of the 12 members of the Silver Ferns Commonwealth Games gold medal winning team.

Several players like superstar shooter Grace Nweke (Sydney Sirens) and the Heffernan twins, Kate (Adelaide Thunderbirds) and Georgia (Sunshine Coast Lightning), have signed multi-year deals.

World.title: Tech stocks end long-time top KiwiSaver performer's golden run
World.content:
Audio player for " When does my property become relationship property? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2235001%2Ftech-stocks-end-long-time-top-kiwisaver-performer-s-golden-run

Simplicity's growth fund has knocked Milford out of the top spot for returns over 10 years, in new Morningstar data.

The latest quarterly update for the September quarter shows that Simplicity's growth fund returned 9.9 percent a year over 10 years. It is the first time the fund has a sufficient performance history to report a 10-year return.

Milford, which has traditionally been top of the table with its active growth fund, slipped to third at 9.6 percent a year, behind Quay Street's Growth fund at 9.7 percent.

Milford returns have slipped in recent months as a result of its approach to the recent tech boom.

Milford recorded growth of 0.9 percent over three months compared to 1.7 percent for Simplicity and 2.7 percent for Quay Street. AMP delivered 13.6 percent over a year and Simplicity 11.7 percent, compared to Milford's 3.4 percent.

It recently produced a webinar for investors that tackled the question of the active growth fund's performance.

Chief investment officer Wayne Gentle said while people talked about sharemarkets delivering very strong returns recently, that was driven by a few very large tech companies.

"The striking feature of markets is that it has a narrow set of drivers. There has been a narrow set of US companies dominating returns. Those companies have been responsible for a disproportionate amount of that return. Mathematically they've been pulling the market up on their own.

"When we're talking about 'markets hitting all-time highs', that's not the average performance of the average company," he said.

Milford said it was achieving its returns with less risk than the other funds.

Gentle said over 10 years the active growth fund had captured 91 percent of market gains but only 77 percent of market falls.

While Milford remained heavily invested in technology stocks - including exposure to the AI theme - concerns about concentration, geopolitics, inflation and debt meant it was not invested in the same proportion as markets such as the US.

"Over the last 12 months, we've been quite cautious about that outlook. That caution has not been rewarded in equity markets to this point," Gentle said.

Bonds and traditionally defensive equities had also disappointed.

"Our traditional diversifiers over the last 12 months have not done the job they have done in the past in terms of protecting and providing that superior risk-return outcome."

He said bonds had come under pressure following the oil price spike and had not rebounded as strongly as technology stocks, while safer equities had also suffered.

He rejected suggestions Milford had "missed" the AI theme.

"We have been heavily invested in technology firms and continue to be," he said.

Head of KiwiSaver Murray Harris said passive funds would have much larger exposure to tech stocks because they made up a larger part of major indices.

"Nvidia I think is about 9 percent of the index ... we've got 3 percent, 3.5 percent exposure to it as at the end of September. It's one of our largest holdings but we're not going to hold it at an index weight.

"So by the very nature of the more diversified mix of our portfolio and managing that risk we're a bit slower because we wanted to really understand the theme around tech, that's impacted our one-year returns and they're not where we would want them to be.

"But we would rather be in that situation than having made a wrong call or going too big into a theme without doing all the research we wanted to do."

REcent results such as the Alphabet announcement on Friday highlighted that potential disappointments could cause worry in the market, he said.

He said he expected the top performers in each category to move around more in future.

"There's been a bit more convergence now across sort of probably the top four or five providers.

"And just depending how things play out quarter by quarter and who's got more exposure to what or how they're managing risk, or if the index continues to climb and the passive funds will continue to do better, then you're going to see those rankings move around a bit. But like I said at the start, we've never set out to be number one and don't expect to be number one forever.

"But we've been very proud of our long-term returns."

Quay Street was the top balanced and conservative fund over 10 years, MAS the top moderate fund, and Generate the top aggressive fund.

Overall, Morningstar said conservative funds had returned 3.8 percent a year over 10 years, moderate funds 4.6 percent, balanced funds 6.8 percent, growth funds 8.6 percent and aggressive 10 percent.

Over the year, SuperLife's Australian Resources fund had the highest performance, up 43.3 percent. Koura's Bitcoin scheme was the poorest performer, down 25.1 percent.

"Despite persistent losses in market share over the past five years, ANZ continued to lead with a 15.9 percent market share at $23.8 billion in assets at the end of the quarter, marginally down in terms of assets in the scheme from last quarter. ASB was in second position, with a market share of 14.7 percent. Fisher, Milford, and Westpac rounded out the top five," Morningstar said.

"We estimate that KiwiSaver providers will charge more than $1.22 billion from KiwiSaver members in the next 12 months to manage their KiwiSaver funds, at an average fee of around 0.81 of a cent per dollar invested."

World.title: For the fans who became heroes, Samoa vs Tonga is bigger than a grand final
World.content:
Ahead of their sold-out Rugby League World Cup match on Sunday, the new faces of the eternal rivalry between Tonga and Samoa didn't quite go straight from the stands onto the field, but they went pretty close.

Four years ago, when the two met in the last World Cup, Francis Manuleleua was hunched over in his bedroom in South Auckland, watching the game on his phone.

He was 18, with the rugby league world at his feet, and after Samoa held on for a pulsating 20-18 victory, he snatched up a flag and marched into the street because his life had changed forever.

Loading...

"Growing up I was always picked in the Kiwi teams, Under 16s and Under 18s and that, so there was a feeling of wanting to pull on that black jersey in either league or union," Manuleleua said.

"But after that 2022 World Cup, seeing all the boys play, how much it meant to them, that's when it changed for me and I thought to myself 'this is the jersey I'd want to put on if I ever get the opportunity'."

Across the Tasman, Sua Fa'alogo was part of the same celebratory throng, wherever the four winds could take Samoans from their islands.

The parades of the Samoan and Tongan fans have become legendary. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

The 23-year-old was born and raised in Samoa, in the village of Si'umu, and lived there until he was nine, when his parents moved to Melbourne to find a better life for him and his eight siblings.

Leka Halasima's story was similar: he was born in Tofoa, Tonga, before moving to New Zealand as a boy.

In 2024, a few months after his NRL debut and well before every league fan knew his name, he watched his two nations go head-to-head in the Pacific Championship, cheering on the Mate Ma'a in a 25-24 victory.

Halasima has gone from admiring his heroes to playing alongside them. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

"Then the next year I was playing with them," Halasima said.

Now the 21-year-old Warriors tyro is doing more than just playing, he is starring alongside the heroes of his childhood and taking forward what they started.

"For a young person like me, I've been a fan since that 2017 World Cup and to go from being in the stands cheering to playing alongside people like Jase (Jason Taumalolo), who I look up to, it's an honour. It's a privilege," Halasima said.

Fa'alogo, Manuleleua and Halasima are not just three of rugby league's brightest young stars; they are part of a new generation inheriting a relationship thousands of years in the making.

Samoa creates rugby league magic The passion of the Pacific shines through in Samoa's rugby league team, and the pride the people have is evident on the island.

The history and culture of Tonga and Samoa are proudly separate and distinct but also irrevocably intertwined by centuries of love and blood and faith, first back in the islands and now within the great Pasifika diaspora.

Today, that relationship plays out in all its colour and splendour on the rugby league field, in grand occasions that prove Tonga and Samoa are a people as much as they're a place.

That place can be wherever either nation plays on their own, but it happens the most when they face one another.

Tonga and Samoa can meet anywhere in the world and their people will find them. (Getty Images: Michael Steele )

It's been this way long enough that players like Manuleleua, Fa'alogo, and Halasima grew up on occasions like this and dreamed of being part of it.

"Since the draw came out, I've been thinking of this day. I'm pretty sure every islander around the world can't wait for it," Halasima said.

"This is pretty much finals footy, this is what it's all about."

Manuleleua played in the NRL grand final for Newcastle earlier this month in what was the most important night of his young life — until Sunday.

Tonga and Samoa renew rugby league's greatest international rivalry Between them they have a population smaller than Canberra, but when they meet on Monday morning for a shot at the semi-finals, Tonga and Samoa will be the talk of the rugby league world.

"This will probably be the biggest game I've ever been a part of it. A grand final is pretty big too, but the rivalry between Samoa and Tonga runs deeper than footy," Manuleleua said.

"A few of my mates are Tongan, and we know deep down we have that hatred for each other when it comes to coming up against them.

"As soon as we cross that white line there's no friends, but after those 80 minutes we'll get together, have a beer and everything will be all sweet."

These games can happen anywhere, because while the islands are always home, the Pasifika diaspora has taken them to the world, and another home can happen wherever Samoans or Tongans come together.

Last year's Samoa-Tonga game attracted more than 45,000 people. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Four years ago it happened in Warrington, 12 months ago it happened in Brisbane in front of 45,000 people in a game that felt like the State of Origin of the new century, and on Sunday it will happen in Parramatta.

Manuleleua's parents are coming over from Auckland but his siblings, he jokes, will have to make their own way.

Halasima will have his partner and newborn son there, as well as his parents, sisters, aunts, and uncles coming from New Zealand and up from Melbourne.

For Fa'alogo it will be an even more special day because his father, Eti, has never seen him play for Melbourne or Samoa in the flesh but he will be there on Sunday to watch his youngest become a part of history.

Sunday will mark a special occasion for Fa'alogo. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

"I can't wait. He's done so much for me," Fa'alogo said.

"I just want to give back to him for everything he did, for bringing me over and trying to give me the opportunity for a better life."

The game itself is a coin flip. Tonga is bigger, stronger and more battle-hardened; Samoa is faster and has more strike as proven by their big win last year.

The former is already locked into a semifinal spot, and the latter may well be by kick-off depending on the scoreline between England and Papua New Guinea, but this is a game that is bigger than a World Cup and larger than life.

The fresh faces feel the legacy of the history between the two nations even as they write its latest chapter, and they want to pass it down just as it was passed to them.

Earlier this year, Fa'alogo went back to Si'umu as part of a trip with the Storm.

He went to his old house and his old school and caught up with family.

Wherever he went, children followed. It has been that way ever since he made his NRL debut in 2023 and his Samoan debut a few months later, but Fa'alogo might not ever get used to it.

"I was shocked," Fa'alogo said.

"Back then I was one of them."

World.title: Australia's Cape Town desperation evident on another pulsating Test day
World.content:
If there was any doubt how much the Cape Town Test matters to Pat Cummins's Australian team, one only needed to clock the cooing pack of them careening towards Cameron Green and Mitchell Starc an hour into the evening session of day three at Newlands.

The catch Green claimed to send his teammates into raptures was straightforward enough, its genesis and aftermath a little more dramatic.

Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, set fair on 62 and attacking everything Australia threw at him, had tried to limbo away from a Starc bouncer that followed him like a heat-seeking missile. Not quite agile enough with his Matrix manoeuvre, Ackerman faintly edged the ball flush into his faceguard, from which it ballooned into the cordon.

Unsure of the deflection and with his ears still ringing from the ding on his grill, Ackerman walked over to his skipper Temba Bavuma to discuss a review of the umpire's call, perhaps as surprised as the Australians when Travis Head arrived on the scene to inquire after his health.

But, in all the chaos and confusion, the crucial 15 seconds had passed before Ackerman could signal for a review. He had to depart.

It has been that sort of series, really; so many periods of ascendancy abruptly terminated by moments of genius, madness and confusion, and so many subversions of the pattern recognition Test cricket followers can normally rely on to impose a sense of order on what they're looking at.

South Africa finished the so-called moving day at 4-140 and 40 runs ahead. It would have wanted to be further in front. It could easily have been far worse off.

Earlier, in the latter stages of its first innings of 429, Australia probably let an extra 100 runs go begging. It sets up a perfect scenario even for those Australian fans who are not normally night owls: a thrilling finish on Friday night into Saturday morning.

On a pulsating day that produced 243 runs and 10 wickets, there was a second Test century for the recalled Josh Inglis and 80 for Alex Carey, both of whom fell to the off-spin of Simon Harmer.

In a Test featuring plenty of runs, only Josh Inglis has reached triple figures. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

An obscurity to most Australians before this series, and tipped to be dropped after the first Test, Harmer was in the thick of everything again with four wickets, two catches, a busted finger and plenty of chatter.

Youngster Cooper Connolly, looking entirely at home at Test level, made a patient 29 from 83 deliveries and might have kicked on further with better support from Australia's tail; the loss of 6-59 to finish off Australia's first innings was, as Pat Cummins often phrases such things, not ideal.

Yet it was still a 100-run lead, and early in South Africa's second innings you got the sense the game was about to break right open for an early finish.

In quick succession, Aiden Markram, who has been a thorn in Australia's side, lazily slapped a loose one from Starc into the clutches of Head at mid-off, and David Bedingham, seemingly rattled by a Starc bouncer that cannoned into his chest, holed out with another inexplicable hook.

The Proteas were 2-31, still 69 runs behind, and the hyenas were circling.

Via the counter-attack of Ackerman, then in a slow and steady partnership between Temba Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke, South Africa began its rally. Yet there was one last twist in store with barely 15 minutes left in the day's play.

Having tortured Bavuma for a few hours with his sharp turn out of the footmarks, Nathan Lyon removed the Proteas skipper again, this time a dipping off break that snuck between bat and pad to castle the lunging batsman. Bavuma is not quite to Lyon what Daryll Cullinan once was to Shane Warne, but he is not far off.

Proteas captain Temba Bavuma posed a major threat to Australia. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

On the matter of hoodoos, much has been made in recent days of Cummins's record-breaking streak without a wicket.

It continued today, despite periods in which the Aussie skipper bowled with genuine pace and guile, although his desperation to break his drought was made clear by one ill-advised review. Even when it is 1.6 metre Bavuma in the firing line, it is always difficult to get an LBW call when it hits above the batsman's knee roll.

In truth, the odd brain fade was perfectly excusable due to the ratcheting up of the atmosphere as this game progressed.

Some testiness and conflict in this series was inevitable, but it has manifested in curious ways. Each team's most vocal player — Marnus Labuschagne for Australia, Matthew Breetzke for the Proteas — has been its worst performed.

Breetzke, in fact, finally started to come good late on day three, and will resume tomorrow believing he is the man to turn the game for his country.

Given the way these two teams have echoed each other's efforts in the past few weeks, perhaps that suggests one last tantalising and slightly mad prospect in the Australian chase: how about Marnus Labuschagne as the last-minute hero?

World.title: Quick hits: Marnus caught in ugly exchange after all-time send off
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne was involved in an ugly moment of DRS drama after giving a retaliatory send-off, as Temba Bavuma threw his wicket away in the shadows of stumps.

Here are the quick hits from day three of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. DRS drama and Labuschagne's ugly exchange

It was one of the most contentious moments of the series when, midway through the evening session, with South Africa 2-95 and still five runs behind, Mitchell Starc collected Marques Ackerman with a steepling, searing bouncer.

The South African lost his balance as the ball thudded into what looked to be a mixture of helmet and bat before flying to Cam Green behind the wicket.

The Australians went up and so did the umpire's finger.

Undoubtedly dazed from the contact, the batter regained his composure and met with partner Temba Bavuma.

Eventually, a referral was called for, but only as the DRS timer ticked to zero.

Ackerman called for the review as the timer hit zero. (Fox Cricket)

It was touch and go, but the officials deemed Ackerman had taken too long, despite the severity of the hit.

With the South Africans pleading their case to the umpires, the ever-vocal Marnus Labuschagne could be heard giving his own opinion over the stump mic.

"The timer's up, oh no, see you buddy!" Labuschagne said from his position at the other end of the wicket.

Meanwhile, Travis Head had made his way over to the South African camp.

"Heady, what are you doing mate? He's off!" Labuschagne could be heard saying.

Head, hands outstretched towards batter and umpire in what appeared to be a peace offering, turned back towards his team and replied.

"I'm just checking if he's alright," Head said.

Head made his way over to check on Ackerman. (Fox Cricket)

Reluctantly, Ackerman made his from the middle, but spent some time at the boundary in the futile hope of being called back.

Thankfully, the replays showed the ball had collected a thick edge before crashing into visor, meaning Ackerman was doomed to be out for 62 even if the review had been permitted.

The technology showed Ackerman was rightly given out. (Fox Cricket)

Even so, it was an ugly exchange and one unlikely to endear Labuschagne to either his opponents or those watching on.

2. Bloodied Harmer keeps South Africa in the game

Simon Harmer, left, made the breakthrough in the first hour of day three. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

With an advantage to press home at the beginning of day three, the set Australian pair of Alex Carey and Josh Inglis would have been hoping for at least another full session of batting.

The conditions were perfect, the pitch was flat, and things looked very promising as Inglis reverse-swept his way to a hugely impressive second Test century.

However, neither wicketkeeper-batter would see the other side of the first drinks break, with off spinner Simon Harmer once again doing the damage.

Only moments after ripping a nail and bloodying his fingers while attempting a low catch with his non-bowling hand, Harmer had Inglis caught behind for 102.

Harmer received some treatment on a torn nail before dislodging the two set batters. (Fox Cricket)

It was a brilliant delivery; drifting away, spinning in and kissing the outside edge of the Western Australian's blade.

Four overs later, a similarly exquisite off break had Carey (80) nudging to Aiden Markram at slip, and Harmer, a fingernail down, had dragged his side back into the game.

Australia's tail proceeded to eke out a 100-run first-innings lead, eventually dismissed for 429.

3. Marnus gives it to Bedingham

Labuschagne was in quite a mood on day three.

Before the DRS drama in the evening session, the Queenslander took quite some pleasure in giving it back to Proteas batter David Bedingham.

On day two, Matthew Breetzke had joyously celebrated Labuschagne's five-ball duck by leaping over the pitch and shouting directly at the Australian.

And when Bedingham holed out to Josh Hazlewood during the middle session on day three, Labuschagne responded in similar fashion.

The Queenslander had his chest puffed out as he ran towards the South African, face red and fist pumping, screaming what you can only imagine was something entirely considered and reasonable.

Bedingham was out for 11 and South Africa's second innings was already beginning to teeter at 2-31.

4. A strange moment on the hill

It was an unlikely proposal. (Fox Cricket)

It was a strange morning on the hill.

During the first session, the broadcast cameras found a man holding a sign that read: "Ryan Rickelton, is your mum single?"

The middle-aged gentleman received a good amount of screen time, which he used to blow kisses and adjust his sunglasses in a performance that probably wouldn't have endeared him to anyone in the Rickelton family.

Rickelton, South Africa's wicketkeeper-batter, was stony-faced in response, before pursing his lips and shaking his head solemnly.

The commentators were lost for words at what was an uncomfortable moment for everyone involved — and especially, you'd imagine, for Ryan Rickelton's mother.

5. Bavuma throws it away in the shadows of stumps

Stumps were in sight for Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke.

The South African pair had so diligently rebuilt South Africa's innings after Ackerman's dismissal, and had just eight more balls to survive.

But with shadows lengthening at Newlands and with the pitch offering more and more for the slower bowlers, Nathan Lyon conjured a little bit of magic.

It was the perfect off spinner's delivery; drifting, turning sharply and bowling a swinging Bavuma clean through the gate.

However, it was a wildly inappropriate shot from the usually so-considered Bavuma, and the South African captain couldn't quite believe what had happened.

Bavuma was a picture of regret on his way from the middle. (Fox Cricket)

He grimaced and shook his head as he made is way from the middle for 35, with South Africa finishing the day on 4-140 and just 40 runs in front.

World.title: Wallaby 'incredibly proud' as brother represents Australian Deaf Rugby
World.content:
For as long as he can remember, Wallabies back-rower Charlie Cale has always been able to rely on his older brother Jack.

Growing up in Sydney's northern suburbs, they would often team up together against the eldest of the Cale boys, Sam, in fierce backyard rugby battles.

Even when it came to studying during their school years, Charlie knew Jack was in his corner.

"He helped me with a lot of my schoolwork," Charlie fondly tells ABC Sport.

"There's been a few exams … he's helped me in a lot of ways, actually.

"That's the best thing about Jack. He's always been there for me and anyone else that has needed him.

"He's one of a kind."

Jack's encouragement is repaid by the support he receives from Charlie and Sam, who both keenly follow his career with the Australian Deaf Rugby (ADR) men's squad.

Last Tuesday night in Sydney, Charlie proudly presented Jack, Australia's vice-captain, with his official team tie ahead of the World Deaf Rugby Sevens Championship, which begin in Tokyo this weekend.

Australia's men's and women's squads are among the favourites to emerge triumphant once the tournament concludes on November 3.

Jack Cale (right) pictured with brothers Charlie (centre) and Sam. (Instagram: Tim Cale)

Jack is grateful to have Charlie and Sam's backing as he juggles rugby commitments with his job as a lawyer.

"It's always been really helpful having two brothers to go through a rugby career with," says Jack, who has played for Eastwood (Shute Shield) and Mosman (Subbies) at club level.

"We're always checking in with each other, trying to watch each other's games.

"Charlie, even with the limited time he gets outside of training with Brumbies and Wallabies squads, is always trying to watch our games as well."

Charlie Cale has played six Tests for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

On the international stage

Jack's introduction to deaf rugby came out of the blue.

"In late 2022, I got a phone call from an old coach of mine on a Saturday morning," says Jack, who had played colts and grade rugby in Sydney by this stage.

"He gave me a call and said, 'Mate, there's this deaf rugby trial happening down at Hunters Hill.'

"Of course, I didn't know what he was talking about as I hadn't really heard anything before.

"I went down there and ran around in a bit of a sevens trial, for maybe 20 or 25 minutes.

"I didn't think I'd actually played that well. I didn't touch the ball that much.

"I came off the field and I wasn't sure what to expect."

Jack Cale during his Eastwood playing days. (Instagram: Tim Cale)

A letter arrived in the mail a few months later in early 2023, informing Jack he was selected in the ADR men's squad for the World Deaf Rugby Sevens Championship, which were being held in Córdoba, Argentina in April of that year.

There was one small problem, though.

Jack found out about his selection during the club rugby off-season, meaning he was not exactly at peak fitness.

"I had to get myself fit pretty quickly without any rugby training, which was a bit of a struggle," Jack laughs.

Australia finished runner-up in the men's competition at the 2023 world titles. (Instagram: Australian Deaf Rugby)

Jack worked his way back into shape and seamlessly joined the Australian line-up, which he helped lead in his vice-captaincy role.

They made the final, gallantly losing 20-5 to Wales, while Australia finished third overall in the women's competition.

In Tokyo, the men's squad faces England, Japan, Hong Kong China and Italy in the pool stage, with the top three advancing to the knockout rounds of the tournament.

The Australian women's team were presented with their ties in Sydney on Tuesday night. (Supplied: Alfred Naputo)

Australia is one of six teams in the women's draw, where it plays Fiji, England, Wales, New Zealand and a combined Barbarians team in a single pool.

Australian squads: Men: Tim Anstey (c), Jack Cale (vc), Anau Takiari, Ben Rogers, Charlie Jeffries, Cruz Lemming, Geofrey Reynolds, Kyle Howlett, Josh Chapman, Josh Doe, Royden Chatfield, Tom Witts, Dave Kearsey (coach) Women: Sydnee Cooke (c), Amy Reid, Ashanti Pennell, Bridie Searle, Bianca Roberts, Cathy Ross, Kari Massey, Khiara McCormick, Olivia Hall, Peta Stephens, Sally Faehrmann, Robbie Pirika (coach)

Each will progress, with the two top-ranked teams moving directly to the semifinals.

Having avoided Wales in the men's round-robin matches, Jack considers England to be Australia's main threat in the preliminary phase.

"You've obviously got to go match by match," Jack says.

"It's important to get through the pool stage as well as we can and then the mindset obviously shifts to the knockout stages.

"I'd consider us in the better pool for the opportunity to do that."

Embracing challenges

To participate in World Deaf Rugby tournaments, players must have an average bilateral hearing loss across both ears of at least 40 decibels.

The level of hearing loss varies from player to player in the Australian teams, which illustrates to Jack the importance of non-verbal communication during matches.

"I stepped into this environment where nothing was said on a rugby field," he says.

"It was a bit of a challenge to get used to that.

"But I also really enjoyed that challenge, being able to communicate with some of those guys whose hearing is a lot more affected than mine is."

The Australian men's team at Tuesday night's tie presentation. (Supplied: Alfred Naputo)

As much as Jack loves playing alongside his Australian teammates, he also gets a kick out of facing them in club rugby.

On one such occasion last year, he and Australian captain Tim Anstey opposed each other when Mosman met Newport in the NSW Subbies competition.

"It's pretty awesome playing against someone like that, who you now travel with on international tours," Jack says.

"But it's also surreal finding out that someone you might have been playing rugby against is also partially deaf and had the same struggles as you growing up, and you're now representing your country with them.

"It's pretty cool."

Tim Anstey (left) and Jack Cale after a Subbies match in 2025. (Instagram: Australian Deaf Rugby)

While Jack relishes every chance to represent Australia, spreading the message of inclusivity is just as important to him and everyone involved in deaf rugby.

ADR states its goal is to give every deaf and hard-of-hearing athlete the opportunity to play the game, regardless of their experience level.

"We want to find as many deaf or hard-of-hearing rugby players as we can," Jack says.

"It's really just word of mouth within deaf and hard-of-hearing communities."

Jack's family is also firmly behind the cause.

"I've got a lot of respect for this [ADR] program," says Charlie, who has played six Tests for the Wallabies.

"It gives these guys a platform and opportunity they may have lacked growing up.

"We know how much it means to Jack and therefore it means a lot to us."

Family support

Charlie got up early in the morning to watch Jack play at the world titles in Córdoba three years ago.

But a friendlier time zone will make it easier for him to follow his brother's progress in Tokyo.

"I don't think I've missed a game," Charlie says.

"I've woken up at 2am or 3am. I love watching him play."

Jack Cale (centre) with his parents Tim (left) and Sue. (Instagram: Tim Cale)

As he did in Córdoba, Jack will have his devoted mum and dad, Sue and Tim, barracking from the sidelines in Tokyo.

The Cale parents do everything possible to watch their three sons play rugby.

"I don't think our mother has missed a rugby game of ours in God knows how many years," Jack says.

"Dad is always on the phone, straight after games, checking in with us and seeing how we've gone."

Just as he helped Charlie all those years ago with his schoolwork, Jack knows he can also depend on the support of his family.

"We're incredibly proud of him," Charlie says.

World.title: WBBL season gets underway with Thunder thumping of Renegades
World.content:
Anika Learoyd has carved out a career-best innings as the Sydney Thunder began its WBBL campaign with a convincing six-wicket win over the Melbourne Renegades in the season opener.
